Title: U.S. CISA adds Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: In early October 2026, Volexity discovered that a threat actor tracked as UTA0576 was exploiting a zero-day vulnerability chain to compromise fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure...
Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the following Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

CVE-2026-111357 (CVSS score of 8.8) – A missing authentication check for a critical function that could allow an authenticated local attacker to gain higher privileges.

CVE-2026-118527 (CVSS score of 4.3) – A predictable identifier vulnerability that could allow an authenticated remote attacker to upload files containing malicious content to a known location on the system.

The vulnerabilities are part of an exploit chain that cybersecurity firm Volexity first documented in mid-October.

“Volexity has identified active in-the-wild exploitation of a vulnerability chain allowing unauthenticated remote code execution in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN devices. Ivanti has published an advisory providing upgrade instructions to customers.” states Volexity. “Systems exhibiting signs of compromise, such as attempts to move laterally originating from the ICS VPN device, should be forensically investigated to ensure no breach has occurred.“

The attacks combined these vulnerabilities with an authentication bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score of 8.6).

In early October 2026, Volexity discovered that a threat actor tracked as UTA0576 was exploiting a zero-day vulnerability chain to compromise fully patched Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliances. The attack combined authentication bypass, remote code execution, and privilege escalation flaws, allowing attackers to gain root access without logging in. The authentication bypass and RCE flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-104935.

After gaining access, the attackers targeted Active Directory credentials and sensitive information, including LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. Volexity worked with Ivanti as soon as it suspected the vulnerabilities were being exploited.

CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 13, 2026.

Ivanti released security updates to address both CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527:

Version 25.1.1.2 and earlier: upgrade to 25.1.1.3.

Version 22.8R2.5 and earlier: upgrade to 22.8R2.6.

Ivanti said it disclosed CVE-2026-104935 first because a fix was already available and ready for testing. When researchers discovered the additional privilege escalation flaws, the company decided not to delay the release of the first patch, which addressed the main attack method. Ivanti also worked with Volexity to share information about the attackers’ techniques, including how they chained the vulnerabilities.

Ivanti had already fixed part of the issue in its July 25.1.3.0 release and was preparing updates for other supported versions. Patches are now available for all the vulnerabilities used in the attacks.

“At the time of discovery of exploitation, Ivanti had a fix developed for CVE-2026-104935 which was already in QA for supported versions, and we made the decision to not delay getting a fix to customers that resolved the primary exploitation path when the LPE was discovered. Because of this, our focus was initially centered on the disclosure of CVE-2026-104935 and providing protection for our customers as quickly as possible.” states Ivanti. “Additionally, Ivanti collaborated with Volexity on their blog post which provided information to arm defenders on known threat actor behavior, including chaining the local privilege escalation vulnerability. These additional CVE disclosures have now been added to this Security Advisory and a fix is available now.”

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix CVE-2026-111357 by November 2, 2026, and CVE-2026-118527 by November 13, 2026.

Title: Northflank security breach leads to abuse of customers' AI API keys
Context: Wiz says attackers involved in some of these incidents have specifically targeted environment variables containing AI service credentials, which can be exploited through a...
Full Text:
Cloud application hosting platform Northflank is warning customers to rotate all credentials and secrets stored on its platform after a security breach led to unauthorized use of customers' AI API keys.

Northflank is a cloud platform that allows developers to deploy and manage applications, containers, databases, and AI applications without managing the underlying infrastructure.

The company disclosed a security incident on October 30, warning customers to immediately rotate their environment variables and API keys after receiving a threat alert from cloud security company Wiz.

Soon after, Northflank told all customers to assume their environment variables had been decrypted and that the secrets stored within them were stolen.

"Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys," Northflank warned in an October 30 update.

Applications commonly use environment variables to store sensitive information, including database passwords, cloud service credentials, authentication tokens, and API keys.

If exposed, these credentials can be used to breach other customer services, potentially leading to data theft or unauthorized charges through API keys.

Northflank later confirmed that multiple customers had reported unauthorized use of AI API keys stored on the platform.

"Users have reported unauthorised use of AI API keys supplied to the Northflank platform," the company said.

"If you have not already rotated your user-provided secrets stored in Northflank, please do so immediately."

Customers were also advised to review their AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity and report suspicious usage to Northflank and their AI providers.

According to Northflank's published incident timeline, Wiz warned them about the breach at 11:43 UTC on October 30, which the company's engineers reviewed one minute later.

Northflank quickly responded with a network policy patch, followed by additional patches at 12:50 UTC and 13:05 UTC. The company also requested assistance from Wiz's incident response team.

The company has not disclosed how attackers gained access to its systems, how many customers were affected, or whether attackers stole or abused credentials other than the reported AI API keys.

As part of its response, Northflank enabled credential rotation for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MySQL, and Redis.

The company also enabled audit logs for all customers, including those using free accounts, to help them investigate any suspicious activity.

Northflank continues to advise customers to rotate secrets stored in workloads, secret groups, and global secrets, and to disable public access to add-ons where enabled.

BleepingComputer contacted Northflank with questions about the breach, its impact on customers, and whether stored credentials were accessed or stolen, but has not received a response.

Black October

The breach comes amid a series of attacks targeting AI development platforms, which security researchers believe are valuable targets because they store API keys that can be used to access expensive AI services.

In a report titled "Black October for AI Developer Platforms," Wiz identified at least nine security incidents affecting AI development platforms during the month, including Northflank, Railway, OpenCode, Warp, and Lightning AI.

The Railway incident also involved potential exposure of decrypted customer environment variables, while OpenCode disclosed exposed AI API keys. Warp reported a breach that exposed AI agent logs and user telemetry data.

Wiz says attackers involved in some of these incidents have specifically targeted environment variables containing AI service credentials, which can be exploited through a practice known as LLMJacking.

LLMJacking involves using stolen credentials to access AI models using another organization's API keys, generating massive API charges or allowing the stolen access to be resold.

In two cases investigated by Wiz, compromised enterprise credentials were used to make approximately 2.5 million Amazon Bedrock API calls, generating approximately $100,000 in AI usage.

The researchers also discovered infrastructure linked to services reselling access to AI models, although they could not link those operations to the initial breaches or large-scale abuse.

Wiz has not confirmed that all nine incidents were conducted by the same attackers. However, many of the incidents involved attempts to steal AI API keys.

Northflank also referenced Wiz's research in its incident updates, noting that customer reports of unauthorized AI key usage may be tied to the attacks seen by the researchers.

Title: New Android SMS of Death exploit can remotely crash unpatched phones
Context: A security researcher has released a proof-of-concept exploit for a recently patched Android vulnerability, dubbed "SMS of Death" and tracked as CVE-2026-58882, that lets...
Full Text:
A security researcher has released a proof-of-concept exploit for a recently patched Android vulnerability, dubbed "SMS of Death" and tracked as CVE-2026-58882, that lets attackers remotely disrupt cellular service or crash phones by sending a specially crafted text message.

The zero-click denial-of-service flaw can interrupt ongoing calls, including emergency calls, without requiring any interaction from the target. What's worse, Android processes the message before it reaches the SMS inbox, leaving victims with no visible indication of what caused their phones to crash.

According to the vulnerability researcher, Mark Blah, Google reportedly patched the vulnerability in its October 2026 Android security updates for Android 14 through 17. However, the flaw is not listed in Google's October security bulletin, and older Android 12 and 13 devices remain vulnerable because they did not receive the fix.

Blah published a technical analysis of the flaw, caused by improper validation of a header-length value in Android's WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu function.

To exploit the flaw, an attacker can send the following malformed eight-byte WAP Push message to targeted phones:

01 06 88 80 80 80 00 BE → sent as a data SMS to port 2948

When this value is translated into a signed 32-bit integer without a bounds check, it becomes -2147483648.

When Android attempts to allocate memory using this negative value, it triggers a NegativeArraySizeException that crashes the com.android.phone process.

As the com.android.phone process manages cellular functions, the crash disrupts mobile connectivity and disconnects ongoing phone calls, including calls to emergency services.

The researcher says the attack can also cause repeated crashes when carriers attempt to redeliver malicious messages or Android tries to process messages already stored on the phone.

When testing the flaw, the researcher found that sending 20 malicious messages could cause phones to get stuck in reboot loops. On one Android 12 device, the phone rebooted into recovery mode approximately every 90 seconds, requiring the user to perform a factory reset to recover.

A GitHub contributor named Sakis discovered a way to remove the malicious messages using Android Debug Bridge (ADB), but the process requires more advanced technical knowledge and access to a computer.

The researcher has published a proof-of-concept exploit that can send the malicious messages from another Android device.

Google's fix, titled "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," prevents the crashes by catching exceptions triggered when Android processes the malformed text messages.

The patch also deletes malicious messages from the SMS database to prevent them from triggering repeated crashes.

Android security updates are generally installed automatically on supported devices, but their availability depends on the device manufacturer and carrier, and a restart may be required to complete installation.

Now that a working proof-of-concept exploit has been released, Android users are strongly advised to install the latest security updates to protect their devices.

Title: Reddit to lock content behind logins to fight scrapers
Context: Reddit announced in a post by co-founder Steve Huffman that the site will gradually become a "logged-in service," offering limited access to visitors without accounts
Full Text:
Reddit announced in a post by co-founder Steve Huffman that the site will gradually become a "logged-in service," offering limited access to visitors without accounts.

For the past 20 years, the discussion platform has let users browse almost all its content without logging in, but according to Huffman, Reddit has now grown to a size where this is no longer sustainable.

The two main points for this upcoming change are the need to offer users more personalization and to address the increasing problem of content scrapers.

To tackle this, a new pilot test will begin in selected markets outside the United States in the coming months, requiring users to log in to access the site's full content.

However, what content will be restricted, what countries will be impacted first, and rollout timelines have not been determined at this time.

Huffman said they currently believe it’s important to keep the front page accessible to all, and allow people arriving from search results or other external sources to see at least the page the URL points to.

With users logged in, Reddit expects to gather more data from upvotes to help users find relevant content, join communities, and participate in discussions.

"Our goal is to help you find what’s most relevant to you and drive the community, connection and belonging that makes Reddit, reddit,” explained Huffman.

“This change will do that, helping surface what’s most relevant to you and quickly getting you to where you want to go—whether that's your favorite subreddit, a game you want to play, or a thread you're looking for.”

More logged-in users will also let Reddit deliver more relevant ads to each member, supporting the platform's revenue stream.

One of the bigger problems this change is meant to address is content scraping.

Reddit says most unauthorized data access happens through its logged-out pages, so limiting access will help on that front. For AI platforms and search engines that want access to the data, Reddit will continue to license it under commercial agreements.

For those concerned about privacy, Huffman said they will not require users to submit their real names or identification documents. To further strengthen privacy on the platform, Reddit will also re-release a read-only incognito mode in its app.

Users will also be able to opt out of personalized advertising, which will presumably disable some internal tracking and profiling.

Title: From Beginner to Bug Hunter: Learning Cybersecurity in the AI Era.
Context: Build the foundations you need to check a finding Before chasing your first payout, learn how the systems you plan to test work
Full Text:
Finding a real security flaw and getting paid for it is an appealing goal when you are learning cyber security. Bug bounties give you a chance to test your skills on real software and help its developers make it safer.

Headlines about programs closing or pausing under a flood of AI reports can make that route feel less certain.

Earlier this year, curl, the widely used data transfer tool and library, ended its paid bounty program after similar problems.

As a beginner, these decisions raise a practical question about where to put your effort.

A useful starting point is understanding what went wrong, then building the skills to produce findings that someone else can verify.

Why some bug bounty programs are pulling back

A bug bounty program rewards eligible security findings under a defined set of rules. Developers must still review each submission, reproduce the issue and assess its impact.

A convincing report about an imaginary vulnerability can consume time that a small security team needs for genuine problems.

When curl ended its program on January 31, 2026, maintainer Daniel Stenberg explained how the quality of submissions had deteriorated. He confirmed vulnerabilities fell from above 15% in previous years to below 5% starting in 2025. Across its lifetime, the program had helped uncover 87 confirmed vulnerabilities and paid researchers more than $100,000.

Those figures describe curl’s experience specifically.

Google’s pause also has a defined scope: supply chain submissions and outstanding reports remain unaffected. Its wider vulnerability rewards programs paid researchers $17.1 million in 2025. The closures and restrictions show pressure on particular programs, while other opportunities continue.

Learn cyber security hands-on, right in your browser

Join 8 million+ learners and start free, with no setup needed.

Start Learning

A glimmer of hope

In April, Stenberg reported that submission quality had improved and the share of confirmed vulnerabilities had returned to roughly 15% to 16%.

He observed extensive AI use in those reports. Researchers were finding real problems, although the growing volume still created work for maintainers.

For someone learning, the lesson is to take responsibility for the evidence behind a finding. Generating a report is easy compared with establishing whether its claim holds up.

Build the foundations you need to check a finding

Before chasing your first payout, learn how the systems you plan to test work. For web security, that means understanding HTTP requests, login sessions, permissions and how applications handle data.

Basic networking and command line skills help you investigate what is happening when a tool produces an unexpected result.

Practise these ideas in an environment designed for learning. You can make mistakes, repeat a test and inspect the result without affecting a live service. Choose a specific skill for each session, such as explaining a request or identifying which account is allowed to access a resource.

TryHackMe’s Cyber Security 101 learning path covers networking, Linux and Windows fundamentals, web application basics, and offensive and defensive security. Working through a structured path gives each new tool a purpose and helps you understand the evidence it produces.

After a lab, write down what you changed, what happened and why. Then repeat the task with your notes closed. Being able to explain and reproduce the result is a useful way to check your progress.

Use AI to support your learning

AI can help explain an unfamiliar error, suggest questions to investigate or review the clarity of your notes. You will get more useful practice if you attempt the task first and give the model a specific point of confusion.

After inspecting a lab request, for example, ask the model to explain how the session cookie relates to the logged-in account. If you are stuck, ask for one hint and describe what you have already tried. Then test your next step and explain why it worked.

Finish the session by doing the task again without assistance. If you can explain which evidence supports the finding and what would disprove it, you have learned something you can use beyond that exercise.

Make every report possible to reproduce

Imagine an authorized training application with two test accounts. Changing an invoice identifier returns a successful response. To establish an access control flaw, you still need to show that one account can access the other account’s private test invoice and that this violates the application’s intended permissions.

Record the behavior you can demonstrate, including the conditions required for it to happen. Keep any claim about wider impact tied to evidence.

Before submitting the finding, check that your report includes:

The affected asset or software version, with confirmation that your testing falls within the program's scope.

The setup and exact steps needed to reproduce the issue, including any required account permissions.

The expected behavior and the actual result, supported by relevant requests, responses or other evidence with sensitive information removed.

The demonstrated security impact, with any assumptions or untested possibilities clearly identified.

Give your first month a clear purpose

A month of focused practice can help you establish useful habits. Adjust the pace to your starting point and measure progress by what you can explain and repeat:

In week one, work through networking, operating system and web basics. Draw a simple request flow and explain where identity and permissions are checked.

In week two, choose one vulnerability type and practise it across several authorized labs. Keep a short record of the evidence behind each result.

In week three, use AI for hints after making your own attempt. Revisit an earlier lab without help, then examine the logs or other evidence a defender could use to spot the activity.

In week four, write a complete report for a lab finding. Ask a peer to reproduce it from your instructions, or follow them yourself from a fresh setup and fix anything missing.

By the end, you should have a record of your reasoning and a report you can improve. Continue practicing wherever you still need help. Readiness for a live program depends on your skills and its rules, so use the month as a starting point.

Keep your career options open

Bug bounty work is one way to apply security skills. The same habit of checking evidence matters in security operations, incident response and penetration testing.

When you investigate a lab, practice explaining how a defender could detect the issue and what a developer could change to fix it.

Bounty income depends on a finding being valid, eligible and covered by the program’s payment rules.

Learning will be easier to sustain if you judge progress by the skills you are building. Save clear lab notes and share write-ups where the training platform permits them, so you have concrete work to discuss as you explore security roles.

For your next session, choose one exercise, make your own attempt and keep the evidence that explains the result.

And if you need guidance along the way, TryHackMe offers the ultimate path to get you started just as you would in an actual security environment.

Title: Chainalysis discloses data breach from "offensive agentic techniques"
Context: Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers...
Full Text:
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis has disclosed a security incident after attackers used what it describes as "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its internal systems and tools.

The company says some customer information was accessed, including names, email addresses, user IDs, and organizational role labels, but claims there is no evidence that sensitive investigation data or authentication credentials were exposed.

Chainalysis says attackers accessed internal systems and tools

Chainalysis provides blockchain analytics tools used by law enforcement, government agencies, cryptocurrency exchanges, and financial institutions to trace cryptocurrency transactions and investigate crimes such as fraud, ransomware, and money laundering.

On Friday, roughly 5:14 PM ET, Chainalysis published a security incident disclosure along with the full text of the email sent to affected customers.

The disclosure says the company detected an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier this month, and has since been patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems.

The accessed data includes user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organizational role labels for users provisioned on the platform.

Chainalysis is still determining which records were accessed for each organization and will provide a detailed breakdown once that analysis is complete.

A Chainalysis spokesperson confirmed the incident to BleepingComputer and said the company is working with external cybersecurity experts. It is also using large language models (LLMs) to support a broader security review of its platform.

"Based on the investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens," the company said, adding that the incident is unrelated to the recent Binance theft.

Customers are advised to enable two-factor authentication (2FA) and watch for unexpected password reset requests, authentication prompts, and scammers impersonating Chainalysis, particularly those offering fund recovery or recruiting services.

What are "offensive agentic techniques"?

Chainalysis has not shared technical details about the intrusion, including which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were accessed, or how long the attackers had access.

It is unclear whether the attackers used existing agentic offensive security frameworks, such as ARTEX, or custom-built AI agents capable of autonomously identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting them, and chaining together subsequent actions.

ARTEX has recently been used by threat actors, including in the ConnectWise supply chain compromise, according to Microsoft.

The term "agentic" generally describes AI systems capable of executing multi-step tasks with limited human intervention, potentially allowing attackers to automate portions of the intrusion process rather than relying on traditional hands-on exploitation.

A relentless week of security incidents

The Chainalysis disclosure comes amid a relentless week of security incidents affecting the cryptocurrency and technology industries.

On Friday, Binance linked the roughly $6.3 billion theft, now the largest crypto heist on record and attributed to North Korean state-backed hackers, to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.

Separately, hardware wallet maker Trezor warned of a suspected cryptocurrency-stealing implant reported in a Trezor Safe 5 device sold by a Southeast Asian reseller. The implant can reportedly read the recovery phrase shown on the device's screen and transmit it over a mobile network.

Meanwhile, a malicious version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor extension marketplace, planting persistent SSH backdoors on developers' machines.

Chainalysis says it will share further updates with affected customers as its investigation progresses.

Context: The development comes as adversarial use of AI has ramped up in recent months, with various threat actors using the technology to automate different stages of the attack...
Full Text:
American blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor accessed non-sensitive customer data.

However, the company noted that the breach did not result in unauthorized access to its investigation content, authentication credentials, or session tokens.

"This month, Chainalysis detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools," Chainalysis said Friday.

"Some non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed, including such information relating to your organization and users."

The company said it's patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems in response to the incident.

The mention of "offensive agentic techniques" indicates that an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool was used to execute the attack, although Chainalysis offered no details on the specific methods or tactics employed.

"We are seeing an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyber attacks, and we are taking a whole-of-company approach to make sure our security posture meets the evolving environment and our customers' expectations," it said.

The development comes as adversarial use of AI has ramped up in recent months, with various threat actors using the technology to automate different stages of the attack lifecycle and target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries.

This includes a China state-backed threat group known as Vapor Panda, which is using ARTEX, an agentic penetration testing framework, to conduct attacks at scale, compromising about 140 targets in a span of 11 days as part of broad access operation.

"AI mainly improves established attacks by making them faster, more personalized, and easier to scale," Abnormal AI said. "Agentic intrusion chains and prompt injection are more distinct because they depend directly on deployed AI systems."

Title: Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
Context: Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings
Full Text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

Title: Syrian Hacker Gets Prison Time in US After Over a Decade on the Run
Context: A Syrian man tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA) has received a 42-month prison sentence in the US, more than 12 years after he was first charged
Full Text:
A Syrian man tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA) has received a 42-month prison sentence in the US, more than 12 years after he was first charged.

Ahmad Umar Agha, who used the online handle Th3Pr0, was sentenced on Thursday by a federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia. According to the Justice Department, he evaded US authorities for more than a decade.

Prosecutors say the hacking conspiracy Agha took part in was directed by figures close to Bashar al-Assad, among them the head of Syria’s General Intelligence Directorate. The scheme began as early as August 2011 and continued until January 2024.

The DOJ described Agha as a central figure in the operation. He compromised around 47 targets, a mix of Western news outlets, companies, NGOs, and government bodies in the US and allied countries.

Among the intrusions highlighted by prosecutors was the 2013 takeover of the Associated Press’s Twitter account. Agha used it to publish a fabricated report claiming that President Barack Obama had been hurt in two blasts at the White House. The fake post triggered a flash crash that briefly wiped $136 billion off the combined value of the Dow Jones Industrial Average’s component stocks.

Agha also gained access to the company hosting the Marine Corps’ recruiting website and sent its traffic to an image calling on Marines to defy their orders.

He twice went after the White House’s social media presence by targeting the email credentials of White House employees. In one case he obtained them, but his attempt to use that access to dupe other staffers into handing over the accounts did not work.

The intrusions left many victims with large bills for cleanup and security overhauls. A firm providing online publishers with content, advertising, and outbound links lost around $35,000 per day for about six months. A global NGO spent roughly $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, retrained more than 800 employees, and upgraded its security, with total losses of $480,000.

Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged by criminal complaint in June 2014. The case was unsealed in March 2016, when the FBI put both men on its Cyber’s Most Wanted list and offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to Agha’s arrest.

A grand jury indicted the pair in May 2018. Dardar has yet to be caught.

Title: Attackers Exploit Critical Drupal Commerce Core Vulnerability CVE-2026-118539
Context: Drupal warns that attackers are exploiting a critical authorization flaw in Commerce Core, putting vulnerable online stores at risk
Full Text:
Drupal warns that attackers are exploiting a critical authorization flaw in Commerce Core, putting vulnerable online stores at risk.

Drupal warns that threat actors are exploiting a highly critical security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118539, in its Commerce Core module. The vulnerability is caused by missing authorization checks.

“This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs. The module doesn’t sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor.” reads the advisory. This vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild.”

The module allows websites to sell products and services through shopping carts, checkout forms, and APIs.

“Missing Authorization vulnerability in Drupal Commerce Core allows Forceful Browsing. This issue affects Commerce Core versions: from 0.0.0 to 2.41, from 3.0.0 to 3.3.13.” reads the advisory.

Researchers Dan Puccetti (dpuccetti), Marcus Johansson (marcus_johansson), and Robert Snyder (rsnyd) reported the vulnerability.

The maintainers at the open-source project confirmed that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild.

Drupal recommends that users update their installations to the latest available release. Those running the 3.x branch should upgrade to version 3.3.13, while users on earlier releases should move to Commerce Core 8.x-2.41.

In May, Drupal warned that attackers were exploiting an SQL injection flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-9082, in its database abstraction API. The vulnerability could allow attackers to gain higher privileges, access sensitive information, and execute malicious code remotely.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog.

Title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Run Attacker Code in Your Session and Read Private Chats
Context: A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at...
Full Text:
A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed.

The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category.

The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared via its public link. It could be sent the same way as any real shared chat: by email, as a chat message, as a support ticket, or as a social post.

The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version of the attack, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once. In a later version, Parameter set the page to open Preview on its own, so opening the link was the only step.

What the Attacker Could Do

Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server controlled by the researchers.

The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly, rather than copying what happened to be on the screen. Because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. "Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account," the researchers wrote.

The work was a controlled test. Parameter does not report any real-world use of the flaw, and ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users.

How the Link Broke Out of Its Sandbox

Here is how the chain worked, according to Parameter. ChatGPT can turn a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page through a feature called Preview. Because that page can hold any code, ChatGPT runs it in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, where it cannot read the main ChatGPT page around it.

That sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation.

The shared chat also contained an interactive graph, and drawing it loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page. Loading MathLive left a listener running there that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard.

A message passed between browser frames is safe only if the receiver checks who sent it. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender, and that the message was allowed to carry raw HTML. The Preview could then reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page.

That HTML built a new frame that the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com. A script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it.

ChatGPT's content security policy limits where a page's scripts may come from. It blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube, which is why that step worked.

What OpenAI Fixed, and What Users Should Do

Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on.

The researchers traced the problem to three design choices that lined up:

MathLive acted on a message that changed its settings without checking which frame had sent it.

That message was allowed to carry raw HTML as keyboard-layout data.

The HTML could create a frame that was not sandboxed and inherited the chatgpt.com identity.

The YouTube step was only the final workaround, not the cause. Blocking it alone would still leave an untrusted Preview able to push HTML into the main site.

ChatGPT users do not need to do anything. The fix is on OpenAI's side, with nothing to install or reset.

Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix. OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report.

Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together.

The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list.

What the test data shows

The SecureIQLab Cloud WAAP v5.0 validation, an AMTSO-certified test published in August 2026, ran 12 enterprise platforms through 1,608 attack scenarios and 1,487 legitimate-traffic scenarios. Complete Security Scores ran from a perfect 100% for the top product down to roughly 61% for the weakest. The spread inside a typical shortlist is that wide, and a shortlist drawn up in 2023 or 2024 may no longer describe the products on it.

The second number matters as much as the first. A platform that blocks every attack and also blocks legitimate requests cannot stay in blocking mode for long, and false positive avoidance varied almost as widely across the same twelve products. Those percentage points become alerts, tuning hours, and exceptions your team carries every day.

3 questions for every vendor on the list

Ask for API coverage protocol by protocol. REST is one protocol among several in a modern estate; GraphQL, SOAP, WebSockets, and gRPC all carry production traffic, and the v5.0 results showed coverage varying widely by protocol inside a single product, with WebSockets the weakest area across the group. A headline API score hides that.

Ask how long it takes to reach a tuned, low false-positive state on your traffic, and measure it over two full weeks of real traffic during the proof of value. Time to protection and tuning effort are the costs you pay after the contract is signed.

Ask how the deployment and licensing model behaves as the portfolio grows. Each delivery model, SaaS, native in-cloud, or reverse proxy, has its own latency and onboarding profile, and each licensing unit, request, bandwidth, or application, bends the cost curve differently as traffic grows. Model 24 to 36 months of growth with each vendor, starting from your own traffic baseline.

An honest aside: no one platform suits every environment. If your dominant requirement is a developer-centric edge platform or raw DDoS scrubbing capacity above everything else, weigh those needs explicitly, and validate any shortlist, Imperva included, against your own traffic in a proof of value.

Title: Yoba Malware Hides a Crypto Miner Behind Legitimate OpenAI and Anthropic Binaries
Context: “The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first...
Full Text:
Yoba malware uses fake ChatGPT and Claude apps to sideload malware through signed installers and deploy a cryptocurrency miner.

Check Point Research has spent two months tracking a campaign it calls Yoba, which uses the popularity of AI tools to spread a custom malware chain. The attackers build fake GitHub projects that pose as AI desktop applications such as GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus. The projects look convincing and run on real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them seem legitimate to potential victims.

“These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload.” reads the report. “In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.”

The lure is simple. Each project has a repository, a GitHub.io page describing the software, and a ZIP release with the malware. The repositories show no fake stars or forks, yet they still rank among the top Google results, most likely through SEO poisoning that optimizes titles, descriptions and hosting domains.

The first repository appeared around July 2026, but the first malicious releases landed only on August 30 and 31, and a third followed about five days later on September 4. Each repository uses a different Outlook address, and commit times point to UTC+4, UTC-4 and UTC+3, which Check Point reads as a deliberate attempt to hide the actor’s real time zone.

Here’s the trick that gives the report its title. Each ZIP holds a legitimate signed executable from OpenAI or Anthropic, named Setup.exe, next to a malicious winmm.dll. The signed program loads the DLL on its own, a technique known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.

The ZIP files were not even password-protected. Attackers often use passwords to prevent security tools from automatically unpacking and scanning files. However, these binaries already had very low detection rates because they used anti-sandbox and other techniques to avoid analysis. The DLL’s compilation date is another clue: it was built on the same day it was added to the archive, unlike the legitimate files around it.

The dropper, called YobaDropper, checks the environment before running. It calculates a hash of the name of the program that launched it and continues only if the name is Setup.exe. This means that sandboxes that run the DLL on its own will fail this check. When that happens, the process does not exit. Instead, it sleeps 200,000 times for 5.5 seconds each, a total of about 12.73 days.

The malware also avoids victims in CIS countries by checking the keyboard layout. It excludes Russian, Belarusian, Tajik, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Georgian, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Turkmen, Uzbek, and Tatar. Interestingly, Ukraine, which has often appeared in similar exclusion lists, is not included.

Next, the malware requests administrator privileges. If the user does not have them, it displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” and exits. The victim must then restart it with administrator rights.

Once it has the required privileges, the malware creates a folder called WMProcess under ProgramData. It copies the legitimate WMPDMC.exe file from System32 into this folder and places the second-stage payload there under the name wmpdui.dll.

The malicious code achieves persistence by using a scheduled task dressed up as Microsoft. The author is set to Microsoft Corporation, the description says it collects device metadata for Windows Media Player, and it starts three minutes after boot as Local System. The task launches the legitimate program, which sideloads the malicious DLL.

The second stage, YobaLoader, shares code with the dropper, which points to the same developer. It only runs under WMPDMC.exe and uses a different seed for its hashing than the dropper does, which separates the stages and weakens hash-based detection. Its job is to find its payload without a classic command server.

It goes to a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub, and downloads the channel’s profile picture. The last 50 bytes of the image seed a domain generator that builds names from word lists in the form adjective-noun-verb-number on dedyn[.]io. Change the picture and the operator gets a new domain.

Then it asks Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS service for a TXT record on that domain. The reply is signed, and the loader checks the signature before decrypting it, which gives a link to a payload on Catbox. Check Point says this reliance on DoH and common hosting aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway protections, and the campaign avoids dedicated command-and-control infrastructure, using Telegram, Tor, Catbox and DoH instead.

The operator can choose how the payload runs. It can inject it into svchost.exe, save it as an executable after removing the Zone.Identifier mark, or run it as a hidden PowerShell script while bypassing execution policies.

“Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.” continnues the report.

The miner uses Tor to connect to an encrypted mining server. It can start its own Tor components, use about 85% of CPU threads, and pause mining when the user is active. It resumes after 240 seconds of inactivity and can load the WinRing0 driver to optimize mining performance.

However, YobaLoader is not limited to cryptocurrency mining. Its DNS tasking system allows operators to deliver any PE executable or PowerShell payload, meaning future attacks could distribute other malware families.

Earlier versions appeared in June 2026. They used Cursor.exe for sideloading, a startup shortcut for persistence, and excluded only Russia. They also used .aber[.]ir instead of dedyn[.]io and included anti-debugging and anti-VM checks that later versions dropped.

Check Point believes the attackers may have Russian origins and mainly operate in the UTC-4 time zone, but this is an assessment, not a confirmed attribution.

Defenders should look for suspicious WMPDMC.exe copies under ProgramData, fake Microsoft scheduled tasks, Telegram-related traffic, DNS lookups for dedyn[.]io through dns.google, and unexplained high CPU usage.

“The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.” concludes the report. “Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.”

Title: Critical Linux kernel flaw allows remote root attacks on MPTCP servers
Context: Security researchers at Anthropic have developed an exploit for a critical Linux kernel vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute commands as root...
Full Text:
Security researchers at Anthropic have developed an exploit for a critical Linux kernel vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute commands as root on servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listeners.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, also affects ordinary TCP connections, although remote code execution has not been publicly demonstrated on servers without an MPTCP listener.

Multipath TCP (MPTCP) is a TCP feature that lets a single connection use multiple network paths at the same time to improve performance and reliability. It is commonly used in environments where devices have multiple network connections, such as Wi-Fi and cellular networks.

CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free vulnerability in the kernel's IPv4 TCP networking code that received a severity score of 9.8 out of 10 from the Linux kernel CVE team.

The vulnerability affects Linux kernels dating back to version 4.4, including widely used distributions such as Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and Rocky Linux.

According to the Linux kernel advisory, the vulnerability stems from a race condition in how the kernel handles TCP connection requests, potentially causing a use-after-free condition.

"tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it," reads the advisory.

"Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req(). tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice."

A similar issue can occur during TCP request socket migration when net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req is enabled, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program is used.

Although triggering the vulnerability requires no authentication, Red Hat says exploiting the race condition is more complex than just sending a malicious network packet.

Red Hat classifies the vulnerability as a potential denial-of-service issue that could cause a kernel crash, assigning it a lower severity score of 5.9 because exploitation is complex.

However, researchers at Anthropic demonstrated that the vulnerability could be exploited for remote code execution under specific conditions.

An Anthropic report explained that an unreleased Claude AI model developed an exploit that bypassed kernel address space layout randomization (KASLR) and executed arbitrary commands as root on a Linux server running an MPTCP listener.

According to Anthropic, the exploit took about 53 minutes to achieve remote root code execution, showing the vulnerability could be exploited for more than denial-of-service attacks.

While MPTCP is not typically enabled by default in applications, some software enables it automatically.

Beginning in Go 1.24, the programming language enables MPTCP by default for TCP listeners on Linux as long as the kernel supports the feature. Due to this, some Go-based network services may enable MPTCP listeners without administrators knowing.

Linux distros begin releasing patches

The vulnerability was fixed in the upstream Linux kernel and backported to maintained kernel branches. However, security updates have not yet been pushed out to all affected Linux distributions.

According to Canonical's security tracker, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS, and 26.10 remain vulnerable, with kernel fixes in progress as of October 30.

Red Hat also lists RHEL 8, 9, and 10 as affected, with fixes planned for future updates. RHEL 7 is not affected because its kernel does not contain the vulnerable code.

In mitigation guidance, Rocky Linux support provider CIQ confirms Rocky Linux 8, 9, and 10 are also affected and shared temporary firewall protections for affected systems.

According to Debian's security tracker, the vulnerability was fixed in kernel package version 6.1.190-1 for Debian 12 (Bookworm) and 6.12.113-1 for Debian 13 (Trixie). Fixed packages are also available for Debian testing and unstable.

Other Linux vendors, including Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux, and SUSE, have also released fixes for some affected kernel versions.

The vulnerability does not affect macOS, which uses Apple's XNU kernel rather than the Linux kernel.

Administrators are advised to check their distribution's security advisories and install updated kernel packages as they become available.

For systems where patches are not yet available, restricting access to trusted networks or IP addresses can reduce the risk.

CIQ also recommends temporarily blocking IPv4 TCP packets containing IP options before they reach the vulnerable TCP processing code, and shared examples of nftables rules that can block this type of traffic.

The company cautions that disabling MPTCP alone is insufficient because the underlying vulnerability can still be triggered through ordinary TCP traffic.

There are currently no confirmed reports of CVE-2026-98432 being exploited in the wild.

Title: A Supply Chain Attack Put Malicious Anthropic Claude Extensions on Thousands of Devices
Context: “Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first...
Full Text:
The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.

The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.

“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.

What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”

Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”

David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”

Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

Title: Crypto's biggest withdrawal.
Context: Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts.
Full Text:
Binance suffers a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. Attackers exploit a critical GitLab flaw. Russian disinformation targets U.S. elections. Treasury sanctions North Korean IT worker operations. A cyberattack halts Polymarket trading. GCHQ loses track of thousands of storage devices. An abandoned Mac app leaves security risks behind. Japan Airlines reports a third-party breach. An AI-powered command-and-control framework emerges in the wild. Our guest is Josh Devon, Co-founder & CEO of Sondera, winner of the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

Today is Friday October 30th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Binance suffers the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has suffered a staggering $6.3 billion theft, reportedly the largest cryptocurrency hack on record. Researchers at TRM Labs and Chainalysis attribute the October 29 attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation. Attackers moved funds across ten blockchains, with most of the theft occurring in just 20 minutes. Binance says its preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which may have provided access to systems authorized to move funds. The company found no evidence that private wallet keys were stolen. Instead, attackers apparently manipulated transaction-signing infrastructure, including an Ethereum feature that allowed them to automate withdrawals. Cryptocurrency issuers and networks have frozen billions in stolen assets, but estimates suggest attackers still control between $2.4 billion and $3.3 billion. Binance has promised to reimburse affected customers, while significant questions remain about the security controls protecting its wallets.

A maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability is under active exploitation.

Attackers are actively exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated remote code execution. CISA has added the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97229, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems by Sunday. The vulnerability involves an integer overflow in GitLab’s regular expression compiler, allowing attackers to execute malicious code through specially crafted CI/CD configurations. GitLab patched the flaw earlier this month and has released additional threat detections after observing exploitation attempts. The Shadowserver Foundation reports nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it’s unclear how many remain vulnerable. The latest discovery follows several serious GitLab security issues this year, including another recently exploited vulnerability that could expose sensitive credentials and other secrets.

A Russian disinformation group targets U.S. elections.

Researchers say a covert Russian influence operation is targeting Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas with fabricated allegations of misconduct. Analysts at Alethea and Clemson University attribute the campaign to Storm-1516, a Russian disinformation group that spread similar false accusations during the 2024 presidential election. The latest attack involved videos that researchers at Graphika believe were AI-generated. Initially attracting little attention, the videos gained traction after several influential accounts on X amplified them. One received more than 850,000 views in its first 24 hours. U.S. intelligence assessments indicate Russia has recently intensified its election interference efforts, particularly in competitive Senate races. While much of the activity targets Democrats, intelligence officials haven’t concluded that Moscow is explicitly favoring either party.

Treasury officials sanction Russian and North Koreans over fraudulent IT worker operations.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russian and North Korean nationals and companies accused of supporting Pyongyang’s fraudulent IT worker operations. Two Russians allegedly laundered millions in cryptocurrency earned by North Korean operatives working remotely for American companies. Treasury also targeted North Korean managers overseeing IT workers in Russia, along with a company accused of using artificial intelligence to help operatives secure U.S. jobs. The broader scheme involves North Koreans using stolen identities to obtain lucrative technology positions, then funneling earnings back to Pyongyang. Some workers have also stolen sensitive information and extorted employers. U.S. officials say the proceeds help fund North Korea’s weapons programs. The sanctions follow a Justice Department operation targeting laptop farms used to disguise workers’ overseas locations.

Polymarket suspends trading following a cyberattack.

Prediction market Polymarket temporarily suspended trading Thursday after a cyberattack involving a third-party service provider disrupted its international platform. The company says trading has resumed and promises to reimburse affected users, but hasn’t disclosed the extent of the losses or identified the attacker. Blockchain security researchers traced more than $2.1 million in suspected cryptocurrency theft to a single account. Security firm Hudson Rock identified the compromised provider as website performance company DebugBear, which separately acknowledged a security incident and urged customers to remove its embedded code. Researchers discovered malicious code apparently designed to identify cryptocurrency wallets and transfer their assets to an attacker-controlled account. Polymarket removed DebugBear’s code from its website. There’s currently no evidence that other DebugBear customers were compromised.

GCHQ laments missing storage devices.

Britain’s intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of storage devices potentially containing sensitive information. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner says USB drives, hard disks, and memory cards remain unaccounted for years after the problem was first identified. Some devices may contain intercepted communications and other highly sensitive intelligence data. The watchdog expressed frustration over GCHQ’s slow investigation. The agency acknowledged shortcomings in its tracking system but says it has implemented corrective measures. Officials are still determining how many devices are actually lost.

An abandoned Mac app causes security headaches.

An abandoned version of the once-popular Popcorn Time streaming app left hundreds of thousands of Macs potentially vulnerable to attack. Researchers at Eye Research discovered that Time4Popcorn installed a persistent update checker that could download and execute code with elevated privileges, even years after users stopped opening the app. With the developers long gone, attackers could potentially hijack expired update domains to distribute malware. Researchers found no evidence of exploitation, but estimate 250,000 to 350,000 Macs were affected. They took control of an abandoned domain and used the update mechanism itself to disable the vulnerable checker on more than a million Macs and Windows PCs. Other vulnerabilities remain, however, and some update domains are still uncontrolled. Researchers recommend uninstalling Time4Popcorn entirely.

Japan Airlines suffers a third-party data breach.

Japan Airlines says a breach at its technology provider, Amadeus IT Group, exposed personal information belonging to 92,000 customers. Compromised data includes names, reservation codes, and flight details. For approximately 2,000 passengers, attackers also obtained passport numbers, contact information, and frequent flyer numbers. The airline says payment card information and flight operations were unaffected.

The disclosure comes amid a wave of cyber incidents in Japan, including breaches affecting millions of customers at a Sony-owned internet provider, Burger King Japan, and gaming company Capcom. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called for emergency cybersecurity measures, warning of growing risks from stolen personal information. Japanese and American defense officials have also discussed strengthening cooperation against cyber threats as the country grapples with the recent attacks.

An AI-integrated command-and-control framework is found operating in the wild.

Cisco Talos researchers have discovered an AI-integrated command-and-control framework called NIK C2 operating in the wild. The Windows-based malware combines credential theft, keylogging, surveillance, and remote access with direct access to OpenAI’s API. Attackers can use AI to analyze stolen information during an active intrusion, potentially accelerating their operations. The malware can even use a victim’s own OpenAI API key, potentially charging them for the attacker’s AI requests. NIK C2 also includes screen-locking ransomware that demands cryptocurrency payments without encrypting files. Its capabilities extend to lateral movement, security evasion, and persistent access. Talos observed active infrastructure and multiple versions of the malware, suggesting ongoing development. Researchers warn that integrating AI directly into malware could significantly reduce defenders’ opportunities to detect and interrupt attacks.

We bid farewell to the captain who inspired a generation of innovators.

We say goodbye today to Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86.

His was a remarkable life. From a difficult childhood in a working-class Yorkshire home, he found his way to the Royal Shakespeare Company, where he spent decades mastering his craft. And then, approaching 50, he took a chance on a science fiction television series that he wasn’t entirely convinced would succeed.

And in doing so, he became Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

For those of us who grew up with Star Trek, it’s difficult to overstate what Patrick Stewart brought to that role. Picard was thoughtful, principled, intellectually curious, and deeply committed to the idea that humanity could become something better. He valued diplomacy over violence, reason over impulse, and the dignity of every individual. He was a leader who listened, who questioned his own assumptions, and who understood that having the authority to give an order didn’t necessarily mean it was the right order to give.

And there’s something else worth remembering. Star Trek inspired generations of scientists, engineers, programmers, and technology professionals. People who watched those shows as kids and went on to build the technologies that shape our world today. The communicators, the tablets, the voice-controlled computers, the extraordinary networks connecting people across unimaginable distances. For countless young viewers, Star Trek wasn’t just entertainment. It was an invitation to imagine what technology might make possible, and then go out and make some of it real.

Patrick Stewart helped make that future feel worth pursuing.

He also reminded us that intelligence and kindness weren’t mutually exclusive, that leadership could be compassionate, and that even in a universe filled with extraordinary technology, the most important questions were still fundamentally human ones.

Now, you might reasonably ask, “What does this have to do with cyber security?”

Well, as it happens, Captain Picard was something of an early adopter of multifactor authentication. Whenever the Enterprise’s auto-destruct sequence needed to be activated or canceled, the ship required authorization codes and confirmation from multiple senior officers.

Even in the 24th century, apparently, you couldn’t just blow up the Enterprise with a single password.

Sir Patrick Stewart gave us many wonderful performances over a long and extraordinary career. But for generations of us who looked to the stars and imagined a better future, he’ll always be our captain.

Thank you, Sir Patrick.

Title: “Are We Exposed?” What CISOs Need to Know About Their Software Risk
Context: Curl When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer
Full Text:
Recent events have once again highlighted the need to quickly answer the question, “Are we exposed?”

We now face threats to businesses and governments from vulnerabilities and compromises in three fundamental components used in software development: Curl, PHP, and LiteLLM.

Curl

When it comes to Curl and its underlying transfer library libcurl, the threat can affect the very foundation of internet data transfer. With libcurl embedded in many enterprise environments – from backend microservices and container runtimes to automated CI/CD pipelines and shell scripts – this vulnerability carries potential systemic risk. The core threat centers on high-severity flaws disclosed in October 2026, notably a high-severity HTTP/2 use-after-free issue (such as CVE-2026-92392) where a malicious upstream server handling an upload can corrupt client-side memory and, under specific conditions, trigger remote code execution or application crashes on the machine initiating the transfer. Because libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for HTTPS URLs when the server supports it and applications rarely inspect what libcurl does under the hood, development stacks and automated deployment pipelines that have not upgraded to a fixed version can remain exposed to hostile external endpoints.

LiteLLM

Regarding LiteLLM, JFrog Security Research detected the problem within 2 hours, and the errant LiteLLM package, version 1.107.0, has already been removed from PyPI. Reflecting the open-source community ecosystem’s continually improving maturation, the package maintainers have already published a report. But from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on October 21, 2026, software developers, agentic agents, or your build systems could have downloaded that package from PyPI, and affected Docker images remained available until 14:20 UTC. The ripple effect of a compromised package or vulnerable component getting into an environment doesn’t just impact the developers or security team. It also impacts IT Ops and, down the line, auditors. Every change impacts the whole organization. Executives, the business decision makers who determine where to invest and allocate resources, need a way to understand where they sit in this maturity. Do they have complete visibility or not?

PHP

In the case of PHP, two CRITICAL-severity PHP core vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), were disclosed and referred to publicly as PHP2Shell. The bugs can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, according to public advisories. Within days, news outlets reported on the vulnerabilities, and CISA issued an alert urging organizations to patch immediately, including CNBC and the BBC, CISA.

“Are We Exposed?”

When a CISO wrestles with the question of “Are we exposed?”, their triage process should focus on these key issues:

Is it really a threat?

Where is it being used?

What is the business impact?

Do I have a reporting or disclosure obligation under rules or standards that apply to my organization, such as those of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), PCI DSS, or, for product manufacturers, the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?

Did we block it?

How do we fix it?

The CISO’s ability to answer these questions with confidence depends on how well they’ve integrated their tools, people, processes, and security program to provide that visibility and respond quickly to security incidents. The ability to do this, in turn, is a reflection of the maturity of their overall security program and how well they can protect, monitor, and govern the full gamut of software development operations – whether it’s on the developer’s workstation, in agentic workflows, or implemented directly by AI coding agents.

A true assessment of your organization’s abilities to determine your strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats is critical to providing a full 360 view of your risk posture.

Hands-On Assessment Experience

As a CISO, I’ve done these assessments on a number of occasions, for both new deployments and as an ongoing protective measure to help keep the business protected as new threats and vulnerabilities evolve.

These assessments should be broadly based and take into account business objectives, employee capabilities, workflows, data usage, and the maturity of the infrastructure. Covering these bases should give you an accurate compass of where you are and where you need to improve.

This should, of course, include your tools, but should not lead to one of the classic mistakes organizations make, which is over-focusing on tools, simply because they’re the easiest thing to measure. The other areas mentioned above are easy to overlook, but extremely important to a realistic assessment, as tools without the right people and processes won’t achieve the objective of protecting your business.

JFrog’s Security Maturity Assessment

Based on JFrog’s experience working with many of the Fortune 100 customers and through the expertise of our in-house security research team, we’ve actually built our own Security Maturity Assessment. It lets organizations self-assess their software supply chain security program maturity across 11 domains, based on their answers.

I strongly recommend taking a few minutes out of your busy day to complete the questionnaire, as it assesses the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and risks in your software development operations and could help you identify where to start when it comes to ensuring you can truly answer the question: “Are we exposed?”

Takeaways

The question of “Are we exposed?” can be complicated and difficult to assess, but recent high-profile security incidents don’t give CISOs the luxury of taking days to come up with a reply. Corporate executives and board members need fast, accurate answers.

Having complete visibility into your people, processes, workflows, tools, and dependencies gives you the leverage to protect your business under the pressure of the latest attacks.
