Title: Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks
Context: In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million...
Full Text:
When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Dropcatch Domains: A Hidden Risk

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Know Your Internet Services

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

Title: WordPress RCE Flaw Draws Nearly 63,000 Attack Attempts in Just 24 Hours
Context: Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released
Full Text:
Threat actors have been observed attempting to exploit a high-severity security flaw in WordPress Core shortly after patches were released.

The vulnerability, which does not have a CVE identifier, relates to a case of remote code execution impacting WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3. It carries a CVSS score of 8.1 on the CVSS scoring system. Patches for the flaw were released on October 28, 2026.

"This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades," Wordfence said. "This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window."

The WordPress security company noted that successful exploitation requires an "attacker to hit a very narrow window while WordPress is unpacking a complete Core update."

The issue boils down to the fact that affected versions unpack new files part of a full-package Core update into a predictable directory under "wp-content/upgrade." This copy also includes the WordPress installer.

"Because the staging directory is web-accessible on many servers, an unauthenticated attacker who requests the installer at precisely the right moment can interact with the staged WordPress copy and progress to PHP code execution," Alex Thomas, who leads the Wordfence Threat Response Team, said.

A threat actor who is able to win the race condition can gain the ability to execute code on the server, assuming the following conditions are met -

A full-package update containing the installer files

Public web and PHP access to the staging tree

A predictable or discovered staging path, and

Adequate time to complete the attack before WordPress cleans up the temporary files

Although that window has been observed to last only seconds in normal lab environments, threat actors are polling vulnerable paths, such as "setup-config.php," repeatedly in an attempt to trigger the flaw. Over the past 24 hours, Wordfence said it has blocked 62,969 attacks targeting the vulnerability.

"Two of the largest sources repeatedly polled small groups of sites for roughly 14.5 hours, behavior consistent with trying to catch the brief upgrade window," Thomas said. "Other sources tested many staging-directory and version-name variations."

"Not every request used the exact vulnerable path, but the sustained polling and exact-layout probes show that attackers quickly understood the race condition and began targeting it."

With active exploitation attempts already underway, WordPress site owners are advised to update to version 7.1.4 as soon as possible and look for suspicious requests to PHP files located under "wp-content/upgrade," as well as unfamiliar administrator accounts, plugins, or PHP files.

Title: SS7 and Diameter Attacks: How Signaling Flaws Expose Your Phone
Context: This keeps happening Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure
Full Text:
SS7 and Diameter signaling attacks can track, intercept, and impersonate you. Here’s how they work and how to stop them.

Your phone can be tracked, your SMS two-factor codes can be intercepted, and your number can be impersonated, all without malware, a phishing link, or any access to your device.

The attacks happen inside the telecom network, in the carrier-to-carrier control protocols known as signaling, the automated descendants of the old telephone switchboard. Most users never see them, and most carriers can’t reliably stop them.

Signaling attacks aren’t new. Most recently, they made headlines when Iranian-linked actors reportedly exploited outdated network technology to locate the phones of US personnel in the Middle East during the Iran war.

But the vulnerability has been around for decades, and it’s been used for far more everyday crimes, like intercepting bank one-time passcodes. It has even been demonstrated by popular YouTubers: Veritasium hijacked a tech influencer’s calls and texts using only his phone number.

This keeps happening

Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure.

Citizen Lab exposed two long-running commercial surveillance campaigns abusing SS7 and Diameter, with thousands of attacks against targets in dozens of countries.

Congressman Ted Lieu’s phone was hacked on live TV via SS7 on 60 Minutes Australia

Attackers have intercepted SMS one-time passcodes to drain victims’ bank accounts.

What is a signaling attack?

Every call, text, and mobile data session requires your carrier to verify you’re a paying customer and route your traffic to the right destination.

Carriers do this with signaling–background messages that identify your location and forward traffic accordingly. Signaling has been the connective tissue between global providers for decades, and it is one of the most overlooked attack surfaces in mobile security.

Two protocols do most of the work: SS7 (from the 1970s, used in 2G/3G) and Diameter (its successor, used in 4G and most 5G).

Both were designed when a small number of large operators could plug into the system, so they assume that traffic claiming to come from a legitimate operator really does. SS7 has essentially no process for authenticating the machine making a request.

Diameter supports stronger authentication on paper, but operators don’t always deploy basic protections like encryption, and many fall back on the same peer-to-peer trust model.

An attacker with access to the global signaling backbone, through a commercial leasing arrangement or a compromised operator, can send messages that carriers worldwide treat as trustworthy.

How does it work

Signaling lets an attacker ask your carrier questions and make claims on your behalf:

Harvest your IMSI. Knowing your number, an attacker can request your International Mobile Subscriber ID (IMSI) under the pretense of routing a call or SMS. It can be reused for follow-on attacks for years.

Locate you in real time. Queries can return the cell tower you last connected to. Others, normally reserved for emergency responders, can return the actual coordinates your phone reports.

Intercept communications. The attacker claims you’ve roamed onto another network, so your calls and texts are redirected to them. Combined with a stolen username and password, this delivers your SMS second factor to the attacker instead of you.

Impersonate or block you. With your IMSI, an attacker can place calls or send SMS as you. A false roaming claim can also cut off service to your phone.

Disrupt networks. Deliberately misconfigured signaling messages can overwhelm provider systems.

None of this touches your device. It happens in automated transactions you can’t see and that leave no trace on your phone.

Why firewalls and velocity checks fall short

Carrier signaling firewalls reliably block messages sent to or from the wrong place. For correctly routed messages, they often run a velocity check to test whether you could physically have traveled from your last known location to the one now claimed. If you were in New York an hour ago and a Turkish carrier says you’re on its network, the request is denied.

The structural problem is that the firewall’s location data is often hours old. In research presented at the Wireless Security conference in 2025, Cape, the privacy-first mobile carrier, measured Diameter updates from a visited network arriving as infrequently as every two to ten hours.

For subscribers in the US and Germany, over 250 distinct networks are reachable within a single hour of travel time. An attacker with enough operator identities will eventually find one that looks plausible.

Citizen Lab’s report shows this in practice: the actor it calls STA1 repeatedly tried to track a user by rotating through eleven operator identities in nine countries to look like legitimate roaming traffic. They also pivoted between SS7 and Diameter, which most carriers defend with separate firewalls and little coordination.

Consider a target who boards a flight from Nashville to Berlin and powers off her phone. A message posing as China Mobile claiming she’s roaming there gets rejected, because it’s physically impossible.

A message from a carrier in nearby Nassau, Bahamas, looks plausible, and the home carrier can be fooled into routing her calls and SMS to the attacker.

How Cape defends against signaling attacks

Cape is a privacy-first mobile carrier, whose approach is to assume the global telecom system is compromised and build protections that keep communications private anyway. There are four layers:

1. Daily IMSI rotation. Almost every targeted signaling attack starts with an IMSI, and once an attacker has yours, it stays useful for as long as you have it. A Citizen Lab report confirms this, with the same IMSIs being attacked across operations separated by months and years. On most carriers, your IMSI is permanent. You get one when you activate your SIM and you keep it forever. On Cape, your IMSI rotates daily. The databases of harvested IMSIs that surveillance vendors build up over the years are no longer useful against Cape subscribers.

2. No SS7. Cape doesn’t support SS7 at all, and there is no SS7 fallback in the network, so SS7-based attacks have nothing to land on. Many carriers still struggle to retire legacy SS7 infrastructure because some revenue-generating part of their network depends on it.

3. Network Lock. Instead of trusting a network’s idea of where you are, Cape asks your device. When a foreign network requests to attach to your phone, Network Lock queries the Cape app, which evaluates the claim locally at the country level and reports back whether it matches. If an attacker tries to attach your IMSI from another country while your phone is at home, the request is denied and you’re notified. Cape’s systems learn only whether the claim matches, not where you actually are, and Cape never collects or stores your precise location.

4. Continuous penetration testing. Most signaling firewalls are compliance tools tuned to GSMA baseline recommendations. Those recommendations are distributed to more than 1,200 member providers, so the same guidance is available to attackers who can send signaling messages. Cape has third-party firms that specialize in current signaling exploitation techniques to test its infrastructure, then hardens the network against what they find, especially anything affecting subscriber privacy.

Title: Passkeys Are Better Than Passwords. But They Are Not Enough.
Context: The Future of Identity Security Must Go Beyond Authentication Passkeys and identity threat detection address distinct parts of the identity attack surface
Full Text:
For decades, passwords have been one of cybersecurity’s most persistent weaknesses. Users forget them, reuse them, share them, and surrender them to convincing phishing sites. Attackers steal credentials, automate credential stuffing, and increasingly use artificial intelligence to make social engineering more effective.

What are passkeys?

Passkeys promise to eliminate much of this problem.

Built on public-key cryptography, passkeys replace shared secrets with cryptographic credentials. There is no password for an attacker to steal, intercept through phishing, or reuse against another service. Properly implemented passkeys are also phishing-resistant because authentication is bound to the legitimate service.

That represents a significant improvement over passwords and many traditional forms of multi-factor authentication (MFA). But it does not answer a more fundamental question: Just because someone successfully authenticated, should we continue to trust that identity?

Passkeys strengthen authentication. They do not eliminate identity risk.

What Passkeys Get Right

Traditional authentication frequently relies on passwords combined with one-time passcodes, SMS messages, or push notifications. While stronger than passwords alone, these methods remain vulnerable to phishing, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, MFA fatigue, SIM swapping, and social engineering.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Passkeys fundamentally change that model. Instead of presenting a reusable secret, the user’s device holds a private cryptographic key while the service retains the corresponding public key. The private key is not transmitted during authentication.

This provides meaningful protection against phishing, credential stuffing, password database theft, and other attacks built around stealing reusable credentials. Passkeys can also improve usability because users no longer need to remember complex passwords or repeatedly retrieve authentication codes.

Organizations should welcome that transition. The mistake would be assuming that stronger authentication solves the broader identity security problem though.

Authentication Is Not Identity

When passkey authentication succeeds, the system has strong cryptographic evidence that a credential associated with an account completed the authentication process.

But was the account legitimately established? Has the underlying identity been compromised? Is the device trustworthy? Is an attacker operating through an authenticated session?

A perfectly functioning authentication mechanism cannot compensate for an identity that should never have been trusted.

If an attacker establishes or takes control of an account before a passkey is bound to it, the organization may subsequently perform highly secure authentication of the wrong person. The stronger the authenticator becomes, the more important the integrity of enrollment becomes.

What Happens When the Device Changes?

Legitimate users also do not always authenticate from the same device. Phones are lost, stolen, damaged, or replaced. Employees receive new laptops. Consumers switch technology ecosystems.

Passkey synchronization addresses many of these scenarios by making credentials available across supported devices. But organizations still need to accommodate legitimate users who arrive without access to the expected passkey.

At that point, the challenge shifts from authentication to recovery and re-establishing trust. How does the organization determine whether someone requesting access from an unfamiliar device is the legitimate account owner?

If the fallback relies on a password, SMS code, email link, knowledge-based question, or help desk process, attackers may target that weaker recovery path.

The passkey has not been compromised. The attacker has gone around it.

Organizations therefore need a secure way to re-establish identity trust before associating a new authenticator or device with an existing account.

Authentication Is Only One Moment

Another gap emerges after authentication. Many identity architectures effectively operate according to a simple sequence: Authenticate, grant access, and trust the resulting session.

Modern identity-based attacks do not necessarily stop at the login screen. Attackers can hijack authenticated sessions, compromise trusted devices, abuse privileges, manipulate account attributes, or conduct anomalous transactions. In these situations, the authentication mechanism may have worked exactly as designed.

The question cannot simply be, “Did this user authenticate successfully?” It must also be, “Do we still have sufficient evidence to trust this identity and its activity?”

Layer Identity Threat Detection on Top

This is where identity threat detection complements passkeys.

Instead of treating successful authentication as a permanent declaration of trust, organizations can continuously evaluate identity risk. Device characteristics, identity attributes, behavioral anomalies, network intelligence, account changes, transaction context, and threat indicators can help determine whether an identity remains trustworthy.

This does not require adding friction to every interaction. A risk-based model can allow legitimate users to proceed normally while escalating controls when risk changes.

A known user authenticating from an established device and behaving normally may require no additional intervention. The same account attempting recovery from an unfamiliar device, changing critical account attributes, or conducting anomalous activity could trigger additional identity verification.

The model changes from authenticate once and trust thereafter to establish trust, continuously evaluate risk, and respond when trust changes.

The Future of Identity Security Must Go Beyond Authentication

Passkeys and identity threat detection address distinct parts of the identity attack surface.

Passkeys reduce risks associated with passwords, credential theft, credential stuffing, and phishing. Identity threat detection addresses risks surrounding authentication, including enrollment, recovery, device changes, session compromise, and anomalous activity.

As organizations eliminate passwords, attackers will adapt. Instead of attacking the authenticator directly, they will look for opportunities around it.

That does not mean passkeys failed. It means they succeeded in making one part of the attack surface harder.

Passkeys answer an important question: Does this user possess a legitimate credential required to authenticate?

Identity threat detection addresses the question that matters throughout the identity lifecycle: Should we still trust this identity?

Organizations need to answer both.

Title: Bulletproof Host Virtualine Loses Its Domain to FBI Seizure
Context: The bulletproof hosting provider first emerged on the cybercrime forum Exploit in 2024, but claims to have been operating since 2019
Full Text:
The FBI has seized virtualine.net, the domain of a Russian-speaking bulletproof hosting services provider associated with various cybercriminal operations.

According to court documents, Virtualine, also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, has been hosting customers’ illicit services and helped them evade law enforcement takedown attempts.

In posts on cybercrime forums, Virtualine promoted support for various types of cybercriminal activity, including phishing, spam, carding, and more; advertised its ability to move customer services to unaffiliated infrastructure; and claimed it intentionally ignored abuse.

It also allowed users to post and sell explicit images and videos of minors and adults, and supported at least one customer that offered a hack-for-hire service aimed at stealing sexually explicit content from online accounts.

Despite receiving numerous takedown requests from law enforcement agencies in several countries, Virtualine continued to aid the customer and even helped them create a new website for uploading the illicit content. The provider continues to host the new website.

According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, Virtualine has been used, among others, by ransomware groups and an infostealer operator.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Virtualine received more illicit-attributed cryptocurrency than any other TRM-labeled bulletproof hosting provider, despite receiving less total value than several peers,” the company says.

The bulletproof hosting provider first emerged on the cybercrime forum Exploit in 2024, but claims to have been operating since 2019. It claimed to have had the largest collection of autonomous system numbers for malware and botnet hosting in 2025.

Most of the payments Virtualine’s labeled Bitcoin addresses have received came from a Russian drug marketplace (44%) and a large sextortion scheme (17%). A cryptocurrency mixer accounted for 13% of them and ransomware for 5%. In 2026, Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer operators.

“A domain seizure disrupts how customers find and access a service. It does not, by itself, establish that the operator has stopped working, or that customers have lost access to all underlying infrastructure,” TRM notes.

Title: Assad regime hacker who caused $136 billion market drop sentenced to 42 months
Context: “This case emphasizes the grave threat posed by cyber criminals and especially those serving regimes hostile to the United States,” noted First Assistant U
Full Text:
A Syrian man who used a hijacked news agency Twitter account to post a fake report of explosions at the White House has been sentenced to 42 months in prison, the US Department of Justice has announced.

Ahmad Umar Agha, also known as “Th3Pr0”, was sentenced on Thursday by a federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia for his central role in a hacking conspiracy organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad’s inner circle, including the commander of Syria’s General Intelligence Directorate.

The scheme ran from as early as August 2011 until January 2024, and Agha spent more than a decade on the run.

Punishing the press

To spread the regime’s propaganda, Agha hacked approximately 47 Western media outlets, businesses, NGOs, and US and allied government entities.

Prosecutors say the conspiracy punished the free press for reporting on the regime’s atrocities during the Arab Spring and the Syrian Civil War that followed.

“Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad’s regime to silence reporting on the regime’s atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.

The tweet that shook the Dow

On April 23, 2013, the Syrian used his access to the Twitter account of a widely respected news agency to post a false claim that President Obama had been injured in two explosions at the White House. The post caused a temporary $136 billion drop in the value of the stocks that make up the Dow Jones Industrial Average.

He later bragged about the hack in an interview with Business Insider, saying that a steep fall in the Dow “was our goal of that hack attack” and that “it was a big victory for us.”

Marines told to switch sides

Agha broke into the company hosting the US Marine Corps’ recruitment website and redirected visitors to a server displaying an image that urged Marines to refuse their orders and fight alongside the Syrian Army. During the attack, approximately 3,500 potential visitors saw that image in place of recruitment material.

On two occasions, he tried to take over the White House’s social media page by stealing usernames and passwords for the email accounts of White House staff. One of those attempts succeeded, and he used the access in a failed bid to trick other staffers into handing over the White House’s social media accounts.

Costly cleanup for victims

Court filings show that several victims had to spend significant sums cleaning up after the intrusions or restructuring their security.

One company that supplies online publishers with content, website ads and links to other sites lost about $35,000 a day for around six months. A global NGO had to deploy a new set of network monitoring products costing around $250,000, retrain more than 800 staff members and upgrade its security system, bringing its total losses to $480,000.

“This case emphasizes the grave threat posed by cyber criminals and especially those serving regimes hostile to the United States,” noted First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani K. Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia.

Agha and his coconspirator Firas Dardar were first charged by complaint in June 2014 and indicted in May 2018.

Dardar, who remains a fugitive, was charged in a separate conspiracy in September 2015, alongside Peter Romar, a Syrian national then living in Germany. Romar was extradited from Germany and pleaded guilty in September 2016.

Title: CISA says max severity GitLab flaw now exploited in the wild
Context: The company has also released threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances after detecting exploitation attempts
Full Text:
Attackers have started exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability patched earlier this month, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

Tracked as CVE-2026-97229, this critical security flaw was discovered by a security researcher using the 'joaxcar' handle in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, which parses, compiles, and evaluates regular expressions in pipeline configuration files.

CVE-2026-97229 stems from an integer overflow weakness and could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances via a maliciously crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient expression validation.

"GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," it said.

GitLab addressed the security issue in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 and urged admins to patch their servers immediately.

The company has also released threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances after detecting exploitation attempts.

On Thursday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed active exploitation and added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog. CISA also ordered federal agencies to secure their servers by Sunday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04.

Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, the cybersecurity agency encouraged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this flaw to protect their networks against ongoing attacks.

Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 Internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, but it doesn't say how many have already been secured against attacks.

​CVE-2026-97229 is the latest in a string of security issues GitLab has addressed since the start of the year. In January, it patched a high-severity two-factor authentication bypass (CVE-2026-0723) that lets attackers who know the target's account ID circumvent two-factor authentication.

Earlier this month, it also fixed a maximum-severity Regular Expression Compiler flaw (CVE-2026-110264) that could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances.

Almost two weeks later, GitLab addressed another maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-85706) in the repository commits API that can be abused to read sensitive data, such as credentials and other secrets, from vulnerable servers.

One day later, CISA added CVE-2026-85706 to its list of actively exploited flaws after cybersecurity firm watchTowr reported that attackers had already begun scanning the Internet for unpatched GitLab servers.

CISA has tagged six GitLab vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, including two (tracked as CVE-2021-22175 and CVE-2021-39935) in February this year.

GitLab's DevSecOps platform is used by over 50% of Fortune 100 companies and has more than 70 million registered users worldwide.

Title: Photo ID, bank checks, face scan? The UK’s age-check options
Context: Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information
Full Text:
As preparation for the UK’s planned social media ban, Ofcom has set out four ways social media platforms could check whether users are aged 16 or over. The government and Parliament will decide how the ban works in practice.

Ofcom is the regulator for the communications services in the UK. The BBC reports that Ofcom identified four ways to check someone’s age that it considers “highly effective.”

Here’s what those checks would involve:

Photo ID matching: Comparing a live image of you with the photo on an identity document, such as your passport, and checking the age information on that document.

Bank-based checks: Using age information your bank already holds about you, with your consent.

Facial age estimation: Using technology to estimate your age from your face. Ofcom says this technology has improved recently.

Digital ID services: Using a digital identity service to prove your age, rather than presenting a physical document.

Let’s think through what those checks could mean.

Challenges

The challenge isn’t simply checking someone’s age. It’s doing so without turning everyday internet use into an identity check.

Photo ID matching brings highly sensitive documents and facial images into the process, which raises questions about how that information is handled and protected. The risks aren’t hypothetical: as I reported last year, a breach at a third-party support provider for Discord exposed government ID images belonging to around 70,000 users.Banking-based checks can be more privacy-preserving if they return only confirmation that someone meets the age threshold, rather than exposing financial information. But the important questions are what information each party receives, what gets retained, and whether the check can be linked to someone’s activity.

Facial age estimation can avoid uploading an identity document, but it still processes a sensitive image and makes an imperfect prediction. Ofcom acknowledges that some technologies can be wrong by a few years around age 16, so people near the threshold may face an additional verification check.I would expect these checks to stop some underage access but not eliminate it.

Previous restrictions have been followed by workarounds, including increased VPN use, borrowed credentials, and migration to services outside the restrictions. The danger is treating a successful age gate as proof that children are now safe, when it might push them into less regulated spaces.The effectiveness depends on how the checks are implemented. A VPN may help someone avoid a check triggered by their apparent location; it won’t, by itself, bypass an identity or facial check that is still required.

Similarly, Ofcom says matching a live image to an ID is intended to make it harder to borrow someone else’s document. We shouldn’t assume every workaround defeats every method. But Ofcom accepts that some motivated children will get through. The meaningful test is how much harm these measures prevent, weighed against the privacy risks and barriers they introduce— not whether every user has completed a check.

My personal preference is double-blind verification: a provider confirms that you meet the age requirement without learning which service you’re accessing, while the service receives proof of age without learning your identity. Proving you’re old enough shouldn’t mean revealing who you are.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Title: Shufti ties AI agent actions to verified owners and permissions
Context: Shufti launches Know Your Agent (KYA), an AI agent verification solution designed to verify autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of individuals and businesses
Full Text:
Shufti launches Know Your Agent (KYA), an AI agent verification solution designed to verify autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of individuals and businesses. Agentic commerce enables AI agents to open accounts, place orders, and move funds for their owners. A business receiving one of these requests needs to know whether the agent is genuine, who is accountable for it, and whether the action falls within what that person approved.

A valid access token alone cannot answer these questions. Stolen credentials can appear legitimate, and agent impersonation allows fake agents to pose as trusted ones. Shufti KYA addresses these risks in a single flow by verifying the AI agent’s identity, confirming that a real person has authorized the action, and checking the agent’s permissions before it can access data or trigger a transaction.

Shufti KYA helps businesses accept authorized AI agents while blocking unauthorized or high-risk activity that could lead to AI agent fraud or chargeback disputes. It combines agent recognition, trust scoring, spoof-resistant identity verification, and permission checks to distinguish legitimate automation from suspicious or unauthorized activity before it proceeds.

Each AI agent receives a unique time-bound credential that can be revoked. Known agents are recognised by name, and new or unfamiliar agents are assessed through behavioural biometrics. Every agent is assigned a trust score to help businesses evaluate risk. Shufti already supports agents such as Meta Muse, GrokBot and OpenAI Dots, within a week of their launch.

Every agent is linked to an individual or business verified through Shufti’s modular KYC or KYB process, allowing businesses to select the checks appropriate to their requirements. Shufti KYA extends these checks to AI agents; it does not replace them.

AI agent authorization starts with a principal that sets a mandate for each AI agent, covering permitted actions, limits, expiry, and revocation. The mandate is enforced as a policy on every request, while ongoing monitoring helps detect misuse.

Each business sets its own rules within Shufti KYA. A bank can let agents view balances and pay approved billers, while new payees need a further check. A digital assets platform can let agents trade within an approved limit, while withdrawals stay blocked.

An iGaming operator can let agents monitor account activity and communicate bet settlement status, while bets must come from the verified player. A Marketplace can support purchases within customer-defined budgets, while a SaaS business can restrict agents to specific resources and tasks.

As agentic AI takes on more customer-facing tasks, Shufti aims to help businesses carry trusted automation plus agentic commerce while maintaining clear human control over AI-driven actions.

Shufti’s risk-based authorization determines when a request needs more than a mandate check. When an AI agent requests an action outside its mandate or one that exceeds a high-risk threshold, Shufti KYA brings in human-in-the-loop control that requires a liveness check in which the authorizing person completes a brief selfie verification. Shufti’s single selfie liveness is iBeta Level 3 certified, testing resistance to presentation attacks. This adds an extra layer of human oversight of high-risk AI agent actions.

Shufti Know Your Agent also maintains an audit trail of requests, decisions, and revocations linked to each agent and its principal, keeping every action traceable for accountability and review.

“Businesses are already allowing AI agents to act for their customers, and the question of who stands behind each action cannot wait for an answer later,” said Faryam Asif, Chief Technology Officer at Shufti. “Shufti Know Your Agent verifies every AI agent request with a verified owner, a clear mandate, and a record that holds up under review. Our customers can say yes to agent activity with confidence, because they know exactly who approved what, and when.”

Beyond AI agent security, Shufti KYA also supports revenue growth. Businesses can accept authorized agents and generate revenue through agent-driven transactions, while blocking rogue agents and any agent carrying a risk of fraud, unauthorized transactions, or chargeback disputes. This allows businesses to adopt AI agent automation with full human approval over agent permissions and actions.

Title: Bedrock Data routes data exposure fixes to owners and verifies results
Context: The capability is generally available today and included with the Bedrock Data platform
Full Text:
Bedrock Data has announced AI-assisted remediation, which federates the work of fixing data exposure to the data owners across the enterprise. Bedrock Data discovers who owns each exposed dataset, opens a ticket for that owner in the Jira or ServiceNow workflow the enterprise already runs and supplies the context needed to fix it. When the owner closes the ticket, Bedrock Data validates that the exposure is remediated and reopens the ticket if it is not.

Remediation now keeps pace with the rate of data creation instead of accumulating in a centralized security team’s backlog. The capability is generally available today and included with the Bedrock Data platform.

Enterprise data is measured in petabytes, billions of records, millions of documents and thousands of data stores. A centralized security team accountable for that data is small by comparison and cannot fix exposure at that scale on its own. It does not have access to most of the data and does not know how the business uses it. The data owners in engineering, data and business teams do.

Conventional DSPM tools stop at visibility, which leaves security teams with a growing list of exposures and no reliable way to get them fixed. In Bedrock Data’s Enterprise Data Security Confidence Index, 76% of respondents said a lack of automation and too much manual work hold back data security.

AI adoption raises the chance that an unresolved exposure turns into a leak. AI agents and copilots access data on their own, at machine speed, and they follow permissions rather than business intent. Sensitive data left in a test environment or a document shared too broadly was previously unlikely to be discovered.

An AI system can now find it and surface it in an answer. In EY’s 2026 AI Risk and Governance Survey, 85% of executives at companies using AI agents said some of those agents take important actions without real-time human involvement. Reducing data exposure lowers the risk of leaks, misuse and compliance violations, and it enables the enterprise to scale up AI adoption.

“Every enterprise has far more data issues than its centralized data security team can action. Until now, with data growing exponentially, risk accumulation and risk remediation were divergent curves. Data is the responsibility of the lines of business and the data organization, and remediation only scales when they own the fix,” said Bruno Kurtic, CEO of Bedrock Data.

“Bedrock Data finds the owner, sends the issue to the tools they already use, answers their questions inside the ticket and verifies the result. Security teams keep control of the rules and the audit trail, and those curves no longer diverge because remediation now operates at scale.”

Federated remediation runs through existing ITSM systems enterprises already use

Enterprises already track and resolve issues in Jira and ServiceNow, and their teams know those systems. Bedrock Data orchestrates those same systems, federating remediation to data owners at enterprise scale. There is no new tool to deploy and no new training for the people who make the fixes. Security teams can extend or override the default routing with rules written in natural language, for example “send findings on this AWS account to the cloud platform team, unless the finding involves access permissions, then route it to the identity and access team.”

Routing runs continuously as scans find new exposures, so remediation is an ongoing program rather than a one-time cleanup. The data owner makes the fix. Bedrock Data automates the workflow and verifies that each remediation has been applied.

Bedrock Data handles three steps in the remediation workflow:

Bedrock Data findings create tickets and route them to owners. Bedrock Data AI examines each exposure and explains it in context, so the owner understands the problem without a manual investigation. Tickets use the format the customer configures, including custom fields.

Bedrock Data AI answers questions inside the ticket while it is open, for example, “Who has access to this file?”

Bedrock Data policy engine tracks the ticket to closure. When the owner marks the ticket resolved, Bedrock Data validates the fix. If the exposure is gone, the ticket stays closed. If the exposure remains, Bedrock Data reopens the ticket with the reason. If Bedrock Data finds on its own that the exposure has been fixed or is no longer observed, it closes the ticket.

Where the fix is well defined, Bedrock Data can apply it directly. Customers can create a policy that revokes sharing on documents based on sensitivity and other criteria, without triggering a workflow, and notifies the data owner that the change was made. Data owners will be able to opt in to automatic remediation for exposure types that recur often and where they are comfortable automating the response.

“Data risk is my team’s responsibility, but lasting fixes have to come from the teams who run the systems every day,” said Manish Chandela, EVP Information Security, Risk and Privacy at Sportradar.

“Seeing the risk is table stakes. Reducing it means getting thousands of issues fixed without breaking the business. Bedrock Data puts each issue in front of the right owner, with the context to fix it, inside the tools they already use, and then proves the fix held. Remediation stops being a backlog my security team carries and becomes a program the whole company runs, with the evidence our board and auditors expect.”

Verified fixes deliver audit trails for PCI DSS 4.0.1, SOC 2 & NYDFS Part 500

Closing the loop changes what security leaders can show their board and auditors. Every exposure has an owner, a timeline and evidence that the fix held. Auditors working under PCI DSS 4.0.1 and SOC 2, and regulators enforcing NYDFS Part 500, expect that audit trail.

Bedrock Data produces it for every ticket it opens. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that organizations making extensive use of AI and automation in security operations had average breach costs $1.93 million lower and lifecycles 65 days shorter than organizations that didn’t use them.

Title: How to prioritize remediation after a pentest: a practitioner workflow
Context: Would you prioritize the“critical” flaw on an intranet site, containing no sensitive data that attackers could only reach if they’d already compromised your internal network
Full Text:
A practical pentest workflow combines CVSS, EPSS and business impact to validate findings, prioritize fixes and document remediation decisions.

Remediation prioritization after a pentest is the process of ranking and ordering security findings based on their risk, exploitability, and business impact. A penetration test can produce any number of findings, ranging from the very low (zero) to the very high (hundreds).

The security of the tested organization depends on the findings management processes addressing the most important results first.

CVSS alone misranks risk. Accurate prioritization relies on combining CVSS, EPSS, and business context.

68.4% of practitioners say a 500+ candidate finding set would strain the team or be unmanageable, so it’s important to validate first.

81.7% of practitioners see AI-generated findings that need significant manual validation, so validation with concrete proof remains essential.

Document every deprioritization, because that record counts as audit evidence.

Why aren’t CVSS scores alone enough to inform remediation?

When prioritizing pentest results, some practitioners rely solely on frameworks like the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). The logic is sound: the higher a vulnerability’s CVSS score is, the more risk it poses, and the sooner you should fix it, right?

Unfortunately, the reality is much more complicated. Boiling down a complex ecosystem of risk into a one-dimensional number means ignoring the wider business context. In the end, that means you fix vulnerabilities that pose serious theoretical risk first, while genuine exposures get pushed to the back of the queue.

Lets use two hypothetical vulnerabilities as an example.

Vulnerability A is an RCE flaw, CVSS 9.8, on an isolated intranet site.

Vulnerability B is a BOLA flaw, CVSS 6.5, on a public facing production payment API.

Now think about which one you would fix first.

Would you prioritize the“critical” flaw on an intranet site, containing no sensitive data that attackers could only reach if they’d already compromised your internal network? Or would you prioritize the “medium” flaw on an API that processes live credit card transactions, and that any script kiddie could manipulate?

Across an entire organization, or multiple organizations if you’re a consultant or MSP, those critical flaws can really pile up. In one AI pentesting survey of 158 base practitioners by Pentest-Tools.com, conducted in June 2026, 68.4% of respondents said a 500+ candidate finding set would strain the team or be unmanageable.

Approaching risk prioritization by trying to fix every “Critical” finding is going to exhaust you and your team. That’s when people make mistakes, and you end up with a major incident on your hands.

What separates a validated finding from a candidate?

That same distinction, in part, separates a candidate finding from a validated one. For example, vulnerability with a high CVSS score but near-zero exploitability should remain a candidate. To graduate a vulnerability from a candidate to a legally and technically validated finding, it must pass through a strict filter that involves three processes.

The first step is to eliminate as much administrative noise as possible. That means deduplicating findings and removing any that are obviously non-exploitable.

Then, you need to confirm exploitability. That typically means executing a safe, controlled attack path against the target environment to prove that a state change, data exposure, or privilege escalation can actually occur.

Finally, you need concrete evidence. A validated finding cannot rely on a generic tool’s “confidence score.” It must include comprehensive proof that a developer or auditor can immediately follow:

Technical proof tends to include HTTP request/response traces or specific error payloads.

Proof of impact includes things like screenshots or server-side telemetry demonstrating unauthorized data access.

Now, many vendors are going to claim that AI-generated findings ease the strain of exploit validation. In many cases, they’re telling the truth. But as with any AI technology, a healthy level of skepticism is important. According to the same study, 81.7% of respondents encounter AI-generated findings that need significant manual exploit validation at least sometimes.

How do CVSS, EPSS and business context combine into a ranking?

Together, CVSS, Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) scores, and business context create a single risk ranking that reflects real-world danger to the tested organization.

CVSS, as mentioned earlier, measures theoretical severity. It tells you how bad a flaw is in a vacuum, but is entirely blind to context. EPSS measures probability. It tells you how likely an attacker is to exploit a flaw in the wild over the next 30 days, but doesn’t measure the potential impact of an exploitation.

Business context measures operational impact. It tells you the value of the affected asset, how easily an attacker can reach a flaw, and what they can steal. It tells you nothing, however, about the threat itself. Ultimately, business context is expressed as residual risk, the danger left over after you factor in your existing defenses. Calculating it relies on measuring four factors:

Exposure: Whether a server is open to the public internet.

User count: How many people use a system.

Data sensitivity: Whether the system holds sensitive information.

Compensating controls: Whether you have firewalls or antivirus tools actively blocking the attack path.

By checking these boxes, you won’t waste time fixing a “Critical” bug locked in an empty, disconnected server. Instead, you’ll prioritize the “Medium” bug on your public checkout page that hackers are actively trying to breach.

What goes first when dev time is limited?

Sometimes, you’re not going to have much time for remediation. That’s natural. In those situations, prioritize validated findings with high threat activity (EPSS score) and critical business exposure. They’re the findings that pose the most threat to your organization.

Prioritization done well is itself evidence. A ranked, validated list, with a written reason for what was deprioritized, is what a team can defend later.

You’ll need to record the owner (the specific individual accepting the risk), the date of the decision, the technical operational basis for deprioritization (such as an active compensating control), and a hard review date for re-evaluation.

Why does the ranked list count as audit evidence?

A prioritized ranking list counts as valid audit evidence because it proves compliance alignment with several major security frameworks. For example:

ISO 27001 A.8.8 demands that organizations evaluate real-world exposure, take targeted corrective actions, and retain objective evidence that the remediation loop has successfully closed.

PCI DSS 11.4 mandates that penetration testing actively validates and exploits findings, with formal retesting conducted after significant organizational changes.

SOC 2 CC7.1 relies on this documentation to confirm that an organization maintains systemic operational consistency and rigorous vulnerability triage over time.

A ranked, validated list also gives MSPs and MSSPs a clear, auditable record of truth that clients can either accept or challenge with their own evidence. This transparency ensures both sides agree on which real-world risks need to be addressed first.

What does a defensible ranking record contain?

A defensible ranking record contains the validated asset identification, its technical CVSS severity, its real-world EPSS probability, the active compensating controls defining its residual list, the formal sign-off from the risk owner, and the targeted review schedule.

Title: Fresh WordPress Vulnerability in Attackers’ Crosshairs
Context: Threat actors started exploiting a new high-severity WordPress vulnerability within hours of patches rolling out, Defiant warns
Full Text:
Threat actors started exploiting a new high-severity WordPress vulnerability within hours of patches rolling out, Defiant warns.

Patched on October 28 in WordPress 7.1.4, the security defect impacts the WordPress update process and can be exploited for remote code execution.

According to Defiant, it is a race condition in WordPress’s Core update process that can be exploited without authentication. The attack complexity, however, is high. No CVE identifier has been assigned to the vulnerability yet.

The weakness stems from predictable, web-accessible staging paths during the upgrades. New files are unpacked into a predictable directory that is accessible from the web on many servers.

“The attacker needs a full-package update containing the installer files, public web and PHP access to the staging tree, a predictable or discovered staging path, and enough time to complete the attack before WordPress cleans up the temporary files,” Defiant explains.

According to the web security firm, threat actors are already attempting to exploit the vulnerability, polling the vulnerable paths repeatedly in their attempts to hit the seconds-long exploitability window.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

While an attacker does not need an account on the site to exploit the flaw, they do need “to hit a very narrow window while WordPress is unpacking a complete Core update,” Defiant says.

To address the security bug, WordPress now randomizes the staging directory, adds an index guard, and prevents the unsafe promotion of staged configuration data.

“Wordfence telemetry shows that threat actors are already actively attempting to exploit the vulnerability. The first match for our new firewall rule arrived nine minutes after deployment. During the first 21 hours, we recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged setup-config.php installer paths,” Defiant says.

Wordfence has not reported successful compromises.

Fixes for the vulnerability were included in WordPress 7.1.4 and backported to branches through WordPress 4.7.

WordPress 7.1.4 includes patches for 22 security defects, including several XSS flaws, interactivity API issues, an unauthenticated information disclosure bug, and an authorization weakness, and also updates the bundled root certificates to reflect the recent eMudhra revocation.

Title: Chinese Actor Compromises US Government Network Via Chained PHP2Shell Exploit
Context: The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9...
Full Text:
A suspected Chinese nation-state actor chained the PHP2Shell exploit with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access to 25 Palo Alto Network (PAN) firewall and management servers.

The campaign rooted 25 PAN servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, according to an investigation by cyber defense platform provider Dream.

There was a particular focus on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment, resulting in persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

The Dream researchers noted a number of indicators of Chinese nation-state involvement in the campaign, including the narrow focus of the targeting.

“Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts,” they commented.

In addition, a number of tools used in the campaign, such as the large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi, and the internet reconnaissance platform FOFA, are Chinese-based services.

The Dream researchers highlighted the “automated and efficient” nature of the exploits, which took place from 23-24 October, including the targeting of specific PAN-OS versions.

“This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing,” they said.

“There was a clear-cut focus on government targets,” the researchers added.

Palo Alto Networks Confirm Compromise

Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 verified Dream’s findings in a blog published on October 29. It said that around .02% of its global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and were impacted by the campaign.

All the affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

“Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available,” Unit 42 wrote.

Palo Alto Networks has recommended that customers review its mitigations for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and apply patches immediately.

Chained Exploits Achieves Access in Under 15 Minutes

The attackers developed two separate exploits and chained them together into one request to target the PAN-OS servers. One of these was the widely reported ‘PHP2Shell’ exploit, made up of two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The exploit, which affects the PHP server-side programming language used by around 70% of websites, was leaked in October before a scheduled disclosure and release of patches. This resulted in many websites being taken down, including by governments, while emergency fixes were applied.

Read now: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

In the campaign identified by Dream, the threat actors tailored the exploit specifically for PAN-OS, targeting PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server.

This was chained to a second exploit, a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem known as Fragnesia and tracked as CVE-2026-46300. The attackers used this flaw to overwrite authentication rules, allowing root access to be achieved without a password.

“Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes,” Dream explained.

Threat Actor Narrows Focus to US Government Servers

Once the exploit was ready, the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. It narrowed down its targeting through a number of stages, using scanners to identify which devices were connected to the internet, their geographic location and what PAN-OS version they were running. The latter was focused on the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30.

This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls located in the US, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.

These targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target.

Of the 240 targets, 24 firewalls were successfully rooted. For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker only planted a webshell and did not carry out any further post-exploitation activity.

However, the two other firewalls, which belonged a US government-affiliated environment, saw the attackers establish persistent access. This included building an 8-port reverse SSH tunnel, which connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure.

The attackers quickly used its access to one of the government servers to compromise a third government server via same PHP2Shell and Fragnesia exploit chain. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

As this third server centrally managed all of the government organization’s firewalls, compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials and network settings.

This allowed the threat actor to exploit the server’s connectivity to Active Directory to steal data such as credentials, although the researchers cannot determine the full extent of the accessed data.

“What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure,” they warned.

Dream said the campaign demonstrates that finding a vulnerability is only one part of identifying weaknesses across an organization’s systems, particularly with the growing use of chained exploits.

“Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise,” the firm added.

Title: Why Urgent Security Fixes Aren't Fixed. Observe, Prove, Act, Confirm Gets Them Moving
Context: The alert is critical
Full Text:
The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything.

Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits.

Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts.

The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect

Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today.

In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments.

Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today.

Figure 1. Operational pressures and configuration drift can delay enforcement.

Build Confidence Before Enforcement

Safe remediation follows four stages: Observe, Prove, Act, and Confirm. Evidence carries the proposed response through each stage, with review and approval where required.

Observation starts with data your security and IT systems already produce. Vulnerability findings, IPS traffic, device utilization, endpoint policies, and configuration states show what surrounds the proposed change.

Then comes proof, and the method fits the technology. An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode, giving teams evidence about false positives and performance before it progresses to Prevent. Operating system hardening can use a selected test group, with each host rechecked after execution. Endpoint settings can be assessed against the vendor's hardening baseline.

The decision becomes specific to your environment. Security teams explain the protection they expect. Infrastructure and application owners judge the effect on the systems they run.

Figure 2. Validation connects environmental evidence with approval, execution, and confirmation.

Use Existing Controls While Waiting For a Permanent Fix

Patching remains essential for addressing the underlying vulnerability. Testing, coordination, and deployment schedules can extend the time before a patch reaches production, creating a period when additional protection may be needed.

An existing IPS signature or virtual patch can help block the relevant exploit path during that period. Correlating vulnerability data with control coverage shows whether a suitable protection exists and whether it is inactive, in Detect mode, or already enforced.

That context helps teams select the response. A protection awaiting enforcement may be a candidate for validation and activation. An exposure without a compensating control may require urgent patching or another action.

The remediation record should distinguish interim protection from a permanent fix. A compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while the underlying vulnerability remains open and requires follow through.

Keep Approval and Execution Connected

Once an action has been evaluated, organizations can require approval of its scope or permit automated execution through configured workflows. The approved change then runs through the system responsible for the affected control.

IPS changes can use the security management server, operating system hardening can use existing patch management infrastructure, and supported endpoint changes can use the vendor API. This approach lets teams work through the technologies already deployed.

Confirmation completes the process. Policy installation can establish that an IPS protection reached enforcement. Host checks can verify a hardening change. Execution records can show failed or pending actions that still need attention, alongside the user, timestamp, and associated exposure.

Measure the Protection That Follows

Success should include evidence that the intended protection is active after execution. Subsequent security events can show whether a newly enabled control blocked activity associated with the exposure.

Across the measured organizations, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. Over one month, protections applied through remediation subsequently blocked 703.56 million attacks, including 21 million within 24 hours of remediation. These results describe the analyzed environments and provide evidence of protection following enforcement.

Figure 3. Remediation outcomes across the environments measured in the white paper.

Make Safe Remediation Part of Exposure Management

Prioritization establishes where action should begin. Safe remediation gives teams a controlled path for carrying that decision into production, with evidence supporting the proposed change and confirmation showing its result.

Check Point Exposure Management connects exposure prioritization with environmental validation, controlled execution, and confirmation through existing security technologies. Security teams can use that process to reduce exposure while evaluating the operational impact of each response.
