Title: Fake IT help desk callers got by on little more than names and email addresses
Context: More about attack Cisco Claude Code cybercrime cybersecurity malware Microsoft Teams ransomware report scams Social engineering threats vishing voice recognition Share Featured...
Full Text:
Attackers posing as IT help desk staff contacted employees by phone, email and Microsoft Teams in the third quarter of 2026 and talked them into opening remote access sessions, Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) found across several engagements. In one case, that access ended in ransomware.

They knew names and email addresses

“The attackers appeared to know employee names and email addresses, as they contacted users directly by email and Teams and used identities that mimicked legitimate company help desk personnel,” Aliza Johnson, a researcher at Cisco Talos, told Help Net Security.

“They likely had broad, generic knowledge of how IT support interactions typically work as they successfully guided victims into Teams sessions and remote access and showed familiarity with common enterprise platforms like Quick Assist; however, there is no clear evidence of deep company- or victim-specific profiling beyond basic identity and contact information,” she said.

The targets were not limited to senior or technical staff. “The contacted victims varied both across organizations and within the same organization, suggesting the actors were primarily seeking any susceptible user for initial access rather than targeting specific individuals for privileged or specialized access,” Johnson said. Protections built around administrators and executives would have missed many of the people these attackers reached.

“Some of these attacks appear opportunistic. In one case, the victim called a fake IT support number shown in a generic browser-based scam pop-up that did not appear to spoof the victim organization, and later granted the adversary remote access. In another, the attacker launched two phishing waves, likely expecting that at least one target would be compromised,” she said.

In the first of those cases, the victim dialed the number.

One Quick Assist session, then ransomware

In an engagement involving VYPR, a ransomware variant Talos considers new and still operationally immature, the actor used a voice phishing call to get a user to start a Microsoft Quick Assist session. Talos could not confirm what the caller said. RMM software already on the network then ran PowerShell commands that downloaded and installed a Microsoft Software Installer package from a remote IP address.

The VYPR operators built on older leaked Conti-derived source code with minimal changes. To knock out EDR tools, they loaded trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, a technique called bring your own vulnerable driver, and dropped an unusually large number of them, possibly as backups. Data exfiltration ran over multiple days, which Talos does not commonly see in ransomware cases. The group had no data leak site until after the engagement ended.

A script went after Claude Code credentials

On a separate macOS endpoint, infected through a trojanized application, attackers scripted a search of the keychain, the Mac’s built-in password store, for credentials tied to Anthropic’s Claude Code assistant.

“We observed an attacker-controlled account executing the following command to target Anthropic Claude Code credentials, possibly for credential dumping. There was no indication of the actor using these credentials,” Johnson said. The command was /bin/sh -c security find-generic-password -a “[USER_NAME]” -w -s “Claude Code-credentials”. Its -w flag tells macOS to print the stored secret.

In another case, an insider hired under false credentials used privileged access to install GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code. Investigators found no evidence of malicious activity or data theft. The employee’s developer access, which included cloning repositories and connecting to databases, could have let them use those tools to automate malicious actions.

Logs, MFA and help desk checks

Talos IR recommends phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys in place of push and SMS prompts. It also recommends requiring help desk verification before employees can enroll new MFA methods themselves.

Among engagements where the entry point was known, phishing remained the top initial access method at 37 percent, down from over 50 percent last quarter. Exploitation of public-facing applications followed at 33 percent. Credential and secret management problems and weak authentication or MFA each turned up in 33 percent of engagements.

Insufficient logging led the list of weaknesses, appearing in over 40 percent of engagements, partly because attackers deleted logs and partly because customers had not retained or configured them. Talos recommends at least 90 days of centralized log retention, with logs forwarded off each device so they survive tampering and rebuilds.

Title: What exactly is ISOC? And what does it mean for you?
Context: The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection...
Full Text:
Gartner recently released a new category of assessing security tools: the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC). Even though SIEM isn’t going anywhere, a rapidly evolving threat landscape is forcing a shift in industry logic that is reflected in the emergence of this new category.

For years, SIEM has dominated as an all-encompassing category. But SIEMs are no longer sufficient to collect data, support investigations, and manage incidents; instead, the SIEM has separated into distinct architectural layers. SIEM platforms, which remain the security system of record for collecting, normalizing, searching, and analyzing event data, are now distinct from the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) solutions. ISOC is tasked with unifying detection, investigation, case management, and response across security domains and security/observability data pipelines.

As AI empowers attackers and more threat landscapes emerge, this stratification becomes essential. Data management, analytics, and operational response are now separate problems, and, as a result, demand separate solutions. This is where ISOC finds its space: to reduce costs, latency, and operational friction.

The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection investigation and response (TDIR) capability. Reduced complexity is especially key for lean teams who prioritize efficiency and streamlined workflows, and the goal of ISOC is to reduce the friction that comes with conglomerating a wide variety of different security tools to contrive full visibility.

In short, ISOC addresses the pain point that every security team faces today. Instead of juggling an array of disjointed tools provided by different vendors, a single vendor streamlines the production of a providing a flexible and adaptable, yet holistic and transparent security solution. This gives a business the efficiency and flexibility to reduce costs, reduce deployment time, and allay growing SIEM complexities.

Common features of the ISOC, as Gartner writes, include native detection and response services, incident case management, and extended case management of data ingestion. ISOC should reduce the friction between security tools and the latency between data, context, decision, and action. Machine-speed responses are more essential than ever in an age where attackers are all armed with the most advanced AI tools.

Latency challenges in Native Detection and Response, Security Data Ownership, Incident Case Management, Cross-Domain Correlation, and Automation and Agentic Response, and Open Ingestion and Response Fabric are becoming issues that business can’t afford to ignore.

Detection and response must operate on the same underlying security data, not through loosely connected point products. Native controls reduce latency between signal, correlation, investigation, and action. ISOC starts with control of the data layer: ingesting, normalizing, enriching, retaining, and making telemetry available for detection and AI reasoning. If the platform does not control the data model, every downstream analytic or agent is working through integration boundaries.

Alerts, entities, evidence, timelines, and analyst actions are assembled into a persistent incident object. The case becomes the operational unit for investigation and response rather than individual alerts. Endpoint, network, identity, cloud, application, and third-party telemetry must be correlated against a common schema and context model. This is what allows weak individual signals to become a high-confidence attack story.

Automation should operate directly against normalized data and incident context, enabling AI agents and playbooks to investigate, enrich, recommend, and execute actions without repeatedly rebuilding context. ISOC must connect broadly to existing security infrastructure while minimizing translation and API friction.

The objective is a common data and control plane where third-party tools contribute signals and become response surfaces.

Looking ahead

As the SIEM market grows, the market share will be divided to include ISOC vendors, who will expand their offerings to include coverage in identity, cloud/Saas management, and email security.

The market is only reflecting the dynamics that security teams have been feeling for years, which has been exacerbated exponentially by the adoption of AI by threat agents. Simply agglomerating more tools is neither strategic, nor effective. And a single vendor approach is key to striking the right balance between efficacy and simplicity. Finding the right tool portfolio now means finding the right vendor.

The market confirms what Stellar Cyber postulated: modern operational needs demand integrated, unified capabilities. From setting an open integration standard to incorporating AI-native capabilities, ISOC environments are meant to simplify operations without compromising coverage or visibility.

Anticipating the limitations of fragmented security stacks leads to natively unified operational platforms. By normalizing raw data from any source through high-context schema technology, modern ISOC solutions deliver the precise, consolidated out-of-the-box outcomes now expected in the market.

An AI SOC that starts with somebody else’s alert is already too late.

Stellar Cyber collects and normalizes telemetry, detects suspicious activity, correlates evidence, builds cases, investigates incidents, triages findings, and drives response from the same security architecture. That gives people and AI access to the evidence behind the alert – not just the alert itself.

Title: Scammers rebuild fake shopping sites within hours of a takedown
Context: Attackers place phishing pages on compromised websites, exploiting the reputation attached to an established address
Full Text:
One retail scam used more than 1,200 look-alike .shop domains sharing a single IP address. The sites reused HTML, JavaScript and payment-page designs intended to harvest card numbers, expiry dates and security codes, according Akamai’s Fraud and Abuse Report 2026.

A ticket scam used a similar setup. Several websites impersonating official ticketing and hospitality portals for a major sporting event were designed to route payment and personal information to the same collection system. Some checkout flows requested passport or identity-document details under the pretext of arranging ticket delivery or event access.

The addresses gave criminals multiple entrances to the same operation. If one domain was blocked or removed, another could continue directing information to the shared collection system. Stolen information could then support payment fraud, account takeover and identity abuse.

Following the offer

In one documented campaign, a paid social media advert directed consumers to a counterfeit app marketplace. Visitors then downloaded a malicious app that collected sensitive information and abused device permissions.

An example of a recruitment scam (Source: Akamai)

Recruitment scams exploited the expectation that applicants would submit personal details. Fake hiring content appeared across four major social platforms, directing people toward phishing forms designed to collect sensitive information.

Replacing websites within hours

Operators register look-alike addresses in bulk and leave them dormant for weeks or months. This can help a domain build a clean reputation before a scam launches.

Some sites vary their content according to the visitor. An automated security scanner may receive harmless material while an intended victim sees the fraudulent offer. Location and browser information can determine which page appears.

Attackers place phishing pages on compromised websites, exploiting the reputation attached to an established address. Reused phishing kits, hosting arrangements and payment infrastructure allow replacement sites to appear within hours of a website being removed.

Turning passwords into purchases

Credentials exposed through scams and data breaches can provide access to existing accounts.

Automated programs test credentials exposed in earlier breaches across other services. When someone has reused a password, attackers may gain access to saved payment methods, reward points or personal details. They can then change account details and recovery settings to make it harder for the owner to regain control.

In a 30-day sample spanning July and August 2026, Akamai classified 26.6% of recorded login attempts as high or critical risk. These attempts were flagged as potential threats requiring investigation.

Account verification requests accounted for 40% of the high- or critical-risk login traffic examined. Such requests can help attackers establish whether an email address belongs to an account before attempting credential stuffing.

Victims may discover the theft through a purchase notification, missing points or a password that stops working. Businesses handle disputed transactions, reimbursement requests and the work of restoring access.

Account opening abuse starts at registration

Criminals create accounts to collect welcome bonuses, exploit promotions, test stolen cards and reserve products for resale. 8.3% of account creation attempts were linked to suspected fraud in 2025.

Small transactions through fake accounts help criminals check if stolen cards work before attempting larger purchases. Businesses can incur processing fees, chargebacks and penalties. Fake accounts can be used to hoard limited stock, reducing availability for shoppers and supplying resellers.

Verification creates another opportunity. In SMS pumping schemes, automated requests trigger registration or password-reset messages to premium-rate international numbers, generating charges for the business sending them. Some operations involve rogue telecom carriers that share the resulting revenue with the fraudsters.

Title: Smart TVs can harbor unpatched security flaws and track what you watch
Context: The detections include scans stopped at routers, attempted logins and exploit patterns detected and blocked
Full Text:
Smart TVs and connected plugs accounted for a large share of recorded security weaknesses in household devices, according to Bitdefender’s 2026 IoT Security Landscape Report. The analysis covered approximately 10.4 million protected home routers between January and September.

Televisions represented 22.7% of vulnerability observations, followed by smart plugs at 22.4% linked with a known software flaw.

Top vulnerable device families (Source: Bitdefender)

Household electronics can stay in use for five to ten years, while their security support may last two to four years. Once updates stop, TVs, plugs and home storage systems can remain connected with unresolved flaws.

Automated scans dominate detected attack activity

Automated port scans accounted for 90.1% of detected attack-category events, with approximately 4.85 billion scan attempts recorded over the nine-month period.

These probes check for accessible services, including remote desktop connections, remote login services and administration interfaces. Finding an open service can provide a starting point for further attempts to gain access, but a scan does not establish that someone broke in.

Password brute-force attempts accounted for approximately 8.7% of attack-category events. Of the 466.6 million brute-force events reported, approximately 455 million targeted Remote Desktop Protocol, commonly used to access Windows computers remotely.

The detections include scans stopped at routers, attempted logins and exploit patterns detected and blocked. They do not establish how many households experienced a successful intrusion.

Free TV apps can share household connections

Citing findings from security firm Spur, the report describes software bundled into free smart-TV apps that can turn televisions into residential proxies after users accept consent terms.

The household’s broadband connection then carries a customer’s traffic for uses marketed as web scraping, advertising verification and market research. Websites receiving that traffic see the household’s public internet address.

Accepting an app’s terms authorizes the sharing, even though users may not understand how their connection will be used.

Viewing data and household profiling

Televisions can also collect information about what people watch and the devices around them.

Gamers Nexus findings cited in the report describe LG televisions collecting viewing data, voice recordings, geographical location, details of other devices on the local network and information about nearby wireless networks.

Automatic Content Recognition, or ACR, identifies material displayed on a television by matching content samples against a reference database. The technology is used to support personalized advertising.

Connected equipment can occupy several roles: an attack target, a proxy carrying outside traffic, a sensor collecting information or a foothold inside a network.

“Once inside, criminals can stay hidden and move laterally across the home network,” warned Chandan Nandakumaraiah, head of product and cybersecurity at NETGEAR.

Full Text: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. It also promised to cover any losses. About an hour ago at the time of writing, Binance posted an update on the incident that explains what it thinks went wrong. “Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” the post states. Binance hasn’t explained how attackers gained access to the engineer’s laptop. The scant details provided make it hard to rule out a successful phishing attack, or perhaps a supply chain attack on a package the developer used. Binance says it will spill once it knows exactly what happened. Cryptocurrency outfits have a long and inglorious history of falling victim to cyberattacks, perhaps starting with the 2011 raid on Mt Gox, to incidents allegedly perpetrated by nation-states, and, just last week, another situation possibly involving an AI-powered attacker. ®

Title: Binance Suffers Security Breach Affecting $6.3 Billion in Assets, Nearly $3 Billion Frozen
Context: 2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as...
Full Text:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that a "security incident" on its platform has impacted about $6.3 billion worth of assets.

The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said nearly $3 billion of those assets have been frozen on-chain so far.

Tether and Circle said they have frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT and 800 million USDC related to the incident, respectively. The Arbitrum Security Council is said to have executed a transaction to freeze about $30.5 million from the Binance Exploit.

"Initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," Binance said in an update.

The company said there is no evidence of a wallet private key leak, adding it will cover all losses from the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) fund and its own funds.

Out of an abundance of caution, Binance has also taken the following steps -

Temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed

Revoked the affected address authorization;

Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds

"We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," Binance said.

In an update, Binance said it expects withdrawals to resume in 48 hours, after its team "completes a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses."

The development makes it the biggest cryptocurrency heist recorded to date, surpassing the theft of about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025. The incident was subsequently attributed to North Korea.

"Our current estimate on the amount stolen is approximately $5.912 billion at time of theft, nearly 4x the amount stolen in the next largest crypto heist," blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis said in an X post.

Attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor

TRM Labs has attributed the record-breaking hack targeting Binance to threat actors from North Korea with high confidence. The blockchain analytics company linked it to TraderTraitor, which was also behind the 2025 Bybit heist, based on what it said were "robust on and off-chain intelligence sources."

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," TRM Labs said.

"The laundering observed so far, built on large swaps through market makers and lending protocols, differs from the bridge-heavy pattern that followed Bybit."

TRM Labs said preparation for the attack was underway at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers taking over a Binance hot wallet to send its "entire balance to an attacker-controlled address" -

At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted a single transaction containing 50 authorizations. Each was signed by the Binance hot wallet, and each pointed it to a sweeper contract that accepts instructions only from the operator. Every wallet keeps a running count of its transactions, called a nonce, and an authorization works only at the count the wallet has reached at the moment it executes. The Binance hot wallet processes a steady flow of withdrawals, so its count keeps moving forward. By preparing signatures for 50 consecutive counts, the attacker guaranteed that one would still be valid when the transaction executed. One matched, which was all the attacker needed. The signatures were produced in advance as a batch.

Three minutes and 24 seconds after the delegation, the operator instructed the Binance hot wallet to send its entire balance to an attacker-controlled address. That single transaction moved 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT.

The most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance's hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains. The batch of 50 pre-signed authorizations suggests the access may have been limited in time, or that signatures had to be requested through a system. Binance has yet to publish a root cause.

Chainalysis has also linked the hack to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) with a high degree of confidence, stating it "observed funds stolen by DPRK in last month's Bitget exploit commingling with funds stolen from Binance."

"The ability to quickly identify and understand illicit activity is increasingly important as North Korea increasingly uses sophisticated automation to move and obscure stolen funds," the company noted earlier this month. "Investigators must keep pace with these tactics while applying the judgment and expertise needed to make sense of complex on-chain activity."

So far, Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial have frozen about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council has frozen about $30 million in ETH and ARB. The attacker continues to retain control of more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, plus smaller amounts on other chains.

Elliptic's chief scientist and founder, Dr. Tom Robinson, told The Hacker News cryptocurrency assets with a total value of $6.43 billion were stolen from Binance, assessing North Korea-linked actors perpetrated the theft, citing similar tradecraft and co-mingling of funds from another hack attributed to them.

"Rather than stealing Binance's private keys, the attacker appears to have been able to get Binance's own systems to sign transactions on their behalf," Elliptic said.

"This closely resembles the Bybit theft, in which North Korean hackers compromised a developer's machine at the wallet provider Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the transaction that Bybit's signers approved. In both cases, it was the infrastructure and people around the wallets that were compromised, not the cryptography."

The company also noted that 2.84 billion of funds have been frozen, while the attacker is in control of around $3.33 billion of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer and are spread across about 43 wallet addresses. This includes 511,861 ETH (1.15 billion), 18,270 BTC ($1.43 billion), 233 million XRP, and 670 million TRX.

The links to North Korea are based on the following factors -

Funds stolen from Binance and funds linked to the Bitget exploit have been sent to the same Ethereum address, 0x15104a9ce0f08a8f0075a0869ae80e795fe0feb7.

Attackers funded their wallet with three small Tornado Cash withdrawals, tested the attack code in advance, and executed pre-signed transactions in a single burst, similar to what was observed in Bybit and KelpDAO exploits.

The likely use of social engineering to trick employees into executing malware under the pretext of a coding test or a bogus project, a technique employed in DMM Bitcoin and Bybit hacks.

Despite these commonalities, Elliptic has urged caution in attributing the activity to North Korea, citing deviations from previously observed laundering patterns in terms of speed and methodology, as well as the absence of a root cause.

"DPRK launderers typically swap stolen stablecoins for native assets within minutes," Robinson said. "The attacker held the stolen USDT for 37 minutes on Ethereum and 46 minutes on Tron without converting most of it. North Korean-linked groups typically move funds faster and more efficiently. The use of market makers and DeFi lending protocols differs from the bridge-heavy laundering seen after the Bybit hack."

"Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions."

"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual."

The company has since revealed that its ongoing investigation has "uncovered additional points of breach" that goes beyond the compromised laptop, and that it's "doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it."

Title: PHP2Shell plus Fragnesia: A dangerous new route from web server to root
Context: The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide
Full Text:
The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned of a high severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers are chaining with PHP2Shell bugs in the wild.

Identified as CVE-2026-46300, it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions.

Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino, CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee.

“PHP2Shell allows for remote access, but that access is typically limited by the account used to run the PHP service,” he said. “By chaining with CVE-2026-46300, that attacker can get unlimited access.”

Researchers at Dream Security have discovered that this attack has already been used to breach 25 servers, including three affiliated with the US government.

Federal agencies have been ordered to patch the flaw, which is known as Fragnesia.

Anatomy of an attack

PHP is a widely-used, open source server-side scripting language that serves as the backbone for websites like WordPress, which powers 43% of the web, as well as Mailchimp, Drupal, parts of Slack and Zoom, and numerous others.

Last week, the PHP Foundation disclosed two flaws in the PHP scripting language that could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both rated a critical 9.2 in severity on the common vulnerability and scoring system (CVSS). The two vulnerabilities are collectively tracked as PHP2Shell. As a result of the disclosure, some government and enterprise websites shut down entirely while awaiting patches.

CVE-2026-46300, dubbed Fragnesia, is a new development in the saga. It is identified as part of the Dirty Frag vulnerability class, a set of local privilege escalation (LPE) bugs in the Linux kernel.

The Dream researchers described an attack they tracked in the wild, in which threat actors built a persistent tunnel into an internal network “within hours.” They developed two distinct exploits, stringing them together to target any Palo Alto Network firewall running a vulnerable build of PAN-OS, and achieved root access in a single HTTP request without any credentials.

After rooting the firewalls, the threat actor launched attacks against Active Directory (AD), giving them the ability to extract credentials and discover hidden files, folders, and other sensitive resources, according to the Dream researchers. The researchers confirmed that the threat actor then possessed a full AD user group listing and “complete organizational blueprint,” private keys and complete network topology, including the IP, hostname, server role, and VPN gateway, and had accessed decrypted service account credentials allowing direct AD queries at any time.

The adversarial actor also parked nearly two dozen firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, “ready for exploitation at any time.” The Dream researchers noted that the breach did not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack, but did include some AI-assisted tooling like Claude Code and AI-powered offensive security platforms configured with Chinese large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi.

“The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure,” the Dream researchers wrote.

Plenty of material for attackers to work with

The two PHP bugs gave an attacker code execution privileges using the web service account, and the kernel bug is what turned that into root, explained Aaron Beardslee, manager of threat research at Securonix, who noted, “The kernel bug writes its payload into the page cache rather than to disk.”

Once an attacker has the ability to execute code, the damage they can do depends on the permissions and credentials available to that process, he explained. Application configuration files, database credentials, and access to internal services can provide “plenty of material for an attacker to work with.” They may also be able to execute commands, retrieve additional tooling or establish persistence.

“Web servers have an unfortunate habit of knowing more about the rest of the environment than anyone intended,” he pointed out.

The chain’s post-access sequence, as described by the researchers, was: Root the perimeter host, stand up a reverse Secure Shell (SSH) tunnel to an internal management server, recover a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) service account credential, then “enumerate domain users and groups, spray passwords, and attempt to create backdoor accounts in Active Directory.”

PHP has “been holding up a substantial chunk” of the internet for decades, and these vulnerabilities live in the runtime itself, Beardslee noted. An enterprise’s WordPress installation can be fully patched, plugins can be current, but the underlying PHP process can still be vulnerable to unauthenticated code execution.

The reported victim count (25 servers so far, mostly firewall appliances, on a government affiliated network) is the part everyone will quote, but it is not the interesting part, he said. Counts differ, and attribution is “openly contested.” None of them is what matters to defenders.

“What matters is that the privilege escalation step in this chain is invisible to disk-based integrity checking,” Beardslee said, “and that the standard remediation advice destroys the evidence of it.”

Remediation

Unfortunately, CVE-2026-46300 is a low-level Linux kernel bug, so the only remedy is to upgrade to a patched Linux version, said DataBee’s Miserendino. There are some options short of full patching, but those could break the system, or at a minimum require IPSec encapsulating security payload (ESP) to be disabled. But that can introduce additional flaws.

“Patch the kernel, and capture memory first on anything you suspect,” Beardslee recommended, noting that the Fragnesia fix is not included in the Dirty Frag patches. “The triage order matters more here than it usually does, because the reboot is what erases the evidence.”

As well, audit the core built-in kernel modules esp4 and esp6, which are responsible for handling the IPsec ESP network protocol, on every internet-facing Linux host, he advised. If nothing terminates IPsec there, “the modules have no business being loaded,” and unloading them removes the vulnerability path without waiting for a maintenance window.

And check which hosts hold a directory service credential, then alert of LDAP binds from anything that isn’t on that list, he said: “This is the control that catches the chain at the stage where it stops being a web server problem and starts being a domain problem.” Further, he said, re-point identity detections at “the source, not the tool.”

Title: A deep dive into China’s Volt Typhoon suggests it is preparing for an assault on infrastructure
Context: ” The report, released on Wednesday, said that Silent Train is built around “rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that are exploited on...
Full Text:
In a deep dive into the Silent Train attack tactic used by China’s Volt Typhoon cybercrime group, Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs highlighted evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as “strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises.”

The report, released on Wednesday, said that Silent Train is built around “rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation and continuously refreshed. This approach allowed Volt Typhoon to carry out exploitation and post-exploitation activity securely while reducing the risk of detection, attribution, and disruption.”

Multiple intrusions via Silent Train have been confirmed in the wild, Lumen said, all on high value targets.

Its report described at least four confirmed and one likely zero-day vulnerabilities exploited by Volt Typhoon, which targeted network and endpoint management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators and control plane infrastructure that provide visibility, administration and access across enterprise and customer environments. It noted that victims included telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, emergency services and other essential operations.

Lumen said the nature of these victims “indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region.”

Although the Silent Train attack has been in the wild for years and was tracked by various cybersecurity teams, the level of operational details that Lumen reported Wednesday went well beyond what had been known.

In fact, Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, who tracks this space, said the Lumen report “may be one of the most valuable pieces of research published this year.”

Key findings

Some of the report’s key findings described the surprising speed and efficiency of the attacks.

“Sessions were often remarkably efficient. Operators could exploit and assemble chains of devices in under two minutes, and on their way out they would leave no evidence for defenders to uncover,” Lumen said. “Their operational tempo suggests the use of a semi-automated, on-demand provisioning process.” But a strict process remained consistent throughout many attacks, it pointed out.

“Another noteworthy aspect was Volt Typhoon’s consistent assignment of specific device types to positions within Silent Train chains,” the report said. “We noticed that device types were reserved for specific operational roles that never deviated. Intelbras modems only appeared as overseas relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi devices served as US-based hops that interacted with victims. Similar patterns appeared across every other device type in Silent Train.”

It observed that, despite having enough global infrastructure to swap device types between overseas and US hops, Volt Typhoon maintained these fixed roles throughout three years of monitoring, and its VPS infrastructure also used separate providers and locations rather than a shared environment.

The report concluded that attack infrastructure “was deliberately compartmentalized across layers, complicating attribution and reducing the risk that access to one device or provider would expose more of the network. The underlying infrastructure changed constantly, but the architecture and role of each layer remained highly structured.”

Laying the foundation

Analysts and consultants noted that the attacks didn’t necessarily engage in damage or theft initially, but instead laid a foundation for a later attack.

“I wouldn’t say this is necessarily a novel approach, but it is a clever one,” said Sav Wheeler, malware research engineer at Malwarebytes. “Holding off on taking advantage of compromised resources until an opportunity presents itself is itself a strategic form of resource management.”

Mike Wilkes, enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, agreed that the delayed gratification is a dangerous attack group tactic.

“P0wning th,e control plane of telecommunications and critical infrastructure is both logical and, sadly, often rather easy” he said. “Why attack individual systems when you can compromise the infrastructure that manages, connects and authenticates them? The strategic objective isn’t necessarily immediate disruption. It’s establishing the ability to disrupt, manipulate or deny services at a time of geopolitical advantage.”

Dickson also agreed, saying that the published details show a pattern that “is not espionage for its own sake. It looks like access being banked for a crisis in the Pacific.”

Rethink defenses

“That breaks the usual defender playbook,” Dickson said. “A blocklist does nothing against an address that was a relay for four hours last Tuesday. The indicators expire before anyone can publish them. This is also a direct response to the KV-botnet takedown. Take out the bridge and they build a ferry.”

He added, “a network management console is built to see everything, reach everything, and change everything. Those are exactly the powers an attacker wants. We spent a decade building higher castle walls and then hung the master key ring by the gate.”

But it is the speed of Silent Train that worries Dickson the most. Although an enterprise can’t out-rotate an adversary that rebuilds its network in two minutes, “it can make the destination much harder to reach. Take every management console, SD-WAN orchestrator, and admin portal off the open internet and put it behind a VPN, a jump host, or a dedicated management network. Patch control plane technology first, not last,” he advised.

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the implications of the Silent Train deep dive will force CISOs to rethink much of their defensive strategies.

“IP-based defenses are nearing the end of their usefulness against this class of adversary. When the network origin is disposable, identity, behavior, and timing are what remain visible,” he said. “An adversary willing to burn an exploit on a router to protect an exploit on an SD-WAN orchestrator is telling defenders exactly how much that access is worth.”

Another concern, said Mahaptra, is revealed by the way Lumen was able to detect much of the attack methodology, something that will likely elude most enterprise SOCs.

“Lumen detected Silent Train because a backbone carrier can see the entire chain,” Mahapatra said. “No single enterprise ever sees more than its own segment. Organizations in the sectors on this victim list should formalize threat notification arrangements with their carriers, because the detection that worked here happened outside every victim’s network.”

He advised enterprises to also watch their own edge devices for outbound behavior. Lumen documented FortiGate and Cisco appliances, PRTG, CyberPanel and even Mirth Connect healthcare integration servers serving as final hops, some for one to three months, he pointed out; outbound SSH to unfamiliar hosts, reverse tunnels built with tools such as Chisel or FRP, and traffic on unusual high ports “can indicate that a company’s appliance is serving as the attacker’s domestic face for an intrusion elsewhere.”

Mark Child, an associate research director with IDC, also is concerned about the tactical methods of Silent Train.

“Silent Train abandons persistence,” Child said. “Instead of maintaining a permanent network, Volt Typhoon rapidly assembles and dismantles transient infrastructure. This makes it more effective against network-centric defenses: IP blocklists, threat-intel feeds of IOC addresses, geofencing, and takedowns. Those all assume infrastructure that sticks around.”

However, he noted, “it is not more effective against good endpoint and behavioral detection on the target.” No matter many hops there are, the exploitation, credential theft and admin-tool abuse still execute on the server.

“The real force multiplier is the choice of target,” he said. “Hitting a management platform delivers admin access to thousands of devices and trusted paths to downstream customers, with no lateral movement, which removes the lateral movement signals EDR usually relies on. For endpoint security teams, IP-based detection loses value here. Behavioral monitoring of privileged management servers, and what they do to endpoints, becomes the decisive control.”

Title: OpenAI doubles ChatGPT Pro usage limits after backlash over planned 50% cut
Context: 4 million installs caught hijacking searches Hackers exploit Cisco SD-WAN flaw to deploy custom KeyDrift malware CISA warns of Fragnesia Linux flaw chained in PHP2Shell attacks...
Full Text:
OpenAI says it won't reduce usage limits for the $100, $200, and $500 ChatGPT Pro plans, as well as Business Premium, and it also promised to keep Dots usage independent.

In a post on X, Tibo, who is the face of ChatGPT and Codex on X, confirmed that the changes take effect immediately and primarily affect ChatGPT Work and Codex, which share usage allowances under eligible subscriptions.

OpenAI had previously planned to reduce the included usage allowance for existing Pro 200 subscribers after October 29, despite keeping the subscription price at $200 per month.

However, OpenAI has now reversed that decision following customer feedback.

"We are doubling all usage limits for all Pro 100/200/500 tiers and Business Premium, effective today," Tibo announced on X.

"We heard your kind feedback and won’t be reducing usage limits for Pro 200, so your Work and Codex usage will stay the same."

OpenAI is also keeping extended usage limits for Dots

Alongside the subscription changes, OpenAI is continuing to offer extended usage limits for Dots, its always-on AI assistants.

"We're also going to continue offering extended limits for Dots for now, and usage of your dot will still continue to be separate from your default usage," the company explained.

OpenAI won't provide exact numerical usage limits for each tier, but the changes give Pro subscribers more room to use Work and Codex without paying for a more expensive subscription.

Title: Researchers find bugs in 5 AI developer tools, with OpenAI and Microsoft flaws still unpatched
Context: Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a...
Full Text: Multiple vulnerabilities in five popular AI developer tools could allow attackers to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof browser address bars. Researchers say flaws in OpenAI's Codex and Microsoft's VS Code remain unpatched, potentially putting developers who use affected configurations at risk. AI security startup Forever Security discovered vulnerabilities in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, VS Code, and Codex, and disclosed four of the flaws to the affected vendors. GitHub independently fixed the Copilot vulnerability without receiving a report from Forever Security. All five share a common security weakness: embedded browsers granted capabilities beyond those available to conventional browsers. Each tool “enriched its embedded browser beyond what a normal browser allows, and those enrichments undermined the traditional threat model - as agent input, as the authority on a tab’s own address, or as reach onto the host,” Forever researcher Gal Weizman wrote in a Thursday report. Forever dubbed this class of vulnerability “Embrace,” short for EMbedded BRowser, and said the flaws led to code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Here’s what each of these looks like, starting with Cursor. Cursor: arbitrary code execution Typical web pages can’t run commands on the host computer because a web page’s JavaScript cannot talk to local apps. Cursor’s integrated browser, however, allows a page to call the agent’s composer. The agent reads this as instructions and follows them, but the instructions remain hidden from human users. This opens the coding agent up to prompt injection attacks that could allow an attacker to execute commands on the host machine. The researchers disclosed the vulnerability to Cursor on September 10, and the vendor silently patched the flaw on October 1. According to Forever, Cursor did not publish a security advisory about the issue or respond to the researchers' disclosure. Cursor also did not reply to The Register’s request for comment. GitHub Copilot: address bar spoofing Under normal browser operations, a webpage cannot change the content of the address bar. “Copilot’s browser preview works differently,” Weizman wrote. “Some pages change their address without loading a new page, and the app cannot always see that. So Copilot let the page tell the app its own address.” The app checked only whether the text looked like a web address, starting with http, https or file, but it didn’t check where the tab really pointed to. This can be abused to trick the embedded browser into displaying a spoofed URL - such as github.com/login - in the address bar, while loading a fraudulent website - like a phishing page - underneath. The researchers found the address-bar spoofing flaw in GitHub Copilot 1.1.27 on September 26. GitHub independently fixed the flaw in a later Copilot build (1.1.29) on October 13 without receiving a vulnerability report from Forever. We reached out to GitHub and did not receive a response. Claude Desktop, Codex, and VS Code: arbitrary file read All three of these vendors’ coding assistants allow local HTML files opened in the built-in browser to escape its boundaries and access other files. Both Claude Desktop and VS Code allow local pages access to their respective project folders, but the researchers found that these restrictions did not apply to web workers – a browser feature that allows JavaScript to run in a background thread, separate from the page's main thread. This means a local page can start a worker, and the worker can bypass restrictions to reach any file on the machine. Codex, however, didn’t have this same restriction, meaning a local page could read any file directly without a worker. Weizman said his team disclosed the issue to Anthropic on July 23, and the AI vendor declined the Claude Desktop bug report as invalid for a “workspace trust” gated security boundary. A day later, however, Noma Security reported the same flaw, according to Weizman, and Anthropic accepted the report as valid. Anthropic did not respond to The Register’s questions about either bug report or Forever’s timeline of events. Forever disclosed the Codex bug to OpenAI on July 27 and didn’t get a response. The flaw remains unpatched, but an OpenAI spokesperson told The Register that it's aware of the issue and working to address it. On September 10, Forever disclosed the VS Code vulnerability to Microsoft and says the vendor also labeled it as an invalid workspace trust gated security boundary issue. The researchers claim it remains unpatched. Microsoft did not respond to our request for comment.®

Title: US Probes Suspected Hack Behind Military Base Freezer Failures
Context: This is the first time Reuters has reported that the US incident is being treated as a suspected cyberattack
Full Text:
The Pentagon treats August freezer failures at US military bases as a suspected hack and is working with French investigators after a supermarket attack.

The Pentagon is investigating freezer failures that spoiled food at US military bases in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to four officials who spoke to Reuters. One official said US investigators are also in contact with French authorities about a similar attack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets in France earlier this month. This is the first time Reuters has reported that the US incident is being treated as a suspected cyberattack.

“The Pentagon is ​treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar ‌with the matter.” Reuters reports.

“One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier this month.”

It is still unclear who is behind the attacks. Reuters could not determine how far the investigation has progressed or whether investigators have identified the cause or those responsible. The Pentagon said a unit of US Cyber Command is working closely with other government agencies and law enforcement. The Army’s Criminal Investigation Division confirmed that its Cyber Field Office is involved and is working with French law enforcement to investigate the freezer outages in Europe.

The incidents hit commissaries, the on-base stores where military personnel buy food. At least six were affected in late August, according to Reuters’ review of the bases’ Facebook posts and website updates. Stars and Stripes named Fort Irwin, F.E. Warren, Naval Station Newport, Columbus and Travis among the confirmed stores, and some outlets count up to 14 sites in 11 states, though not all are confirmed.

Source: Signal and Silence Blog

In at least one case the freezers didn’t just stop. Their temperatures were cranked up overnight, which left mounds of wilted or melted food in the morning. Fort Huachuca in Arizona said on August 26 that its freezer went into defrost mode and heated up all the food, adding that trust us when we say it was spoiled.

The Pentagon wasn’t the first to speak. A recently created blog called Signal and Silence reported the freezer failures and the possibility of sabotage on August 28, while Stars and Stripes reported the involvement of military investigators and Britain’s Daily Telegraph reported the contacts with the French. The French Embassy in Washington had no comment. Frozen food is the one asset where damage takes hours and evidence takes the form of puddles.

The French attack is the clearest example. Hackers took control of the cooling units in more than 350 stores and raised the temperatures. Frozen food aisles were emptied, and some units got so hot they caught fire. One supermarket owner said the total cost could reach tens of millions of euros.

The same thing happened in Arizona: attackers made the units hotter instead of just turning them off.

Reuters could not tell which brand was used at the US bases, and Danfoss, which is the manufacturer targeted in French supermarket attacks, did not reply. A public research report on Danfoss controllers came out before the incidents, but nothing shows a link to the bases.

There is a history of attacks on refrigeration systems. Danfoss reports that hackers targeted supermarkets in Russia and Israel in 2022 by exploiting outdated cooling controllers. In December 2025, US prosecutors accused a Ukrainian woman of belonging to a hacking group that disrupted refrigeration at a meat plant in 2024, ruining more than 2,000 pounds of meat.

Earlier this year, the Global Food Safety Initiative urged food safety experts and IT leaders to work together to protect refrigeration systems.

Title: Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools
Context: Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the...
Full Text:
Attackers are managing to sneak low-grade phishing emails through brand name email security products, as evidenced by a recent Anthropic impersonation campaign.

The campaign, described in a new blog post by Cofense, won't impress anybody. Since September, an unidentified threat actor has been sending out emails around the world, pretending to grant early access to Anthropic's cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technology. Their goal: stealing Google and Microsoft account credentials.

To avoid being relegated to spam folders, the attacker has been using novice tactics: shortening their malicious URLs, adding CAPTCHAs to their phishing flow, and leveraging legitimate video conferencing tools. The only remarkable thing about the campaign, really, is that it actually seems to be working.

Fake Emails Steal Google, Microsoft Credentials

Even as far as phishing campaigns go, this one's pretty lazy.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

Attackers are appealing to targets with VIP invites to a "private preview" of Anthropic's supposed "new social media AI tool." Emails emphasize that this special early look is "private, invitation-only."

Right off the bat, there are ample reasons to be suspicious. The email titles have a grammatical error. The email sender's name includes a typo — "Austin from nthropic" — and their domain belongs to GoTo Webinar, not Anthropic. Visually, the messages are barebones, possessing no visual elements that even attempt to impersonate Anthropic branding.

If for some reason someone actually clicks on the fake registration link — a link that doesn't point to an Anthropic or even a conferencing app domain — they'll end up on a fake Zoom meeting page. If, further, the victim doesn't catch that a GoTo Webinar invite led to a Zoom call, they might choose to sign into Zoom via Google or Microsoft Single-Sign On (SSO). If they choose Google, they won't even be prompted for a password, thus making half of this malicious campaign completely useless, even to the attacker running it.

Inconsistent brand impersonations and missing or broken data theft flows are endemic to AI-generated campaigns; Cofense couldn't confirm if AI was used here. "However, due to the multiple variations of Zoom pages, it's likely generative AI was used," Cofense researcher Jacob Malimban says.

He points to one bit of additional evidence: Beginning Oct. 28, the threat actor began spoofing Anthropic's website instead of Zoom's. The similar but slightly off format of the Anthropic spoofing page, he says, also suggests AI generation.

Related:10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years

How Weak TTPs Beat Email Security Solutions

The overall package is so maladroit that one can only wonder how such an email bypassed any spam filter in the first place. In fact, Cofense found these emails getting through market-leading email security products like the Proofpoint Secure Email Gateway (SEG) and Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Cofense pointed to a few little details that might help explain why.

First, the emails are sent from a legitimate email address, customercare@gotowebinar[.]com — a shared sender address that any GoTo Webinar user might use to distribute webinar information. The legitimacy and ubiquity of this shared address shields the sender from scrutiny.

Second, the malicious registration link in the emails was run through a URL shortener, Zapier, eliminating a security product's ability to interpret red flags in the domain itself.

Lastly, the phishing flow incorporates two separate CAPTCHAs. The first — a Cloudflare CAPTCHA, presented before the fake Zoom or Anthropic page — is meant to stop an automated scanner in its tracks.

The second CAPTCHA — placed between the fake Zoom or Anthropic page and the fake SSO page — is a malicious twist on the form, designed to block VPN services, Tor browsers, and other tools defenders might use. "Some phish kits used that specific type of CAPTCHA before. It appears to have been actively developed by threat actors to detect the tools of both automated and human activity, as well as see if the IP address was proxied," Malimban explains.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

None of these tactics will knock anyone's socks off but, in the gestalt, they seem to do the trick.

Takeaways for Cybersecurity Awareness Month

To Keeper Security chief information security officer (CISO) Shane Barney, it's no surprise that threat actors are successfully bypassing perimeter email defenses, even with cookie cutter tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

"The reality of modern cybersecurity is that Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) will always have blind spots," he says.

Barney adds that organizations should assume phishing emails will end up in employees' email inboxes, and therefore security teams need to build defenses that focus on identity.

"If an employee is tricked by a fake Anthropic lure and their Microsoft or Google credentials are compromised, strict least-privilege access policies, phishing-resistant multifactor authentication and privileged access management are what prevent the attacker from moving laterally, elevating privileges and accessing sensitive data," he advises. Lastly, he adds, "Utilizing a centralized password manager that validates domain URLs before autofilling credentials provides a critical last line of defense against the lookalike domains used in this attack, neutralizing the threat at the point of interaction."

In the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month 2026, and its emphasis on avoiding and reporting phishing scams, Malimban adds, "We hope that employees are trained using Secure Behavior Management to recognize and report phishing. To defend against suspicious account access, organizations should have robust account monitoring, like with CISA's free tool (Logging Made Easy). All in all, having multiple controls and defense in depth is necessary to defend against modern attacks."

Title: A leak in the chain of command.
Context: Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs.
Full Text:
DHS suffers a massive data leak. Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods. Cisco patches a firewall zero-day. A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories. Online scams overtake phishing. NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance. CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation. The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline. A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations. Our guest is Yonald Chery, CTO from Technology Advancement Center (TAC), discussing securing operational technology in our critical infrastructure. Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

Today is Thursday October 29th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

DHS suffers a massive data leak.

A massive leak of Department of Homeland Security records has exposed information on more than 41,000 employees and contractors, potentially providing adversaries with a detailed roadmap of the department’s operations.

The archive, dubbed “Icepick,” was published by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets. It reportedly contains data from DHS’s Okta identity management system, including employee contact information, reporting relationships, and access permissions for sensitive systems.

WIRED’s analysis identified references to undercover operations, surveillance programs, facial recognition tools, and investigative platforms. The records cover roughly one-seventh of DHS’s workforce, including thousands of ICE and Customs and Border Protection personnel.

Security experts warn the information could facilitate targeted phishing, impersonation, and intelligence gathering, particularly when combined with other leaked datasets.

DHS says it’s investigating a potential breach. Okta maintains its systems were not compromised.

The hackers, calling themselves the Department of Peace, framed the release as an act of government accountability.

Researchers reveal Volt Typhoon’s sophisticated methods.

For years, U.S. officials have warned that China’s Volt Typhoon hacking group poses an extraordinary threat to American critical infrastructure. Now, researchers are revealing the sophisticated methods behind those warnings.

As Kim Zetter writes in her Zero Day newsletter, Lumen Technologies’ Black Lotus Labs has uncovered what it calls Silent Train, a covert network of compromised routers, servers, and internet-connected devices that Volt Typhoon uses to infiltrate sensitive American networks.

The attackers construct elaborate chains of compromised devices, sometimes in less than two minutes, routing their activity through multiple countries before reaching their targets. Each chain is typically used for a single intrusion, then dismantled. The hackers erase logs, remove evidence, and disappear, sometimes after spending just minutes inside a network.

Researchers tracked more than 27 classes of compromised devices and identified at least four exploited zero-day vulnerabilities.

The targets include government agencies, defense contractors, telecommunications providers, military research institutions, and operators of energy, water, and transportation infrastructure.

Many victims are concentrated in Hawaii, California, and Texas, locations strategically important to U.S. military operations in the Indo-Pacific.

Researchers believe the campaign combines espionage with preparations for potential disruption during a conflict involving Taiwan. They’ve observed attackers stealing military-related documents, mapping networks, and collecting credentials that could provide future access.

And that access can persist long after the initial intrusion. Volt Typhoon sometimes returns weeks later using stolen credentials and entirely new routes.

The result is a carefully maintained network of potential access points into critical American systems, built to remain largely invisible until the attackers decide they need it.

Cisco patches a firewall zero-day.

Cisco has patched an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting its ASA and Firepower Threat Defense firewall software. The high-severity flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, allows unauthenticated attackers to remotely crash vulnerable devices with SSL VPN enabled, causing unexpected reboots and service disruptions. Cisco confirmed exploitation earlier this month but hasn’t identified the attackers or their targets. The company urges customers to install security updates immediately. Administrators unable to patch can mitigate the vulnerability by disabling secondary authentication on affected VPN tunnel groups.

A suspected coordinated supply chain attack targets public GitHub repositories.

Radware researchers have uncovered a suspected coordinated supply chain attack targeting 61 public GitHub repositories, including projects from Google, Brave, and Trivy. They identified 83 malicious submissions, most posted within just 43 minutes, using 74 GitHub accounts, many potentially compromised.

The attacker concealed malicious commands inside HTML comments in issues and pull requests. When vulnerable CI/CD workflows processed that content, the commands could execute automatically, attempting to steal environment variables, credentials, and access tokens.

Researchers confirmed malicious command execution in two cases but found no definitive evidence of stolen repository permissions or compromised downstream software.

The suspected objective was to gain access to repositories and potentially distribute malicious code through trusted open source projects.

Researchers recommend restricting workflow permissions and treating externally submitted content as untrusted.

Online scams overtake phishing.

Online scam detections doubled over the past year, overtaking phishing for the first time, according to Akamai’s latest State of the Internet report. Researchers recorded 6.4 million scams during the second quarter of 2026, including fraudulent stores, investment schemes, and payment scams.

Phishing also increased 61%, with AI helping criminals create convincing lures and launch shorter, more agile campaigns.

Meanwhile, a separate report from the Identity Theft Resource Center highlights the devastating human consequences. More than 80% of surveyed U.S. scam victims reported suicidal thoughts, while nearly nine in ten who sought institutional assistance received no response.

Many victims subsequently paid supposed recovery services, potentially exposing themselves to further fraud.

The findings illustrate both the growing industrialization of online scams and the troubling lack of support for their victims.

NIST shares post-quantum cryptography guidance.

NIST has released guidance to help federal agencies meet deadlines for transitioning sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography. Under a June executive order, agencies must adopt quantum-resistant key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. The guidance recommends prioritizing sensitive, long-lived data vulnerable to future quantum decryption, while allowing hybrid encryption approaches for particularly critical systems. NIST also urges agencies to assess their cryptographic supply chains, warning that meeting the deadlines will require immediate, coordinated action.

CISA warns a VMware ESXi vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA warns that attackers are exploiting a VMware ESXi vulnerability that allows administrators to perform certain operations without generating audit logs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-41709, has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. CrowdStrike attributes earlier exploitation to the China-linked group Warp Panda, which reportedly used the zero-day to conceal activity during intrusions targeting U.S. organizations, including law firms. Despite its low severity rating, the vulnerability can significantly hamper forensic investigations. Federal agencies have two weeks to apply patches.

The Federal Election Commission takes systems offline.

The Federal Election Commission has taken several systems offline following reports of an attempted cyberattack, just days before the U.S. midterm elections.

The disruption affects electronic filing, campaign finance searches, and reporting tools, preventing organizations from submitting required disclosures detailing political spending. The FEC says it has identified an issue and is implementing a fix, but several services remain unavailable.

The timing is particularly sensitive, with record amounts of money flowing into congressional campaigns. Security experts warn that interruptions to financial disclosures could undermine transparency and public confidence.

Importantly, the FEC regulates campaign finance but does not administer elections. The incident has no direct impact on voting systems or how ballots are cast.

The agency says it’s working to restore services.

A Ukrainian national gets prison time for ransomware operations.

A Ukrainian national has been sentenced to nearly six years in a U.S. prison for his role in the Nefilim and Hive ransomware operations. Thirty-six-year-old Artem Stryzhak pleaded guilty to participating in attacks that encrypted victims’ systems and demanded ransom payments, including attacks against healthcare organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Stryzhak joined Nefilim in 2021, agreeing to surrender 20% of his ransom proceeds in exchange for access to its malware. He later became an early Hive affiliate, participating in attacks against seven organizations, including healthcare providers and law firms.

The FBI helped one victim recover its files without paying.

Authorities are still searching for alleged Nefilim administrator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. The State Department is offering up to $11 million for information leading to his arrest, conviction, or location.

Bitcoin mining gets you in hot water.

A company that previously turned space heaters into bitcoin miners now wants to bring cryptocurrency into your shower.

Heatbit has introduced Bitwater, an $899 replacement heating element that uses twenty bitcoin-mining chips to heat household water while generating cryptocurrency.

The idea is straightforward: Bitcoin mining produces heat, so why not put that heat to work? The company says Bitwater fits many conventional electric water heaters, operates without noisy fans, and sends mining proceeds directly to the homeowner.

The economics, however, are a little less refreshing.

A conventional heating element costs less than $30. Heatbit has shared estimates suggesting mining could generate roughly a dollar a day, potentially recovering the premium in about three years. But those returns depend on volatile cryptocurrency economics, hardware longevity, and household hot-water demand.

Shipments are planned for early 2027.

Our return on investment desk reports it would take over three hundred years of bitcoin mining to break even.

Whether Bitwater ultimately saves money remains uncertain. But at least your morning shower might finally contribute to your retirement portfolio.
