Title: Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps Abuse Signed Executables to Deploy Crypto Miners
Context: "The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first...
Full Text:
Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba.

The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader.

"The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis.

To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google.

Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below -

github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop

gpt-5-6.github[.]io

github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io

github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io

gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io

github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io

opus-5-0[.]github[.]io

"Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone."

Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components -

Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable

winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable

The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment.

Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks.

YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData."

The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload.

The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks -

Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub").

Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io."

Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input.

Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat").

"By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said.

The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions.

"The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."

Title: NIK C2 Malware Can Use Victims’ OpenAI Keys for AI Queries
Context: Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays...
Full Text:
A new AI-enabled malware framework has been found that can fall back on victims' own OpenAI API keys for artificial intelligence requests, charging the usage to the victim while obscuring who made the requests.

Cisco Talos observed the command-and-control (C2) framework, dubbed NIK C2, in the wild, according to research published on October 29.

Its Go-based implant gave attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging and surveillance capabilities, while an integrated OpenAI client let them send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.

NIK C2 Routes AI Requests Through Victim Machines

The AI capability is built into the implant rather than requiring operators to process collected information separately. Talos said attackers could supply a prompt and model choice through the C2 panel, with the implant sending the request to OpenAI from the victim's machine and returning the response to the operator.

If the operator supplied no key, the malware read an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable on the infected machine instead, which Talos called a deliberate design. An organization with an OpenAI API key configured on a compromised Windows system could therefore end up funding the attacker's AI requests.

Read more on AI API key abuse: Attackers Steal METR API Key and Burn $600,000 in AI Credits

Talos said OpenAI's billing system would charge the victim's payment method and its access logs would show the victim's key as the one making the requests, leaving no trace attributable to the attacker.

Malware Framework Combines Theft and Ransomware

Beyond its AI functionality, the Windows malware supported more than 52 commands covering credential theft, browser data collection, cryptocurrency wallets, Wi-Fi credentials, keylogging, screen capture and remote access. Talos said it also offered lateral movement and multiple defense-evasion capabilities.

The framework also contained a screen-locking ransomware module that displayed customized ransom demands in Bitcoin or the Tether stablecoin (USDT). Talos said the module encrypted no files, leaving no forensic trail of file-modification timestamps or encryption markers, and that a screen lock is considerably faster to deploy than file-encrypting ransomware.

The company said it observed at least three versions of the implant and found its infrastructure active during the research. That led it to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is a fully functional framework rather than a proof of concept.

Talos said NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft "by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows."

Title: Belgium's tax agency confirms cyberattack, pulls services offline
Context: FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while...
Full Text: Belgium's finance and tax agency has pulled "several" digital services offline after a cyberattack on the organization. FOD Financiën confirmed the attack on Wednesday, saying that MyMinfin, the agency's main online tax portal, as well as other online services, are temporarily unavailable while they start the initial investigations. "This measure helps limit the risks and makes it possible to carry out the necessary technical interventions to ensure the security of our systems," it said in a public announcement. FOD Financiën added that "this has consequences for tax deadlines in the near future," referring to the October 31 extended deadline to submit tax filings for specific types of income, such as sole traders and earnings from foreign companies. The agency confirmed the deadline will be extended to November 16, by which time MyMinfin, the platform through which such filings would normally be submitted, should be back up and running. The detail offered up in the public statement reflects the early stage of the investigation; not much is known, although there is nothing to suggest data was compromised. "Data protection is a top priority for the FOD Financiën," it said. "At present, there are no indications that a data breach has occurred or that data has been compromised. This aspect is also being closely investigated and followed up. "In the meantime, a large part of our other applications remains available with full or partial functionality. We are closely monitoring the situation and doing everything we can to make the affected services available again as soon as possible." Spokesperson Francis Adyns told local news outlets that the attack was thwarted within hours, and that it was unable to gain access to applications or data. "The attack could not be sufficiently expanded within our environment to take over applications or gain access to data," he told Nieuwsblad. "Elements that were potentially infected were isolated. As a result, MyMinfin, Tax-on-web, and Biztax went offline, but the hacking was successfully stopped. "The various services must be restored in an isolated environment. This requires considerable time to realize, with the necessary caution to rule out new risks." ®

Title: Malicious Firefox extensions impersonate popular crypto wallets
Context: Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets
Full Text:
Socket’s threat researchers found three malicious Firefox extensions that impersonated the Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget crypto wallets.

Once installed, the malicious extensions stole recovery phrases and private keys, which would provide the attacker with full control of a wallet.

A crypto wallet is an app, browser extension, or physical device that lets you manage cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin. Despite its name, it doesn’t actually hold your coins. Those are recorded on a blockchain, a shared digital record of transactions. Instead, the wallet manages the secret digital keys that let you access and spend them.

When you create a wallet, you may be given a recovery phrase: a list of words you can use to restore access. Write it down and store it offline. It’s a backup of your keys, not just an ordinary password. Anyone who gets hold of it can take control of your funds, which is why fake wallet extensions try to steal it.

Cybercriminals listed three fake wallet extensions on Firefox Add-ons, impersonating Phantom, Jupiter, and Bitget. The genuine wallets offer extensions for other browsers: Jupiter lists Chrome, Brave, and Edge; Bitget’s extension is for Chrome; and Phantom says its Firefox extension is no longer supported.

The malicious extensions looked for 12-, 15-, 18-, and 24-word recovery phrases, as well as Ethereum and Solana private keys. They could read input fields, detect pasted text, and scan screens displaying recovery phrases.

A recovery phrase or private key is a bearer secret: whoever holds it controls the wallet and can move its assets. The Phantom variant’s backend logged captured secrets, sent them to a Telegram bot, and automatically moved funds to hardcoded payout addresses. Those addresses covered Ethereum, BSC, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Avalanche, Solana, and Bitcoin. The Phantom variant could read a phrase both when it was typed during import and when it was displayed on a reveal screen.

How to stay safe

Socket says all three listings were live on Firefox Add-ons during its analysis and have since been removed. But if you find one of these extensions in your Firefox browser, you should:

Remove the extension. Use the three-dot menu next to it and choose Remove.

Title: CREST Urges Whole-Ecosystem Approach to Financial Cyber Resilience
Context: CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and...
Full Text:
Cyber resilience in financial services should be built across the wider ecosystem of institutions, supervisors and specialist providers rather than treated solely as each institution's own responsibility, a new framework has argued.

CREST, the global non-profit accreditation body for the cybersecurity industry, said its whitepaper, Cyber Resilience in Financial Services: A Whole Ecosystem Approach, provides a maturity pathway for jurisdictions to assess their capabilities and coordinate improvements across three domains.

The paper, published on October 29, argued that weaknesses in shared infrastructure, technology providers, cyber firms or public authorities can undermine resilience across the wider financial system.

CREST Sets Out Three Domains For Financial Cyber Resilience

Under the framework, financial institutions are responsible for protecting critical business services and demonstrating their controls work under pressure.

Financial supervisors are tasked with setting proportionate expectations, overseeing individual firms and understanding systemic risk, while cyber service providers are expected to deliver specialist advice, assessment, threat intelligence, testing and response capabilities.

The framework maps each domain through five stages of cyber maturity, with the three pathways planned together. Institutions progress from incomplete basic hygiene to advanced, threat-led assurance and continuous improvement. Supervisors move from mapping their sectors and establishing mandates to adaptive, cross-sector oversight, while providers progress from unvalidated services to specialist financial-sector capabilities.

CREST said the pathways are illustrative, not a new compliance standard. Its three priorities were ecosystem-wide measurement of maturity, a common language across the three domains and faster development wherever one part of the ecosystem lags.

Read more on financial-sector cyber regulation: FCA Updates Cyber Incident and Third-Party Reporting Rules

Framework Calls For Multi-Year Cyber Maturity Programs

CREST suggested supervisors or other market participants set out multi-year programs so the three domains develop in parallel, warning that requirements outpacing readiness can produce limited assurance. Its roadmap begins in years one and two with institutions mapping critical services and closing urgent hygiene gaps while supervisors publish a baseline and strategy.

Years three to five would bring independent assessment and risk-based testing for institutions, tiered requirements from supervisors and independent accreditation for providers. Years five to 10 would focus on threat-led penetration testing where proportionate, system-wide exercises and a diverse community of accredited specialist providers.

The whitepaper also warned that moving prematurely to mandate the highest international accreditations could shut out local providers where no route to accreditation exists. It pointed to measures including mentoring, partnerships, training and CREST's Cyber Accelerated Maturity Programme (CREST CAMP).

"Financial institutions, supervisors and cyber service providers each have a distinct role, and the strength of the system depends on their capability developing together," said CREST CEO Nick Benson.

Title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Leads Benchmarks for Finding, Exploiting, and Patching Vulnerabilities
Context: One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability...
Full Text:
Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

"It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55).

One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon.

Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection.

The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program.

Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.

The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks."

"GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said.

"GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task."

Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software.

This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft.

"These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said.

"These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
Context: The Cofense researchers found that attackers are exploiting this fact by sending what seems to be an invitation email from a legitimate sender; when users click on the link to...
Full Text:
Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact.

New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview.

In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so.

“It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Fear of missing out is the oldest lure in the book.”

Every organization is trying to figure out where AI fits, he noted, and a private preview of Anthropic’s newest technology is exactly the invitation an ambitious employee would want to accept. “The attackers did not pick Anthropic at random,” he said. “They picked whatever is hottest in the news cycle. Next month, it may be another name.”

How attackers lure users with spoofed Anthropic invites

GoTo Webinar is a widely used platform, and its meeting invitation emails are typically not blocked by security tools. The Cofense researchers found that attackers are exploiting this fact by sending what seems to be an invitation email from a legitimate sender; when users click on the link to register for the fake webinar, they are instead sent to a compromised URL.

The email offers what the researchers call a “tantalizing” offer: “This private, invitation-only virtual session brings together a select group of participants to a focused conversation on AI systems, research, and the future of frontier models,” it reads.

A URL shortener circumvents email security tools, and the attackers use subdomains and dashes (-) to hide the malicious URL. The link itself appears to have been generated by Zapier, a legitimate company whose tools are designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI compatible with Model Context Protocol (MCP).

The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com (GoTo Webinar’s website is actually www.goto.com). The text contains no obvious spelling errors, and the email contains GoTo Webinar branding. However, the researchers noted, the email sender’s name is “Austin from nthropic,” with the “A” missing.

“Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign,” they pointed out.

If the phishing link is clicked, a Cloudflare CAPTCHA page appears, and must be completed before the login prompt is presented. This serves as the first of two checkpoints to prevent security tools from scanning attackers’ websites.

“Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure,” the researchers explained.

Once the CAPTCHA is completed, victims are led to a Zoom-spoofing invitation page. If they want to “attend” the fake event, they must register, and they are prompted to enter their work email address. When they click “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft,” yet another CAPTCHA page appears.

Both CAPTCHA pages seem to be good at detecting and blocking analysis by VPN services, scanners, Tor browsers, and other security tools, the researchers noted. Also, because there are two distinct CAPTCHA pages, such tools may not be able to follow every step in the attack.

“A CAPTCHA was built to keep bots out,” Dickson pointed out. “Here, it keeps the security scanners out and lets the victims in.”

The fake Google and Microsoft login pages differ a bit, however. The spoofed Google page does not capture passwords, only usernames, which the researchers surmise is due to a misconfiguration; the spoofed Microsoft page does collect both usernames and passwords.

But both are “remarkably similar” to their respective legitimate pages, and their subdomains are “tricky.” The fake Google URL is goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu, while the Microsoft URL closely mimics real Office and Sharepoint domains, using office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com.

Once credentials are submitted, neither login offers a confirmation message, nor does it redirect to legitimate vendor pages. But by that point, attackers have already succeeded at exfiltrating credentials. That means they could compromise an account, access the sensitive documents in that account, or use it as an initial attack vector to further infiltrate the enterprise, the researchers explained.

They advised checking if the branding of a message remains consistent from the email to a login page, searching for small inconsistencies such as minor misspellings, and reminding employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate.

“Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry, especially now with the use of AI,” the researchers noted.

It’s not the employees’ fault

The AI industry’s habit of gated previews and waitlists does not help in these situations, Dickson noted; it trains people to expect exactly this kind of invitation.

“Start with the cracks the attackers left showing,” he advised: The sender supposedly came from “nthropic,” the email carried GoTo Webinar branding, the registration spoofed a Zoom meeting page, and the login pages were from Google or Microsoft. That’s three brands in three clicks, he noted.

The fake login domains, like office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com, are built to be skimmed, not read, he pointed out. And, while the Google page collected only usernames, which may be a configuration error, the threat actors behind this campaign will likely fix that.

“Training helps, but I would not hang the defense on an employee squinting at a URL at 4:45 on a Friday,” Dickson said; how much a stolen password is worth is a leadership decision, not a test the employee fails.

Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) such as passkeys makes a stolen password far less valuable, he noted. But enterprises ultimately have a short to-do list to allow them to defend themselves from this sort of scam, Dickson said:

Verify any AI preview invitation through an account team or a known contact.

Treat branding that changes from email to meeting page to login page as a red flag.

Roll out phishing-resistant MFA. If someone entered credentials on one of these phishing login pages, reset them and review that account’s activity.

“Bottom line: This campaign uses trusted tools to defeat defenses built on trust,” Dickson said. “The employee should not be the last line of defense.”

Title: Shadow AI Across Government: It's Three Problems, Not One
Context: That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking
Full Text:
Most agencies and contractors now have a generative AI (GenAI) policy. Far fewer can tell you what their people are actually running.

That gap has a name. Like shadow information technology before it, Shadow AI is what happens when AI tools, services, and components enter an organization outside the processes meant to govern them. The difference is that shadow IT mostly showed up as an unapproved application.

Shadow AI can create risk at three points:

Data that leaves your environment.

AI-generated code your developers commit.

AI models and other components your builds pull down.

Those three are usually discussed as one risk. They are not. They have different failure modes, different owners, and almost no overlap in the controls that address them. An organization can have an excellent acceptable-use policy and still have no idea which AI models are running inside its own software.

None of which is an argument against adoption. The productivity gains are real, and the organizations getting the most from these tools are not the ones that tried to ban them. They are the ones that made the sanctioned path the easiest path to take. That only works if you can see which path people are actually taking.

Here is what each problem is, who owns it, and what closes it.

The Adoption Already Happened

Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that 45% of employees are now regular users of AI on corporate devices, authorized or not — up from 15% a year earlier. Two thirds of those users accessed AI services through non-corporate accounts, which means the activity is largely invisible to the organization paying for the device.

Shadow AI is now the third most common non-malicious insider action in the report's data loss prevention findings. And the most common category of data sent to external AI services is source code.

That last detail is the one worth sitting with, because it connects all three problems. Source code leaving is a disclosure problem. The same assistant that received it returns code and dependency choices that come back in. And the models behind these tools increasingly arrive as components inside your own applications.

One behavior, three exposures.

Problem One: What Goes Out

This is the problem most policies already address, and the one most people mean when they say Shadow AI. An employee pastes contract language, personnel data, or controlled unclassified information (CUI) into a public chatbot to summarize or rewrite it.

Ownership: Security and privacy teams, records officers, and acceptable-use policy owners.

Controls: Provide a sanctioned platform people prefer, use data loss prevention and network controls, name approved services, and give staff practical guidance.

Verizon's findings show why prohibitions alone may not work: employees may turn to personal accounts, moving AI use further out of view rather than stopping it.

For Department of War (DoW) components, this is already written down. DoW Instruction 8430.01 bars entering non-public departmental information into generative AI services unless the service resides on departmental systems and is approved for departmental use. Both conditions, not either.

What does not close it: anything in your software supply chain toolchain. No repository control, bill of materials, or scanner sees a developer paste code into a browser. If a vendor tells you otherwise, press on exactly which telemetry they are reading.

Problem Two: What Comes Back In

Your developers are using coding assistants. The output is unverified input, and the accountability for it does not transfer to the tool that produced it.

DoWI 8430.01 is explicit on this point for defense work: AI-generated code is treated as unverified, and developers and their teams remain fully accountable for what they ship. It also asks software efforts to maintain a record of the models, versions, and significant datasets used to generate or test software, kept with the software evidence package and treated as analogous to a software bill of materials (SBOM).

The subtler issue is that a coding assistant does not only write code. It chooses dependencies. An assistant suggesting a package is making a supply chain decision on your behalf, at a speed and volume no review process was designed for, which is a different problem from whether the code it wrote is correct. We covered that specific question in more depth earlier this month.

Who owns it: engineering leadership and application security.

What closes it is treating assistant output as you would a pull request from an unfamiliar contributor. Human review, software composition analysis (SCA) on everything it introduces, and a record of which models were in the loop, which is both a DoW requirement and the only way to answer the question later.

Problem Three: What Your Builds Pull Down

The third problem is the least discussed and the hardest to see after the fact: AI models and machine learning packages entering your environment as components.

Sonatype calls components retrieved straight from public repositories, bypassing the repository manager, shadow downloads. Sonatype Research Labs audited 9,658 Hugging Face requests across a set of customers in the first half of 2026, as part of our Beyond Traditional Packages report. Nearly 7% were blocked or rejected by policy. Of the 674 models blocked, 55% were stopped on model acceptability and 18% on security grounds, which says models are raising governance questions traditional policies were not built for.

A model is not like a library. It arrives as opaque weights, it may carry a license with terms on how its output can be used, and its published name tells you very little about what it was built from — open models are routinely fine-tuned, merged, quantized and re-released under a new publisher. Three federal exclusion orders now name a single model developer and reach products "developed using" its implementations, which makes model provenance a procurement question and not only an engineering one.

Who owns it: platform engineering and whoever runs your repository manager.

What closes it: one governed path in. Route model pulls through a proxy repository so every request is visible in one place, block direct downloads from the corporate network, and lock client configuration so the path cannot quietly be bypassed. Sonatype Firewall can then audit or quarantine models at that boundary before a developer gets them. Start in audit mode to see what your teams are actually pulling, then move to quarantine. At scan time, Sonatype Lifecycle flags a model as a derivative and names the foundation model it came from, and the AI Models Usage dashboard shows which applications are using models, with lineage, commit hash and publishing date.

That last piece matters for a reason beyond engineering. Joint guidance on AI and machine learning supply chain risks, co-sealed by the National Security Agency and seven other national agencies, tells organizations to require an AI bill of materials from vendors as a condition of procurement. Asking your suppliers for something you cannot produce yourself is a difficult position to hold.

What To Do About It

Pick your lane. These are three different jobs and they rarely belong to the same person.

If you own policy. Name specific sanctioned services rather than categories, and pair the policy with a platform people prefer to the alternative. Then confirm your inventory obligation is being met. OMB Memorandum M-26-05 makes each agency head responsible for the security of software on the agency network and directs agencies to maintain a complete inventory. Models are software.

If you own compliance. The obligations people associate with the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) did not go away when Phase 2 was suspended. DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171 and Supplier Performance Risk System scoring are unchanged, and annual affirmations remain in effect. An attestation that does not match the environment is the exposure, and that gap is exactly what undeclared AI tooling creates.

If you own the platform. Start with visibility, not enforcement. Put a proxy in front of model pulls, turn Sonatype Firewall on in audit mode, and spend two weeks looking at what comes back before you block anything. Most teams are surprised, and the surprise is the business case. Then make it continuous — an inventory taken once begins decaying the day it is produced, and the reason to route intake through a single path is that the record maintains itself rather than becoming an annual exercise.

Shadow AI is no longer a question of whether people will adopt these tools. They already have. The question is whether you can identify:

Which services receive your data.

Which models help write your code.

Which models run inside the software you ship.

Three questions, three owners, one answer: you can only govern what you can see.

Title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
Context: 5B+ valuation for entire firm, though portion sold not specified Malware Month Ten years since the first corp ransomware, Mikko Hyppönen sees no end in sight On the plus side,...
Full Text: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims. It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.” The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks. In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online. Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content. Commenting on today’s announcement, Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld. ?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply. "We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play." The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®

Title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
Context: The order asks officials to examine independent verification inside AI laboratories, independent checks of safety assessments, verified shutdown mechanisms, and expanded...
Full Text:
OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls.

The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions.

“If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission.

OpenAI, in its October 20 letter, called for an amendment to California’s Senate Bill 53 (SB 53).

“We support amending SB 53 to require frontier developers to maintain effective shutdown controls and an enforceable duty to use them when unsafe conditions arise, and no lesser intervention would adequately address the risk,” OpenAI wrote.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the two approaches address complementary needs. “The operator must contain the unsafe activity promptly. Independent review must examine both intervention and inaction,” he said.

Newsom’s executive order, N-9-26, directs California’s Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and national experts, to submit recommendations by November 16 on potential amendments to existing AI safety laws. The order asks officials to examine independent verification inside AI laboratories, independent checks of safety assessments, verified shutdown mechanisms, and expanded reporting of critical safety incidents. It does not itself impose these proposed requirements.

Independent verification

Anthropic wants evaluators to assess developers’ safety claims and publish their own findings.

“We strongly support requiring independent verification of what frontier AI companies report about the risks of their models and whether those risks are sufficiently mitigated,” the company wrote.

It proposed requiring developers to publish risk reports at least every six months, covering serious risks from their models, including internally used models substantially riskier than released systems. Evaluators should receive unredacted reports and access to developers’ most capable models and relevant internal information.

Anthropic also proposed that developers pay into a state-administered pooled fund to finance evaluators, rather than pay them directly. It said a team from the independent evaluation organization METR had received employee-like access on a pilot basis, with further partnerships involving SecureBio and Accenture under development.

OpenAI, in its letter, said it supports independent technical assessments but distinguishes them from compliance audits. Technical assessments would examine evidence behind developers’ safety claims and the effectiveness of safeguards; compliance audits would check whether companies follow their published safety frameworks and legal obligations, it added.

OpenAI recommended annual independent compliance audits and focused technical assessments of serious risks arising during model training, evaluation and internal deployment. It also urged California to work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop common assessment standards.

Gogia said oversight requires more than funding. “Credible assurance must survive an adverse finding,” he said.

Beyond a single switch

OpenAI argued that a single kill switch would not address the different ways AI systems operate and are deployed.

“We recommend using the term ‘shutdown controls’ because it will require the development of multiple controls and coordinated action by different actors to stop AI operations when necessary, rather than a single switch,” the company wrote in the letter.

Interventions could include stopping a training run, isolating an AI agent, revoking tool or network access, or suspending a service. OpenAI said responsibilities should extend to inference providers and downstream deployers according to the operations they control. It also noted that developers cannot reliably switch off independently operated copies of open-weight models running on external systems.

Anthropic similarly argued for more targeted safeguards. “We think a more apt metaphor for what frontier AI companies need to build is a circuit breaker,” it wrote, advocating controls that can contain problems at the level of an agent, customer, deployment environment, or model.

For enterprises, Gogia said, contractual shutdown responsibilities should match the controls each party actually possesses. Agreements should specify intervention authority, incident-reporting cooperation, and who can authorize a restart.

“Every assigned duty needs an executable control,” he said, adding that CIOs should test recovery processes rather than assume switching to an alternative model will preserve safe operations. Both companies also called for broader reporting of incidents involving models that circumvent safeguards or take unauthorized actions.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: [New Threat Trend Data] When Bad Actors Use Reality Against Us
Context: In Q3 2026, attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure than in Q2, and threat actors are using native platform features to host fake developer...
Full Text:
“Is it real?” has become a common question across our digital lives thanks to the rise of AI-generated content.

A fair one, with deepfakes and AI-produced imagery flooding nearly every channel we use daily. A skeptical eye is a must, but our most recent Phishing Threat Trends Report reveals why that might not even be enough.

Our 8th Phishing Threat Trends Report tracks how attackers stopped faking infrastructure and started borrowing it. Modern phishing has no need to fool filters with lookalike domains when it can sit directly on trusted ones. This shift runs through every finding in this report: campaigns are routed through hyperscalers, attackers harvest API keys from trusted platforms, and session hijacking via refresh tokens that render "change your password" meaningless. The only thing left that is fake is the premise.

Overall, phishing volume rose 29.8% in 2026 compared to 2025, and one dangerous email now lands in every 733 an organization receives. The bigger shift is not how much arrives but how it is built. Attackers have stopped faking infrastructure and started borrowing it. Check out Volume 8 of our Phishing Threat Trends Report to see what that looks like and where security teams should focus next.

Download the full report here. Read on for some highlights:

Targeting Sharpens as Mass Phishing Declines

Mass, low-effort phishing is fading. Mobile-focused attacks fell 47.3% and 419 scams fell 31.3% compared to 2025. Meanwhile, lures built on research and personal selection are rising. Spear phishing is up 41.1%, scouting is up 33.7%, and company impersonation is up 28%.

Links remain the dominant payload at 66.2%, including QR codes. Attachments account for 19.1%, and nearly one in three phishing attachments is a PDF.

Attackers Are Stealing Permission, Not Passwords

Authentication phishing goes after the sign-in itself. Instead of capturing a password, attackers use device-code logins and OAuth consent to obtain persistent access. In Q3 2026, authentication phishing accounted for 2% of link-based phishing from toolkits, and 25.6% of link-bearing attacks had MFA-bypass capability.

Because the stolen access is a token or a permission rather than a password, a password reset does not end the compromise. Lures for device-code campaigns are also moving from email to Microsoft Teams, through compromised accounts, fake calendar invites, and missed-voicemail alerts.

AI Platforms Become the Newest Phishing Host

Attackers are increasingly sitting on trusted AI domains rather than spoofing their logos. Attacks impersonating AI brands rose 228% between April and August 2026. In Q3 2026, attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure than in Q2, and threat actors are using native platform features to host fake developer consoles, sign-in prompts, and download hubs.

The primary goals are credential and API key harvesting, quota fraud, and malware delivered through on-platform app downloads. For organizations, the risk extends beyond people. Stolen API keys and OAuth grants can turn AI agents into attack tools, redirecting their actions and siphoning the data they process.

Secure Email Gateways Miss Many Phish

Email security is catching less than it should. 41.3% of phishing emails bypass secure email gateways, peaking at 48.3% in July 2026. Real domains, valid certificates, and genuine consent screens are now part of the attack, so filters built on lookalike detection fall short. In fact, 58.1% of the phish that gateways miss still pass DMARC.

When the filter misses, the employee becomes the last line of defense. Real-time coaching and continuous training keep that layer working, especially as lures get more personal and more convincing.

What This Means for Security Leaders

The pattern is consistent. Phishing has moved from fake infrastructure to borrowed infrastructure, and from broad campaigns to targeted, automated ones. Trust signals alone are no longer proof of safety.

Standard secure email gateways and native mail filters were built for a threat landscape that no longer exists. As adversaries abuse genuine cloud infrastructure, deploy specialized reverse-proxy toolkits, and hijack trusted AI platforms, perimeter-based defenses simply cannot keep pace with localized, highly targeted attacks. Your security stack needs to be as agile, adaptive, and geographically aware as the threat actors themselves.

By moving toward an integrated platform fueled by deep behavioral analytics and real-time threat intelligence, your security posture shifts from reactive filtering to continuous, automated defense. Delivering real-time behavioral coaching at the exact moment of risk transforms your workforce into an active line of defense, securing both your human workforce and your autonomous AI tooling across every global operation.

Title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
Context: A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain...
Full Text: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register. Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register. A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said. The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were. This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets. “There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks." The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions. “Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

Title: Imposter abused trust in OpenAI, Anthropic, and 30 others to hunt for secrets
Context: However, institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers...
Full Text:
Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets.

A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider. “It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths,” Cequence’s director of threat research, Will Glazier, said in a blog post.

Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solution management at Black Duck, who reviewed Cequence’s findings, points out that the scanner tested whether websites treated an AI bot’s self-declared name as proof of its identity. “The user-agent header is where a visitor names itself, and setting it costs nothing,” he said.

Glazier said defending against such impersonation requires verifying every claimed identity before trusting it.

While Cequence confirmed observing extensive scanning activity attributed to a single threat actor, it did not report a breach. “On one day in October, the actor reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic,” the company said.

A rotating cast of AI identities hunts for secrets

According to Glazier, the scanner cycled through roughly 32 AI bot identities and targeted organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software. The activity was observed from at least late September through late October 2026.

Instead of crawling publicly accessible pages, the scanner requested sensitive paths associated with configuration and credential files. Working through a list of approximately 90 file paths, it sent bursts of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds before moving on, Cequence said.

The same bot machine was observed claiming to represent OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity within seconds. It also used more than 300 cloud addresses in a single day, making static IP blocklists less effective as a standalone defense.

“Fraud is now polymorphic: AI lets attackers vary their approach every time, so legacy, static fraud defenses decay faster than teams can update them,” warned Patrick Harr, chief executive officer at DataVisor. However, institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers do, he noted.

Nearly all the scanner’s requests were blocked or failed, Cequence noted.

Don’t trust the agent’s name, verify it

Cequence recommends verifying AI crawlers through published address ranges, signed requests, or direct integrations rather than relying on self reported identities. Security teams should also flag bots that request credential files, keep secrets out of web-accessible directories, and assess automated traffic based on its behavior.

Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security, said organizations must extend zero-trust controls and least-privilege policies to AI agents, API keys, and service accounts. He also urged businesses to replace long-lived local credentials with centrally managed secrets.

“When an identity starts looking for sensitive files it shouldn’t need, real-time threat detection must flag and terminate that machine session instantly,” Barney added.

Title: 26,400 Valid Cloud and AI Credentials Found Exposed in Public Gitee Repositories
Context: 2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections PHP Issues Emergency Patches for Two Critical PHP2Shell RCE Flaws as...
Full Text:
26,400 credentials that developers left in public code on Gitee, a Chinese code-hosting service, still worked when a researcher tested them. Anyone who copied one from that code could have used it.

Independent researcher Ben Zimmermann found them by scanning 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and reported the results on October 28. Most were keys for cloud and AI services, led by 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs.

Zimmermann sent the vendors with the most exposed keys a list of their credentials, but he did not contact the developers who leaked them. When he published, he had not confirmed that any of the reported credentials had been revoked. So anyone who has pushed a key to a public Gitee repository cannot assume it has been revoked.

The scan ran for about a month, but Zimmermann did not provide the dates, so it is unclear how long ago the credentials were tested. He also did not say whether anyone else had used them.

He ran two secret scanners, TruffleHog and Kingfisher, over every repository. Both tried each credential against the service that issued it and kept only those that worked, he wrote.

The scanners read each repository's full commit history. A key that a developer later removed from the code could still be found and counted there.

The 26,400 figure counts each credential once, regardless of how many repositories it appeared in. By commit date, 12,242 of the credentials came from 2025, nearly half the total. Some dated to the late 2000s.

What Was Exposed

After the Alibaba Cloud keys, the largest groups were 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, 1,489 keys for Zhipu's BigModel AI platform, and 1,348 OpenAI keys. Smaller numbers were found for GitHub, AWS, Google Cloud and Google's Gemini.

One of the credentials was "an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform," Zimmermann wrote. He did not name the platform or say what the credential could reach.

What a working key lets someone do depends on the service. OpenAI says that a compromised key allows another person to use the account's quota without the owner's consent. That can cause "data loss, unexpected charges," a used-up monthly quota, and interrupted API access.

A YouTube API key is a Google Cloud API key that identifies a project, Google says. Without API restrictions, such a key can be used with every API that accepts Google Cloud keys.

What to Do If You Committed Keys

Treat any key that has ever been in a public Gitee repository as exposed, and revoke it at the provider. Deleting a key from the code or rewriting the repository's history does not revoke it, as noted by TruffleHog's maker, Truffle Security.

Alibaba Cloud: create a new AccessKey pair, switch your apps to it, then disable and delete the old pair. Check for unexpected charges and for resources created or deleted that you did not need, Alibaba Cloud's leak response plan says. ActionTrail shows the key's API calls for the last 90 days, but data operations in services such as OSS and SLS have to be checked in each service's own logs.

Google and YouTube API keys: rotate the key, which creates a new key with the same restrictions, update your apps to use it, then delete the old key. Add API restrictions so the key works only with the APIs you need.

OpenAI: rotate the key immediately from the API Keys page, as OpenAI advises, and set spend limits to help limit charges from a leaked key.

Two Scanners, Different Results

MongoDB makes Kingfisher, and Zimmermann's post was developed with its Kingfisher team.

In this scan, TruffleHog found 12,737 credentials that worked, and Kingfisher found 14,664, but only 1,001 were found by both. Each tool alone found about half of the total.

TruffleHog found almost all of the Alibaba Cloud keys. Kingfisher found all 1,489 BigModel keys, because TruffleHog has no detector for Zhipu's keys, Zimmermann wrote.

Teams that rely on a single scanner should verify its detectors against the services they use.

Gitee and Other Code Hosts

China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology chose Gitee in 2020 as the base for a national open-source code-hosting platform.

Gitee's public API is limited, and a 2021 attempt to study leaked credentials on the site gave up because of it.

Gitee's rate, 3.64 working credentials per 1,000 repositories scanned, is higher than the rates from earlier scans of GitLab (3.11) and Bitbucket (2.39). Those scans used only TruffleHog, Zimmermann wrote.

Based on TruffleHog's results alone, Gitee's rate is 1.76, but that count excludes services TruffleHog does not cover, such as Zhipu. So neither figure shows which platform leaks more.

Title: Online Scam Volumes Double to Overtake Phishing
Context: The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time
Full Text:
Detections of online scams doubled between July 2025 and June 2026, as cybercriminals focused on more direct ways to generate revenue from victims, according to Akamai.

The security vendor’s latest State of the Internet (SOTI) report features data from partner Bolster AI, revealing that scam activity overtook phishing for the first time.

It recorded around 6.4 million online scams in the period April-June 2026, versus 3.2 million in July-September 2025.

This category typically includes fake stores, investment scams, tech support scams and payment fraud, it said.

“The fight against fraud is no longer just an isolated financial function; it is a critical, cross-functional cybersecurity imperative,” said Patrick Sullivan, CTO, security strategy at Akamai. “As autonomous AI agents and synthetic identities redefine how customers interact with brands, threat actors are exploiting these same vectors to conduct business logic abuse and zero-click data exfiltration.”

Read more on digital scams: Social Media Platforms Earn Billions from Scam Ads.

However, phishing – which Akamai defines as attempts to steal credentials, authentication info and data via brand impersonation – also rose during the period.

Phishing detections increased by 61%, driven by reusable phishing kits, industrialized infrastructure, and AI.

The latter has helped to decrease the average phishing attack lifespan by more than 50%, dropping from 48 days (Q4 2025) to 22 days (Q2 2026), the report claimed.

“Adversaries leverage AI to generate dynamic templates, produce multilingual lures at scale, and deploy condition-aware evasion – drastically lowering costs while bypassing legacy defenses,” it explained.

“Conversely, security teams use AI to compress investigation and reduce workflows from days to less than an hour through automated indicator analysis, infrastructure clustering, and evidence collection, disrupting attacks before victims are impacted.”

The Human Impact of Scams

Over 80% of scam victims in the US reported suicidal thoughts following the crime, according to new data from the non-profit Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) published on October 28.

A large part of this is down to the self-blame and social stigma attached to scams, the ITRC claimed. It also blamed “institutional ghosting" for the mental anguish that victims often feel.

“When general consumer scam victims overcame their shame to seek help, institutions frequently compounded the injury,” it explained. “Nearly nine in 10 general consumer scam victims asked an organization for help and were never contacted, and 67.2% reported that the organizations they contacted ‘made me feel it was my own fault.’”

A lack of support can also leave victims exposed to recovery scams.

“Abandoned by legitimate institutions and desperate to undo the damage, 78.9% of general consumer scam victims (and 90.9% of those experiencing suicidal ideation) paid a fee to a third party who promised to recover their stolen money, fix their credit or catch the scammer – compared to just 6.5% of scam victims who connected with the ITRC,” the report said.

Apple’s latest updates include a fix for a CoreGraphics bug that may have been exploited in targeted attacks. The fix is now available for older iPhones and iPads.

Apple released security updates on October 26. Apple first fixed the flaw in iOS 26.7.1. Its latest updates also bring the fix to older devices that can’t run iOS 26, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad.

The iOS 18.7.11 update is a backport: it brings a fix from a newer software version to an older one. Here, Apple has made the fix available to older devices running iOS 18, so they can be protected without upgrading to an operating system they don’t support.

How to update your Apple devices

How to update your iPhone or iPad

For iOS and iPadOS users, here’s how to check if you’re using the latest software version:

Go to Settings > General > Software Update. You will see if there are updates available and be guided through installing them.

Turn on Automatic Updates if you haven’t already—you’ll find it on the same screen.

How to update your Mac

To update macOS on any supported Mac, use the Software Update feature, which Apple designed to work consistently across all recent versions. Here are the steps:

Click the Apple menu in the upper-left corner of your screen.

Choose System Settings (or System Preferences on older versions).

Select General in the sidebar, then click Software Update on the right. On older macOS, just look for Software Update directly.

Your Mac will check for updates automatically. If updates are available, click Update Now (or Upgrade Now for major new versions) and follow the on-screen instructions. Before you upgrade to macOS Tahoe 26, please read these instructions.

Enter your administrator password if prompted, then let your Mac finish the update (it might need to restart during this process).

Keep your Mac plugged in and connected to the internet until the update is done.

Restart your device when prompted.

Technical details

The headline bug is CVE-2026-86950, in CoreGraphics, Apple’s framework for drawing graphics, images and PDF content. It’s an out-of-bounds write flaw, where software writes data outside the memory set aside for it. The result is that “processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution.”

Apple says it is aware of a report that the flaw may have been exploited in an “extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals” on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

That wording indicates Apple believes the bug was used in real attacks against a limited group of users.

Usually, journalists, activists and officials are the targets of this kind of attack. If you think you could be a target of highly sophisticated spyware, you should update, restart your phone, and consider applying Apple’s Lockdown Mode.

Title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
Context: In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at...
Full Text:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.

It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.

Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.

He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.

The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.

An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.

With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.

Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.
