Title: ICO Reprimands Staffordshire Police After Domestic Abuse Breach
Context: Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to...
Full Text:
A UK police force committed a serious breach of data protection law after sharing the home address of a domestic abuse victim with their abuser, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has revealed.

The privacy regulator issued a reprimand to Staffordshire Police on October 28, following the incident in March 2024.

The force had served the abuser, “P,” a Domestic Violence Protection Notice (DVPN) on their release from prison in order to protect the abuse victim, or “data subject.”

However, it erroneously included that person’s home address, which was not previously known to P.

“As a consequence of the investigation into the relevant incident the commission has become aware of allegations that P subjected the data subject to both physical and emotional abuse over a period of several years, resulting in the data subject having to relocate their home address on numerous occasions in order to escape the alleged abuse,” the reprimand noted.

“In this context, the data subject’s current address was highly sensitive information and should have been handled as such.”

Read more on police privacy breaches: Police Scotland Fined After Sharing Victim’s Phone Data.

Despite the serious nature of the breach, the ICO decided not to fine the police force, even though the regulator found that it failed to put in place “appropriate measures” to prevent the disclosure, “including poor completion rates for mandatory training in both data protection and issuing DVPNs.”

It argued that Staffordshire Police had since made improvements to reduce the risk of a similar event taking place in the future. These included increased training completion rates, new leadership roles for domestic abuse cases, new internal procedures and new technology to improve services for victims.

ICO head of investigations, Sally-Anne Poole, said the case is a reminder of the importance of getting the basics right.

“Every organization must be doing everything necessary to protect the personal information in their care, especially where there is a known risk to someone's safety,” she added. “Whether in policing, health or local government, we urge organizations to take responsibility for training their staff and putting appropriate systems in place to avoid these incidents and the harm they can cause.”

Advice for Handling Sensitive Information

The ICO warned back in 2023 that organizations handling the personally identifiable information (PII) of domestic abuse victims could put lives at risk if breaches occur.

It said at the time that it had issued reprimands to seven organizations in the previous 14 months after sensitive PII was breached, including one police force.

The latest revelations will do little to allay concerns that the regulator’s public sector approach – which favors warnings, reprimands and enforcement notices over fines – is not having the desired effect.

After this latest incident the ICO advised organizations handling sensitive PII to:

Ensure staff know how to handle the PII of people experiencing domestic abuse with extra care

Review default templates and processes to ensure PII is only included where legally necessary

Regularly check contact information to avoid disclosing information to an old address, email or phone number

Always double check before any PII is transferred, altered or disclosed

Ensure training is thorough, relevant and tailored to the tasks staff actually carry out

Title: GitHub Launches npm Firewall to Block Malicious Packages Before Installation
Context: The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud
Full Text:
GitHub has announced that it's introducing a new package firewall as a preview to block installation of suspicious npm packages during installation time.

"The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate," GitHub said.

The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

According to the Microsoft subsidiary, the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories so as to deter malware attacks that compromise systems when packages are installed.

This behavior can expose users to severe security risks, especially when artificial intelligence (AI) agents and CI runners automatically install dependencies to complete a task or build without their explicit permission.

The idea is that endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of directly pointing to the public package registries. The firewall then checks package downloads against policy controls such as minimum package age and malware advisories, and blocks downloads that do not meet those policies.

To use the firewall, administrators are required to configure policy controls, such as the ones listed below -

Block known malware by checking against the GitHub Advisory Database for active malware advisories

Block packages based on the severity of vulnerabilities by checking the GitHub Advisory Database for flaws that affect the requested package version. The control defaults to "Critical only" as the severity level that blocks an installation, although users can choose "High or higher," "Medium or higher," or "Any severity."

Block attestation downgrades by comparing attestations for the requested package version with those of earlier versions and stop the download if the requested version does not have an SLSA attestation.

Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks, which can be abused to steal sensitive data.

Block packages based on a cooldown period that prevents versions that are newer than the configured minimum age from being installed. The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day. Users can disable it by setting it to 0.

Users who need access to a package that gets blocked erroneously by the firewall can submit an exception request, which can then be approved by enterprise administrators and security managers.

The development comes as Rust 1.100, which is scheduled for release on November 12, 2026, readies to add support for a configurable minimum publish age, allowing security scanners and maintainers time to flag and block malicious crate releases before they can be installed or used by users.

The value, defined via the "global-min-publish-age" option in "cargo/config.toml," allows users to specify a minimum publication age in days or weeks. If left unspecified, a seven-day waiting period is applied by default to skip releases published within that window.

Over the past year, similar waiting periods have been implemented across open-source ecosystems, including npm, Python, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Ruby, Bun, pnpm, and Yarn, as a way to bolster software supply chain security by reducing the chance that a newly published, unreviewed version is immediately pulled into a build.

Cooldown periods help add friction and slow down attacks in which a bad actor publishes a poisoned version of a popular package after seizing control of a maintainer account, thereby preventing rapid spread through manual or automated installations.

"The tradeoff is that legitimate fixes have to wait, too, unless developers make an exception," Socket said. "Malicious code also doesn't magically become harmless with age. A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown. The value is in buying researchers, maintainers, and registries time to act before the next dependency update carries an attack further."

Title: Vulnerability exploitation rising as the root cause of many breaches
Context: “Phishing is still a major threat, but exploiting a vulnerability can give an attacker a direct route into a system without needing to persuade an employee to click a link,”...
Full Text:
More evidence has emerged that attackers are turning to vulnerabilities rather than phishing as a means for breaking into corporate systems.

Incident response firm LevelBlue’s Q3 findings show that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 14% of initial access cases, up from 4% in Q2. The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated.

In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report — which is based on the combined evidence of multiple incident response vendors and law enforcement agencies — placed exploitation at the center of nearly a third (31%) of breaches, up from 20% the year before and ahead of credential abuse for the first time.

Phishing/social engineering remain the top initial intrusion vector, accounting for 42% of breaches, down from 65% in Q2, according to LevelBlue’s Q3 report.

Living on the edge

Scott Doerr, experienced CISO turned founder of ForeGuard Advisory Group, said the biggest driver of the trend is exploitation of security flaws in internet-facing edge devices such as VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances.

“LevelBlue’s most-exploited CVE lists this year are dominated by those appliances from SonicWall, Fortinet, Palo Alto, Ivanti, and BeyondTrust,” said Doerr. “They’re exposed by design, and a working exploit puts the attacker directly on the network with no user to fool and often no MFA prompt in the way.”

Mitchell Spicer, co-founder and COO of Revelion AI, an autonomous AI penetration-testing platform, backed this assessment.

“Phishing is still a major threat, but exploiting a vulnerability can give an attacker a direct route into a system without needing to persuade an employee to click a link,” said Spicer. “The opportunity is particularly attractive when organizations have internet-facing services that are unpatched, misconfigured, or forgotten.”

AI offers a double-edged sword

AI is adding another dimension to the cat and mouse game between attackers and enterprise security defenders.

“It [AI] is making parts of reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery cheaper and more accessible, which can help defenders find weaknesses but can also help attackers identify potential targets,” Spicer said. “The longer those weaknesses remain exposed, the more opportunity attackers have to find and exploit them.”

Full Text:
A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Dangerous Configurations for Codex, Claude Code Users

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

Grave Risks for Gray Market Users

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

Title: NIST Publishes Guidance to Meet Federal Post-Quantum Deadlines
Context: For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to...
Full Text:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has published official guidance designed to help federal government agencies meet the 2031 deadline to transition post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

President Trump’s Executive Order 14412, published in June 2026, mandated that all US federal agencies transition “high value assets” and “high impact systems” to use PQC for key establishment by December 31 2030 and for “digital signatures” by December 31 2031.

NIST’s new document sets out a transition plan for agencies and organizations that work with the federal government to meet this deadline. The guidance references the post-quantum algorithm standards that NIST published in 2024.

“These deadlines leave little margin: meeting them will require immediate and sustained action by federal agencies and by the technology providers, standards organizations, and infrastructure operators on which federal systems depend,” NIST wrote.

How to Prioritize the PQC Transition

The NIST report emphasized the logistical complexity that comes with the PQC transition. It outlined the approaches that can be taken for different types of systems and data to ensure security teams to take a risk-based approach to the transition.

For example, agencies and federal suppliers should prioritize the migration to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time, due to the risk of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks.

The NIST guidance also accommodates a hybrid option for particularly sensitive systems, which combines conventional encryption with PQC – essentially providing two layers of security. However, this approach would demand more computational resources.

It also sets out how long less critical systems can continue to use conventional encryption protocols.

NIST mathematician Dustin Moody commented: “We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out. It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.”

The report also urges federal agencies to look beyond their own system components and at its entire cryptographic supply chain.

Post-Quantum Preparations Ramp Up

The new NIST guidance follows a series of pledges around PQC transition from other governments and across the tech world.

Governments like Canada, Australia, Japan, and the UK have set deadlines ranging from 2028 to 2030 as milestones for ensuring critical government systems are quantum safe.

While many of these mandates are focused on government and critical infrastructure organizations, they generally come with a push for other sectors to follow suit and set a roadmap for PQC migration.

Large tech firms, including Cloudflare, Google and Microsoft, have set a 2029 deadline for full PQC migration. Meanwhile, Apple, AWS, IBM and Meta, have officially started rolling out NIST-approved PQC algorithms into their products.

Read now: How Cybersecurity Vendors Are Preparing for the Post-Quantum Era

The situation has been made more urgent after warnings from tech companies like Microsoft that advances in quantum R&D mean that cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs) capable of cracking asymmetric encryption could appear sooner than anticipated – potentially within the next five years.

Title: Securing MCP servers before the AI rollout outpaces security
Context: For a first pass, to speed up the assessment, you can drop threats with very low or low likelihood
Full Text:
Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself.

You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely.

What is an MCP server?

MCP servers are like the ODBC of the 1990s. Before ODBC, every application needed custom code to query databases. ODBC defined a single standard on how to talk to databases, and database vendors just developed a driver to talk to their solution.

MCP servers work in the same way: the AI app just needs to use the standardized methods to communicate with the local MCP host, and each available tool (databases, file shares, CRMs) provides an MCP server that translates the MCP transmissions into the tool’s native format. So, you just need a driver on your MCP host to talk to any available endpoint.

Fig.1 – MCP architecture.

Greg Neville

The MCP Hosts will be in your environment, and you can control the ingress and egress traffic allowed for each MCP Host. One MCP Host can also access more than one MCP Server, allowing greater scalability, but it also adds risk.

Fig. 2 – Example marketing LLM application.

Greg Neville

Top priority MCP controls

At this stage, define requirements before the MCP server implementation gets too far. Establish a list of requirements for the initial phase. Focus on the controls that deliver the most value and reduce the most risk.

Input validation and sanitization

Inputs from any indirect external sources outside your control are untrusted and should be treated as high-risk for abuse. Identifying and removing malicious input is vital for preventing misuse of an LLM application. Input validation and sanitization include strong authentication and authorization, detection of malicious code and jailbreak attempts, and filtering sensitive or regulated data.

Output validation and sanitization

These controls often involve enforcing a specific structure to facilitate validation, context-aware encoding and removal of unusual or unapproved data. Incorporate human oversight for higher-risk actions or other high-importance outputs, such as financial reporting.

Network segmentation

Segmenting MCP hosts can reduce the attack surface and limit potential abuse by restricting ingress and egress traffic to authorized systems and ports.

Server hardening

Servers should be configured following comprehensive guidelines such as the CIS Model. Hardening measures include disabling unnecessary or default accounts, closing unused ports and adjusting system settings to minimize vulnerabilities. Ideally, use infrastructure-as-code (IaaC) to make these servers ephemeral and further reduce the risk of a compromise spreading.

Least access principle

Permissions will be key in limiting the blast radius of what an attacker can do. Multiple MCP servers can be used to reduce over-permission by grouping tools that have similar access needs. Limit access to only the users, tenants and workloads that the server needs to provide the service. Also, limit token life to as short as possible in case any token is stolen.

Encryption

Encryption is hopefully a part of the server hardening process but needs to be called out on its own. Deploy encryption at rest and in transit end-to-end, with strong key management practices.

Tool management

Limiting the number of available tools on MCP hosts and restricting their capabilities to the minimum necessary can help reduce risks related to tool misuse and compromise.

Third-party assessments and contracts

Ensure third-party providers implement appropriate security controls, preferably verified by independent bodies such as SOC 2, HITRUST or ISO 27001/2. Contracts should specify control requirements, and any identified high-risk gaps should be addressed through remediation agreements. A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) should be in place if protected health information (PHI) is involved.

Audit and logging

Maintaining detailed logs of AI actions and prompts is crucial for detecting issues like hacking attempts, AI misuse and prompt abuse.

Human-in-the-loop

Human-in-the-loop is critical for any high-risk action that an LLM application may try to take, or any highly critical data that is produced. Verify administrative actions to critical systems before allowing them to execute or be produced.

Pre-production testing

An important, often-overlooked step is to monitor implementation and perform pre-production testing to make sure your key controls work correctly. Some potential tests would be:

Enter fake PHI, SSNs, account numbers or whatever data is appropriate to your environment to make sure those data types are being flagged or blocked.

Test authentication and authorization by logging in and confirming what tools you can see and access.

Test inbound and outbound network filtering to confirm only approved systems are reachable.

Confirm the server(s) have been hardened according to the hardening policy.

Confirm all critical events and actions are being logged.

You’ve tried to work with the CTO and get him to agree to all these controls being implemented, but you don’t see the project plan changing or you’re getting fuzzy dates back. You may need to enlist other executives to help influence the decision.

The risk management approach

If you have a Risk Committee in place, it could help prioritize control requirements and timelines, so they’re implemented sooner rather than later. You need to be open to prioritizing certain controls over others to avoid major roadblocks and delays in moving the product forward. A proper AI Risk Assessment will help determine the applicable threats and controls to your environment, as well as the inherent and residual risks.

For an AI threat list to build your risk assessment, I use the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for my assessments and reporting. Scope the threats and rate their inherent risk in your environment. For a first pass, to speed up the assessment, you can drop threats with very low or low likelihood.

For the Risk Committee, however, communicate the impacts in their language to help them understand. I would communicate the issues in terms of productivity loss, downtime, loss of customer trust, regulatory fines and other industry-specific impacts, such as patient care, trading errors, bad credit decisions, unfair claims or underwriting, worker safety and service availability. Don’t make it a quantitative exercise; keep it qualitative but be prepared to explain your ratings to maintain your peers’ trust.

Good outcomes

At this point, if all went well, you have provided the governance and input to limit risk to the organization. Incidents can and will cause downtime, fines and reputational damage if key controls are not in place. Helping your organization lower the risk of this occurring is a job well done.

Title: MR ROBOT Malware-as-a-Service Targets Indian Bank Customers
Context: Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand
Full Text:
A new Android malware-as-a-service (MaaS) operation has been found renting customized banking trojans to criminals targeting Indian bank customers, with one affiliate intercepting 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

The operation, branded MR ROBOT by its operators, was detailed in research published on October 28 by threat intelligence firm CloudSEK. Its researchers found an operator control panel, a Telegram-based storefront and a malware builder that let affiliates create bank-themed Android trojans on demand.

The lures are distributed through fake Play Store-style pages and messaging-app links, and impersonate banks as well as utility providers and government services.

MR ROBOT Turns Banking Malware into Subscription Service

CloudSEK said MR ROBOT is not a single actor’s campaign but a multi-tenant crimeware platform. Each affiliate receives its own application ID and can generate Android packages impersonating specific Indian banks.

The platform supports a tiered reseller model with sub-admin accounts, and licenses access for set periods through a control panel identified as version 7.0.

The malware intercepts text messages carrying one-time passwords (OTPs), shows fake screens to harvest banking credentials, card details, PINs and identity information, and can silently enable call forwarding. CloudSEK said this reroutes incoming calls, including banks’ fraud-check callbacks, to a number the attackers’ control.

The storefront, a Telegram bot called APK Shield, offered around 36 lure apps, including bank impersonations and fake apps for utility bills, telecom services, traffic fines and government services.

One Affiliate Intercepted More Than 5400 Text Messages

CloudSEK tracked two affiliates. One affiliate’s panel held around 154 enrolled devices and approximately 3270 intercepted messages, while an exposed Firebase database linked to a second held 153 devices and 5407 messages.

That data was collected between July 16 and 30, 2026, and around 4000 of the messages came from bank and telecommunications short codes. CloudSEK said call forwarding was active on 58% of the devices.

Each build receives a fresh signing certificate and can hide from the Android launcher after installation. CloudSEK said MR ROBOT shares call forwarding and per-customer builders with FatBoyPanel and RedWing, operations previously documented by Zimperium, but its kit, storefront and panel had not been publicly reported.

Read more on Android banking malware: Rokarolla Trojan Combines Banking Fraud With Device Surveillance

CloudSEK advised users never to install bank-branded apps from links sent by text, WhatsApp or Telegram, and urged banks to move customers from text-message OTPs toward app-based or Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication where feasible.

Title: Admin dropped the F-bomb in a password to show hackers who was really 1337
Context: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale
Full Text: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims. Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs. A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now. Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights. Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps. At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in. “So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.” Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account. But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [l337 5p34k]. The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. Schloss assumed it wouldn't work and sat on it for a week. During a briefing he had with the IT crew, he presented his findings and then asked who set up the admin account with this funny password. “You could see everyone kind of looking at the senior manager of IT like ‘that was you, wasn’t it,’” Schloss explained. “He’s kind of got this face. I’m like ‘oh shit, like what?’ Turns out that ‘heyhackergof***yourself’ was the actual password for his admin account." On Monday, Schloss tried the username and password combo and, lo and behold, it gave him complete control of the entire network. He was then able to get access to other passwords and many of them were also insults directed at potential hackers. Schloss understood that the team was still angry about a breach they had suffered six months prior and, should they be breached again, wanted to give the finger to the hacker who did it. Unfortunately, their system was still vulnerable because of the outdated machine that was hooked up to the domain and he was able to gain control. The lesson here is really to patch your systems and avoid using insecure legacy OSes whenever possible, because it was an old machine that let Schloss in, not a weak password. Indeed, “hackergof***yourself” in leet speak isn’t a terrible password, just an embarrassing one if it's exposed. ®

Title: PHP2Shell will persist in enterprise environments for years
Context: For example, if a WAF looks only at the first few kilobytes of a request, an attacker can simply pad the beginning of their payload with junk data to push the malicious exploit...
Full Text:
Two critical vulnerabilities were announced last week in PHP, the internet’s most widely used web application runtime, and they came with the familiar warning to patch immediately. But CISOs will have to deal with the long tail of these flaws for years due to widespread PHP integration into third-party products with patching cycles customers don’t control.

NAS devices, firewalls, VPN gateways, printers, building management panels, industrial IoT devices, and human-machine interfaces (HMIs) inside operational technology (OT) networks have web panels powered by PHP runtimes that cannot be patched directly. And many of these runtimes have unsupported versions for which upstream patches are not available.

Vulnerabilities in widely used technologies can linger for years, and some deployments never get patched because they sit inside products that are out of support but still in service. One year after Log4Shell was disclosed in December 2021, nearly three quarters of organizations still had assets vulnerable to the critical flaw in the ubiquitous Log4j Java library, which remained a top attack vector in real-world attacks throughout 2023.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) could be even worse than Log4Shell for enterprises that cannot identify and patch all their assets — and attacks are already under way. On Monday, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, confirming active exploitation. Researchers had previously reported widespread scanning and attempted exploitation, but no confirmed compromise of production systems.

“PHP2Shell has the potential to become a Log4Shell-scale event, but for a different reason,” Sai Molige, senior manager of threat hunting at Forescout, told CSO via email. “With Log4j, the main problem was finding a library you didn’t know you had. With PHP, much of the forgotten infrastructure will be found, but won’t have an upstream fix.”

When patches for third-party appliances and software products can take weeks to arrive from vendors, security teams must reduce exposure by other means, both at the internet edge and inside internal networks. And that’s only after building an inventory of impacted assets, which is not straight forward for these flaws.

The patching challenges

The PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 as the official fixed versions, but relying on version numbers alone is not enough due to the way PHP is distributed. Most servers run Linux distributions that deliver application updates through their own package managers, including long-term support (LTS) distributions that bundle older PHP versions. In many cases, patches will have to be manually backported by package maintainers for those specific distros.

For example, PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are officially end-of-life, even though they’re still widely used. The PHP developers published minimal source backports for those versions to help package maintainers, but PHP 7.3 and older were not covered at all. Vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck found that 42% of the 2.6 million internet-facing PHP hosts it scanned were running end-of-life branches, including 27% on PHP 3.x through 7.3 and 15% on 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1.

Obtaining the fix on LTS distributions requires different approaches depending on the bundled PHP version. On Ubuntu 22.04 it arrives as a free PHP 8.1 update; on Ubuntu 20.04 the PHP 7.4 fix requires a Pro subscription; on Debian 11 the fix for the bundled PHP 7.4 sits behind a Freexian extended-support contract; and on AlmaLinux 8 it arrives as a backport for the retired PHP 7.2, 7.3, and 8.0. Red Hat Enterprise Linux, SUSE, Alpine, and Amazon Linux each draw their own support boundaries and those determine whether a fix exists at all for different distro versions.

The version numbers for backported patches can also be inconsistent with upstream versions, adding to the inventory challenges. For example, AlmaLinux’s patched php-8.3.33-1.el10_2.alma.1 is below the upstream’s fixed version number for that branch: 8.3.36. Therefore, a scanner that reads a PHP version banner could flag a host as vulnerable even when the distribution has applied the fix.

On top of all that, there are pre-built container, virtual machine, and firmware images for all sorts of third-party enterprise products that have their own bundled runtimes and that are much harder to inspect using automated scanners.

“The PHP team has done a good job in a horrible situation,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and CTO at software supply chain security firm Echo. “The problem for most companies is they don’t know where they’re running PHP. It’s in base images and in components that bundle their own runtime, and a lot of it is on versions older than 8.2 that are past end of life.”

There are no public estimates on how many enterprise appliances or IoT and OT devices might run vulnerable versions of PHP, but they exist and some are reachable from the internet. Security firm Flare used internet scans from multiple sources that covered 2,220,231 service records from PHP hosts across 224 countries. In a regional sample across a single US state they identified NAS devices, VPN gateways, remote access portals, building automation systems, and physical access controllers.

“Organizations still view PHP as a basic application dependency, but it’s often embedded deep inside appliances, hosting platforms, and upstream container images where day-one patching simply isn’t an option,” said Tom Kellermann, vice president of AI security and threat research at TrendAI. “The real battle isn’t just the vulnerability; it’s visibility.”

PHP is also found inside industrial devices that can be in use for a decade or more and for which firmware patches take time to develop and deploy. Some of these devices need to be isolated until fixes arrive.

Vulnerability management firm Cogent Security scanned dozens of Fortune 500 customer environments on the PHP2Shell disclosure day and found 2,266 affected assets per company on average, with 926 that were running the PHP service actively and 122 that were exposed to the internet.

The company’s assessment focused on servers and virtual machines, not hardware appliances and OT devices. This highlights that the problem for enterprises won’t be the unavailability of scanners, but their lack of visibility inside all types of assets. As such, organizations will need a combination of strategies to discover all PHP installations in their environments: from versions reported by host-based package managers to network scanners and software bills of materials where available.

Reducing exposure while waiting for patches

Having an up-to-date inventory is important, but a complete map of PHP installations does not solve the issue of runtimes bundled in third-party products, each with its own patching schedule and mitigation instructions that can range from disabling the web management interface to completely isolating the device on the network.

Just to give a few examples, Palo Alto Networks scheduled updates for some of its PAN-OS devices for this week and Siemens advised customers of its RUGGEDCOM APE1808 devices for industrial networks that are also powered by PAN-OS to follow Palo Alto’s advisory. Delta Controls patched its enterprise building management platform enteliWEB, but affected HVAC and room controllers are still awaiting firmware patches. Some NetModule IIoT and industrial routers from Belden are confirmed to be vulnerable but patches are still being developed.

Until patches become available, which could take weeks in some cases, organizations will have to monitor the advisories for the third-party products they use and follow the temporary mitigations instructions for each of them. There will also likely be situations where some products have reached end of life and will never receive a patch, especially those supporting legacy applications organizations still need to keep operational.

For a system that cannot be updated, the measures fall into three groups:

Take the vulnerable web application off insecure network segments

Put firewall controls in front of it

Assess if a compromise may have already happened

In some cases, management over HTTP or HTTPS might not be needed and the same functionality could be achieved over SSH or other protocols. For example, both Belden and Delta advise customers to disable the embedded HTTP server until patches become available. NetScaler advises customers to keep the management GUI and API reachable only from trusted administrative networks.

As far as firewall detection rules go, there are some limitations. At the application layer, Web application firewalls (WAFs) can help, but they cannot block all PHP2Shell exploits that abuse multipart data uploads because they don’t usually inspect the full body of a web request, unlike the PHP engine.

A WAF can scan for known attack patterns, but it doesn’t parse the internal structure of these form uploads deeply enough to catch all possible variations, so attackers can tweak the request formatting to potentially slip past the rules. For example, if a WAF looks only at the first few kilobytes of a request, an attacker can simply pad the beginning of their payload with junk data to push the malicious exploit code past the inspection limit.

Furthermore, if an attacker manages to find the direct IP address of a backend system, they could completely bypass the WAF controls. That doesn’t mean that WAF rules are useless, but they are not a silver bullet against exploits. On the cloud side, AWS, Cloudflare, and Microsoft Azure offer WAF protection rules for PHP2Shell already and there are many local enterprise WAFs that have added detection as well.

The other type of firewall protection is at the network layer via intrusion prevention systems (IPS). The issue with these firewalls is that they could be bypassed if they’re not configured to decrypt HTTPS traffic. IPS vendors have already created detections: Palo Alto has Threat ID 543004; Check Point has IPS protection CPAI-2026-15172; Cisco Talos has Snort rules 67359 and 67360 and Suricata rules 3000650 to 3000652 are also available.

But deploying patches and alternative mitigations does not help systems that have already been compromised. And the longer it takes to implement these measures the more likely it is that attackers might have compromised a server.

“The PHP2Shell flaws went from scanning noise to confirmed remote code execution on a honeypot within days of the October 21 patches, and that gap is where most real damage happens,” said Steve Povolny, vice president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam. “Plenty of sites weren’t patched on day one. Some of those servers were probably exploited before anyone noticed, and installing the fix now does nothing about an intruder who got in last week. Patching closes the door. It doesn’t tell you who is already inside.”

Any detection and prevention effort should be accompanied by an investigation of existing logs including web server access and error logs, PHP-FPM logs, WAF and reverse-proxy logs, CDN logs, EDR and process telemetry, DNS and egress logs, authentication logs, file-integrity monitoring, and cloud audit logs.

How to know if you’ve already been hacked

Things to look for in those logs are PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and a PHPSESSID cookie, multipart/form-data sent to endpoints that do not accept uploads, unusually large or malformed multipart bodies, deeply nested field names, repeated POSTs from one source, and spikes in HTTP 500 errors.

Admins should also look for PHP-FPM, Apache, or httpd worker processes spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, base64, or various code interpreters, unexpected child processes under the web service account, reverse shells, outbound connections from web workers, as well as new or modified .php files in web root directories, upload directories and plugin directories. Abnormal PHPSESSID cookie length or corruption, unusually large session files, and unexplained worker restarts or segmentation faults could also be signs of exploitation, according to researchers from security firm Xint.io.

Title: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN flaw, fixed in February, to plant custom malware inside the systems that control an organization's SD-WAN network.

The malware, called KeyDrift, is designed to copy the keys that encrypt traffic between sites and store them for later use, Cisco Talos said on October 28. Talos calls the attacks historical but does not specify when they occurred or whether any keys were sent.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-20127 and has a CVSS score of 10.0. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrative privileges on these control systems. On a Controller, the attacker can log in as a high-privileged internal account that is not root.

When Cisco disclosed the flaw in February, Talos tracked its exploitation as UAT-8616, a cluster of activity it said went back to at least 2023.

In Cisco's traditional key exchange, each SD-WAN router periodically generates an AES key for its traffic and sends it to the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart). The Controller passes the keys on to other routers. A process on the Controller called vdaemon runs the encrypted control connections that carry these keys.

On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted. For a preset list of edge routers, it pulls out their IP addresses and a 32-byte field. Talos assesses that field as the AES-256 key material that the Controller passes between routers.

LittleFilch encrypts what it collects with RSA and writes it to a file. It can then send that data over UDP to an address listed in a settings file, which it deletes after reading. Talos could not recover that settings file.

The group behind KeyDrift, which Talos tracks as UAT-11473, has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

The group's infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, Talos assesses with high confidence. Silent Train is the name Lumen's Black Lotus Labs uses for a network of hacked small-office, home-office, IoT and business devices.

Lumen says Volt Typhoon used the network to hide its activity. CISA, the NSA and the FBI said in 2024 that Volt Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber group.

Talos links UAT-11473 to Volt Typhoon only through the infrastructure overlap. It does not say the two are the same group, or how UAT-11473 relates to UAT-8616, the cluster it reported in February.

Separately, Lumen said on October 28 that Volt Typhoon was exploiting CVE-2026-20127 by late 2025 and continued to exploit it after Cisco disclosed the flaw in February. Lumen does not tie that activity to KeyDrift.

KeyDrift primarily starts via modified runit scripts that Cisco SD-WAN devices use to launch their services, according to Talos. In one version, the script for the SSH service starts a loader script, conf_sshd, before the real SSH server. The conf_sshd script writes vdaemon's process IDs to a file, and a tool called rsshd injects KeyDrift's main module, PolyFlame, into each of those processes.

PolyFlame runs in memory inside vdaemon. It can act as a TinyShell-like backdoor that runs commands and reads and writes files, or as a relay that forwards commands between its command server and other machines. It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address.

On a compromised Validator, formerly vBond, a fake aaamgr service under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ runs a packed loader, aaamgrd, that decrypts and runs PolyFlame. Cisco's real aaamgr component is a Python package and does not normally run as a compiled service.

There are also signs of timestomping: commands the group ran copied the timestamps and permissions of existing files onto its own files.

Affected Releases and Fixes

CVE-2026-20127 affects the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), regardless of their configuration. On-premises systems are affected, as are Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments, including the Cisco Managed and FedRAMP environments. Cisco added the Validator to its advisory on June 16.

Cisco says it is aware of limited exploitation of the flaw. There is no workaround, and the first fixed releases are:

Release train

First fixed release

Earlier than 20.9

Migrate to a fixed release

20.9

20.9.8.2

20.11

20.12.6.1

20.12

20.12.5.3 or 20.12.6.1

20.13

20.15.4.2

20.14

20.15.4.2

20.15

20.15.4.2

20.16

20.18.2.1

20.18

20.18.2.1

Releases earlier than 20.9 and the 20.11, 20.13, 20.14 and 20.16 trains have reached end of software maintenance.

Until they can upgrade, on-premises customers can limit access to ports 22 and 830 to the IP addresses of known controllers and other known systems. Cisco says this step worked in a test environment, but that customers should check how well it works in their own networks. Such guardrails are already in place for Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments.

Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device.

Checking for KeyDrift

Talos advises organizations to install Cisco's fixes, follow Cisco's Catalyst SD-WAN hardening guide and watch for signs of post-compromise activity. Anyone who finds such signs should start incident response and can ask Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for help.

That advice does not say whether upgrading removes KeyDrift from a device that was already compromised, or whether any keys should be replaced. Cisco's February remediation guide for this flaw warns that there could be "existing exploits which are still in place" from before an upgrade.

KeyDrift uses these files and locations, some given only by name:

File: the run script under etc/sv/sshd/, modified to start conf_sshd

Directory: /etc/sv/aaamgr/, a fake service on a compromised Validator

File: aaamgrd, the packed loader

File: conf_sshd, the loader script

File: rsshd, the injector

File: libdssl.so, PolyFlame

File: libcommon.so, LittleFilch

File: /tmp/system-vdaemon, the list of vdaemon process IDs

File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, LittleFilch's encrypted records

File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf, LittleFilch's send settings, deleted after reading

Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift.

Talos released Snort rules on October 28 that look for inbound KeyDrift command-and-control connections: 67387 through 67416 for Snort 2, and 7:44 through 7:73 for Snort 3. Rules 65938 and 65958, already available, cover CVE-2026-20127 itself.

The October 28 rule update lists the Snort 2 rules as disabled by default, so users of the paid Snort Subscriber rule set must turn them on. The Snort 3 rules appear with no default state.

To check for exploitation of the flaw itself, Cisco says to look in /var/log/auth.log for Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin entries from unknown IP addresses. Before opening a TAC case, customers should run request admin-tech on each control component. The remediation guide also recommends rescanning those admin-tech files with the Check Bug Applicability feature on the Bug Search Tool page for bug CSCws52722.

For US federal civilian agencies, CISA's February 25 emergency directive sets out what to do if a root account compromise is found. They must report it to CISA, deploy fresh Manager, Controller and Validator instances from patched images, and move their edge routers to the new systems.

Title: Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause
Context: And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6
Full Text:
Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Inexplicable Data From Italy's Threat Landscape

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Theory #1: Poor Cybersecurity Hygiene

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Nordic CISOs Handle Rising Cyber Threats Remarkably Well

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Theory #2: A Cyber Risk Network Effect

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

Theory #3: Small & Medium-Sized Businesses Shift the Data

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

Title: China-Linked Hackers Exploited VMware ESX Zero-Day to Reduce Audit Trail Visibility
Context: Attacks mounted by Warp Panda involve the exploitation of internet-facing edge devices to obtain initial access, after which the threat actor pivots to VMware vCenter...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a security flaw impacting Broadcom VMware ESX to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, after CrowdStrike revealed that it had been weaponized by a China-nexus threat actor known as Warp Panda in attacks targeting the U.S. legal sector.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an a case of insufficient logging that could permit permit a malicious actor with admin access to perform certain operations without being logged.

In an advisory released in July 2026, Broadcom revealed that the issue was addressed in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025

VMware vSphere Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025

VMware ESX ESXi80U3j-25429389

VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.4

VMware Telco Cloud Platform ESXi80U3j-25429389

The development comes in response to CrowdStrike's 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which revealed that Warp Panda had exploited CVE-2026-41709 as a zero-day in early 2026 with an aim to reduce audit trail visibility.

Warp Panda "exploits internet-facing edge devices using zero-day vulnerabilities and custom malware to maintain covert, persistent access," it said in the report shared with The Hacker News, adding the adversary "actively circumvents detection by bypassing audit logging, harvesting cloud session tokens, and registering rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices."

The threat actor, also tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), Clay Typhoon, and VerdantBamboo, has a storied history of weaponizing zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure devices.

Earlier this month, Google-owned Mandiant also attributed the hacking crew to the zero-day exploitation of a critical improper origin validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deliver malware families like SAWFLY and BARECLAW.

Attacks mounted by Warp Panda involve the exploitation of internet-facing edge devices to obtain initial access, after which the threat actor pivots to VMware vCenter environments to deploy custom malware like BRICKSTORM and SharpStorm to maintain persistent access without attracting attention.

Select intrusions have also involved the targeting of cloud services with an aim to extract user session tokens to access Microsoft 365 environments sans raising any credential-based alerts. In at least one case, Warp Panda is said to have registered a new MFA device on a compromised account as a way to set up persistent access even if the password is changed.

"Warp Panda represents a sustained and strategically focused China-nexus cyber espionage threat to U.S. entities across multiple sectors, including the legal sector," CrowdStrike said.

"The legal sector's concentration of client communications, merger and acquisition materials, active litigation strategy, and cross-client access makes it a high-value collection target for a state-directed adversary seeking intelligence with downstream operational utility."

In light of active exploitation of CVE-2026-41709, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 11, 2026.

Title: Deploying a Local Ghidra Server for Your Malware Analysis Lab, (Thu, Oct 29th)
Context: Collaboration: several analysts can work on the same samples, with read-only, read/write or admin permissions per repository
Full Text:
Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware. Today, thanks to virtualization, it's convenient to play with snapshots in your lab. Start a new investigation from a clean snapshot and take some more when you reached a critical step. But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! Therefore, it's important to store important data outside the VM.

If you do malware analysis with Ghidra[1], your work lives in "projects". A project is a ".gpr" file and a ".rep" directory sitting on the disk of your analysis machine. Every renamed function, comment, structure and bookmark you added is stored there. And,as said before, hours of work can be lost if your VM has issues or you restart to a clean snapshot. When you create a new project in Ghidra, it always asks you if you want a "shared" or "non-shared" project:

Ghidra ships with a component that many people ignore: Ghidra Server. It is included in the standard distribution (no extra download, no licence) and turns your local projects into "shared projects" backed by a central repository. Here are some reasons why it's useful to deploy one in yout lab:

Persistence: revert your VMs as often as you want; the annotated programs are safe on the server.

Versioning: each check-in creates a new version of the program with a comment. You can go back to a previous state of your analysis or compare versions (like a git repot)

Multiple clients: start an analysis on one box and continue it on another one (another VM, your laptop, a colleague's workstation).

Collaboration: several analysts can work on the same samples, with read-only, read/write or admin permissions per repository.

Confidentiality: everything stays in your lab. No sample or customer-related binary is pushed to a third-party service. This matters when you handle files coming from incident response engagements.

From a requirements perspective, the server is lightweight. I'm running Ghidra 12.1.4 in an Ubuntu container on my Proxmox host, but any small Linux VM will do. Recommended specs:

Small Linux VM or container, kept separate from your analysis VMs

2 x CPU, 4GB (enough for small teams, personal use)

8G of storage (may depends on your volume of samples!)

JDK 21 or newer

To avoid incompatibility issues, use the same version of Ghida between the server and clients. Keep versions aligned!

Important remarks about networking:

Ports TCP/13100 & TCP/13101 must be reachable from clients

Clients must be able to resolve the hostname announced by the server

Don't forget that this server will host malicious pieces of code! Treat it as hosting live malware and keep it in your malware analysis lab network! Nothing is executed there, but the repositories contain the raw bytes of every sample you imported. Sounds legit but never expose it to the Internet. Ghidra Server is a Java RMI service.

The basic setup is pretty easy. There is no official container image, but the distribution contains everything needed to run the server as a regular service. First, create a dedicated account, unpack Ghidra and create the repositories directory:

# apt install openjdk-25-jre-headless unzip # useradd -r -m -d /opt/ghidra -s /usr/sbin/nologin ghidra # cd /opt && unzip ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_*.zip # ln -s ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC ghidra-current # mkdir -p /opt/ghidra-repos && chown -R ghidra: /opt/ghidra-repos

The configuration is in "server/server.conf". Set the repositories directory, the account used to run the JVM, and the server parameters:

ghidra.repositories.dir=/opt/ghidra-repos ???????wrapper.app.account=ghidra # Authentication: local Ghidra passwords, expire after 90 days wrapper.app.parameter.1=-a0 wrapper.app.parameter.2=-e90 # Hostname announced to clients wrapper.app.parameter.3=-ip wrapper.app.parameter.4=ghidra.lab.local # Repositories directory (must be the last parameter) wrapper.app.parameter.5=${ghidra.repositories.dir}

The main authentication modes are "-a0" (passwords managed by the server), "-a2" (PKI with client certificates) and "-a4" (JAAS, to plug into LDAP or Active Directory). Leave anonymous access disabled. I'm using the local authentication scheme (-a0).

The "-ip" parameter is important: RMI returns this name to the clients, which reconnect to it on ports 13101 and 13102. If clients can't resolve it, they reach the server on the first port and then fail. If you want to bind the service to a single interface (your VPN interface, for example), add -i <address>.

Install the service, check it and create the users:

# /opt/ghidra-current/server/svrInstall # systemctl status ghidraSvr # ss -tlnp | grep -E '1310[0-2]' # cd /opt/ghidra-current/server # ./svrAdmin -add xavier # ./svrAdmin -list -users

New users get the initial password "changeme" (yes, unsecure...) and must change it at first login. The svrAdmin commands are queued and processed by the running server within a few seconds.

Now, you are ready to use your brand now server! Repositories are created from the Ghidra client:

File > New Project... and select "Shared Project".

Enter the server name (the one used with -ip) and port 13100, then log in.

Click "Create Repository" and give it a name (mine is "MalwareLab"). The user who creates it becomes its administrator.

Choose a local directory and a project name. This is your local working copy.

Access for other analysts is managed from the client (Project > Edit Access List) or from the server, once the repository exists:

# ./svrAdmin -grant john +w MalwareLab # +r read-only, +w read/write, +a admin

A shared project still creates a .gpr file and a .rep directory locally! That's expected: they contain the connection settings, a cache and your checked-out copies. Importing a binary does not send it to the server. It remains a private file until you right-click it and select "Add to Version Control...". From then on, the workflow is similar to any source control system:

Check Out a program to work on it (exclusively or not).

Check In your changes with a comment; each check-in creates a new version.

Versioned files display a version icon in the project tree; files without it are still local only.

Project > Project Info shows the server and repository you are connected to.

How to restore your project if your analysis VM has been reverted to a clean snapshot and the local project is gone? To get everything back, create a new Shared Project, connect to the server and select your existing repository (don't create a new one). The project tree is populated with all checked-in programs. If a file is still checked out by the old instance of the VM, right-click it, select View Checkouts and terminate the stale entry.

What the server can't give back:

Private files never added to version control.

Changes made after the last check-in.

Your client settings (tool layouts, key bindings, script directories, extensions), stored in ~/.config/ghidra/.

Your client certificate and key if you use PKI authentication. Back them up separately!

Before deploying your own server, you can have a look at the ghidra-server project[2] that offers a free server for the RE community. But don't forget that, like any "cloud" service, you'll share your data!

Happy reversing!

[1] https://github.com/nationalsecurityagency/ghidra [2] https://ghidra-server.org

Title: Bluesky Is Blocking Links to a Major Leak of DHS Employee Records
Context: Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access...
Full Text:
Bluesky is blocking users from opening links to a newly leaked archive of records on more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors, and labels the pages “malicious.”

The files include people’s email addresses and phone numbers, “shared without their authorization,” Bluesky tells WIRED, in violation of its community guidelines. The company says it chose to block the links, rather than remove individual posts, “to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary.”

The DHS records, published Wednesday by the transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets, list employees’ and contractors’ names, contact information, and membership in internal groups, tied in some cases to surveillance and undercover operations. A WIRED investigation found that the files lay out in detail how DHS is organized, from senior leadership to individual immigration agents, and in some cases appear to show who has access to certain technologies.

Users who try to open the archive through Bluesky’s website or app land on a page labeled “Blocked Link,” which says the URL has been identified as “malicious” and blocked for their safety. Bluesky did not respond to questions about whether the block was imposed automatically or whether any government agency had asked the company to restrict access to the data.

The DDoSecrets homepage loads normally from Bluesky. At least one third-party app, Klearsky, opens links to the DHS archive with no warning.

Bluesky promotes a decentralized approach to content moderation that lets users pick independent services that label or filter posts. Its current community guidelines bar sharing “home addresses, personal contact info, financial or medical data, or identification documents.” (A preview of the DHS leak analyzed by WIRED apparently contained work-related contact information one expert described as details that would be printed “on a business card.”) The same guidelines explicitly protect “factual reporting” on matters of public interest that are “related to government transparency and public officials.”

Bluesky started in 2019 as a Twitter research project, later became independent, and opened to the public in February 2024. By August of this year, it counted 45 million registered accounts, and an estimated 10.4 million people used its mobile app in June. Toni Schneider, the founding CEO of Automattic, has run the company since cofounder Jay Graber stepped down in March. Because the network runs on an open protocol, outside developers can build their own Bluesky apps and decide which of the company’s moderation labels to apply.

Emma Best, cofounder of DDoSecrets, says this is not the first time a social media platform has wrongly labeled the organization's website malicious or tried to restrict access to its publications. Twitter suspended DDoSecrets’ account in 2020, prior to the Elon Musk acquisition and X rebrand, and blocked links to its website after the group published BlueLeaks, a 269-gigabyte trove of internal records from hundreds of police agencies and fusion centers. Best says tech platforms often give in to government pressure but insists they cannot prevent the information from spreading. “They can’t stop the signal,” they say.

A group calling itself the Department of Peace gave the archive, dubbed “Icepick,” to DDoSecrets and journalist maia arson crimew. crimew also built a website for searching the records, and Bluesky blocks that site in its website and app as well.

At least one of Bluesky’s competitors has taken a different tack. On X, the Grok chatbot built by X’s parent company pointed curious users to the Icepick website, describing it as a “cleaned searchable web tool” and saying that the complete dataset can be downloaded via DDoSecrets’ website or by torrent. X did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
