Title: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
An unreleased Anthropic AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits, the company said in its latest report.

The exploits were built in the lab after the model was prompted, not seen in any real attack, and Anthropic reported every flaw to the vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in a research post. The strongest claim is not any single bug, but that one model found several separate flaws and combined them into a working exploit, something the company says has until now been the work of a few specialist teams. That capability claim rests on Anthropic's own account.

The patches and the fact that Apple and Google credit Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes can be verified with the vendors.

What a reader cannot check is how much of each chain the model built on its own. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not break down what a person did at each step, and it does not name the model beyond calling it an unreleased, internal research model.

For the one flaw with its own public record, the Windows bug, the record names no finder at all. Here are the five chains, what each would do, the condition each needs, and where the fix landed.

Platform

What the exploit does

Condition it needs

Fix

Chrome

Runs code on the computer, outside the browser's sandbox, from one visit to a web page

One click or page load, stock Chrome on macOS

Chrome 156, October 20

Safari

Lets any website read data from other sites the user is signed in to, such as email or a bank account

One visit to a malicious page

iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2, June 29

Android

Copies photos and other data off a locked, stolen phone

Physical access to the phone, over USB

Anthropic says Google has fixed it; no public record was found

Windows

Crashes a server over the network, and keeps it down by repeating

The server answers HTTP/3 requests

CVE-2026-33096, patched April 2026

Linux

Runs commands as root over the network, with no login and no user action

The server runs a multipath TCP listener

CVE-2026-98432, patched October 15

In the Chrome chain, the model used four separate flaws in turn. A malicious page first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine.

A second flaw escaped V8's memory sandbox and took control of the part of Chrome that renders the page. A race condition in a feature called CacheStorage then let that code read memory it should not reach and learn the layout of the more privileged browser process.

A final use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome's sign-in feature, let the exploit run code outside the sandbox entirely. Anthropic says it reported 62 flaws to Google that were assigned CVEs and fixed as of Chrome 156, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes.

Google's own release notes credit "Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude" for specific Chrome fixes, though not for all 62.

The Safari chain is different because it never runs code at all. It chains flaws to obtain full read and write access to the browser's memory, then changes a single value to turn off the same-origin policy, the rule that prevents one website from reading another's data.

With that rule off, a malicious page can read a user's history and cookies and send signed-in requests to other sites. Apple fixed the use-after-free at the center of the chain in iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2 and credits "Milad Nasr and Nicholas Carlini with Claude, Anthropic" for it.

The Windows chain is the one with an independent paper trail, and it is also the narrowest. It is a denial-of-service attack: a few network packets crash the machine, and repeating them keeps it down, but it does not run code or steal data. Anthropic describes the flaw as an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's QUIC handling.

The public record for the bug it points to, CVE-2026-33096, instead names HTTP.sys, Windows' built-in web request handler, and rates it 7.5 out of 10. No open source ties those two descriptions together as the same component. The CVE record credits no finder, so Anthropic's authorship of this one rests on its own post.

As of late October, the U.S. government's vulnerability enrichment marked the flaw as not exploited, and it was not in the CISA catalog of known exploited bugs.

The Linux chain is the most serious in terms of impact: it runs commands as root over the network without a login. It needs the target server to be running a multipath TCP listener. The model first leaks a kernel memory address to bypass a defense called KASLR, then reuses the same race-condition bug to redirect the program to code the attacker has already placed, resulting in a root shell.

Anthropic says its proof of concept took 48 minutes to leak the address and five more to reach the shell, and that a failed attempt does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep retrying.

The company ties this chain to CVE-2026-98432, a kernel use-after-free rated 9.8 and fixed upstream on October 15; the public record for that CVE describes an IPv4 TCP fix rather than a multipath TCP one, and the two are linked only by Anthropic's post.

Anthropic frames the work as help for defenders. It says it reported each flaw under a coordinated disclosure policy that gives developers 90 days to patch and 45 more before it discusses details beyond a public advisory, and it points security teams to its expanded Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted professionals access to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1.

The reason the company gives for publishing is in its own words: "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

Title: FBI Seizes Virtualine Domain Over Alleged Criminal Hosting and Bitcoin Money Laundering
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine.

The move was in response to the service being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct," the DoJ said.

Visitors to the "virtualine[.]net" domain are now greeted by a message that states it has been seized by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation as part of a coordinated operation between international law enforcement agencies and private sector entities, including the Hessen State Police, the National Police Corps of the Netherlands, the U.K. National Crime Agency, OverRIPE, and Lumen Technologies.

According to court documents, Virtualine, which also operated as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums, claiming that they can be used for phishing, carding, email spam, and port scanning, with the exception of child content and terrorism activities.

In June 2025 on HackForums, the provider is alleged to have boasted that "Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists." Earlier this March, it also began marketing an "additional protection plan" that promised its customers to move their criminal infrastructure to a shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine when receiving official requests from law enforcement agencies.

Snapshots captured by the Internet Archive show that standard plans cost anywhere between $19.99 per month for one virtual CPU, 2GB memory, and 30 GB storage to $179.99 per month for 24 vCPUs, 64 GB memory, and 130 GB memory. Virtualine also offered plans optimized by CPU, memory, and storage, starting from $21.99 per month to $379.99 per month.

"Despite advertising that it does not allow 'child contents' on its server, Virtualine knowingly hosted a website that did so, identified in court records as Vendor 1," DoJ said. "Vendor 1 is a criminal online forum that allows users to post and sell access to nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults."

"Vendor 1 also promotes a hack-for-hire service in which users can pay hackers to access victims’ online accounts without their consent and illicitly obtain explicit images and videos. In January 2026, about one month after Virtualine assigned an IP address to Vendor 1, Virtualine began receiving notifications about sexually explicit images and videos of minors on that server."

The Justice Department said Virtualine continued to host Vendor 1's services despite receiving numerous notices from law enforcement in Germany, Canada, and Australia; the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States; and a victim's attorney.

Virtualine has also been accused of working closely with Vendor 1 to create a new website where its clients could upload their illicit content and download it upon completing a purchase. The website continues to be hosted by Virtualine to this day, the department added.

"Virtualine.net included a number of payment options for Virtualine's customers, including Vendor 1," the DoJ said. "Virtualine accepted payment through BTC [NO-AML], specific unhosted bitcoin addresses that allowed customers to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit."

"The funds Virtualine's criminal customers paid to Virtualine, some of which can be traced directly to various criminal groups, were received by Virtualine and then further laundered to conceal the origin of the funds."

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, in its own analysis, said Virtualine accepted direct Bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without triggering compliance checks at hosted exchanges.

"Virtualine's on-chain footprint has direct exposure to a broad cross-section of the cybercrime ecosystem, including ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses," it said.

Following the site seizure, the operator of Virtualine has published an open letter, refuting allegations that the service knowingly hosted child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The operator also claimed they have taken action on requests for cooperation concerning CSAM within 24 hours. In a post shared on their Telegram channel, they insisted that customer data was safe.

"When we identified prohibited material associated with the customer described as 'Vendor 1,' we ended our relationship with that customer," the individual added, claiming "Virtualine has been part of my life for five years."

"Please do not cast suspicion on me and the tens of thousands of customers who have trusted Virtualine because of the actions attributed to a single customer. I want you to know that I am prepared to respond to your requests concerning 'Vendor 1.'"

In September 2025, the Spamhaus Project revealed that Virtualine had expanded their operations to AS209800. "Thanks to Turkey- and U.S.-based IP address brokers with poor customer vetting procedures, Virtualine keeps obtaining new IPv4 prefixes for enabling internet abuse. AS209800 is currently routed via aurologic GmbH, a hosting provider proliferating several other bulletproof hosting operations."

"A lost ASN does not by itself mean the BPH has stopped," Silent Push said. "The speed of acquiring a new ASN is a crucial part of the problem, and we believe the process for registering an ASN should be tougher."

Update

According to an analysis published by TRM Labs, Virtualine received more illicit-attributed cryptocurrency than any other labeled bulletproof host in 2026, surpassing SecureHost, vpsbg, F0XYF0X BPH (aka Bearhost), and Gerry, despite lower total inflows.

A Russian drug marketplace accounted for nearly 44% of direct inflows, while a large sextortion scheme, a mixer, and ransomware groups were responsible for about 17%, 13%, and 5%, respectively. Direct payers include Coinbase Cartel, The Gentlemen, INC, DragonForce, and Qilin, alongside malware operators such as the StealC infostealer and the Matanbuchus loader.

Other counterparties that have transacted with Virtualine are darknet markets, illicit goods and services operators, bot and malware-distribution services, and sites linked to child sexual abuse material.

"Virtualine is another example of Russia's illicit economy at work: darknet markets, ransomware groups, non-compliant exchanges, and brokers all feeding the same ecosystem," Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Bulletproof hosting is the connective tissue. Seizing a domain matters, but the blockchain record doesn't disappear with it. It shows who is paying, who is getting paid, and where they go next."

A press release from the Dutch police has revealed that dozens of physical servers located in a data center in Limburg were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.

"Through the seizure, the police are in possession of data and information relating to more than 3,000 customers who used the servers for criminal activities," the Politie said. "The secured data will be used for further police investigation regarding customers who used these servers for criminal purposes."

As of October 29, 2026, virtualine[.]org, the domain that hosted the open letter, and the Telegram channel are no longer accessible.

Title: Japan's GMO Offers $1 Million Bounty to Catch Hackers Behind FX Trading Cloud Breach
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Japan's GMO Internet Group is offering up to $1 million in total for tips that help catch the attackers who breached its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service, after refusing to pay an extortion demand.

The reward program opened on October 28 and pays only if a tip helps lead to an arrest or an international wanted notice. The service hosts Windows desktops used for FX trading, and a broker has linked unauthorized trades on some of its customers' accounts to logins leaked from the service.

GMO says the attackers took customer information. It received a demand for about $50 million (about ¥8 billion) on October 21 from people it believes carried out the attack. They have also threatened its customers' trading accounts and data.

On October 27, the attackers posted material on their website that they say is information about GMO and its customers. The site's domain, including its mirror sites, was shut down at about 4 a.m. Japan time on October 28, and GMO plans to act against any new site.

How the Reward Works

GMO Internet Group runs and pays for the program, called GMO Cybercrime Bounty. Tips are sent by email to an address listed on a dedicated website, in Japanese, English, or Chinese, and can be anonymous. The program is open until an arrest, an international wanted notice, or October 27, 2027, whichever comes first.

GMO wants information linking people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency addresses to the attack, extortion, or movement of money, along with evidence of how the crimes were carried out. Guesses, unsupported accusations and reposts of public information generally do not qualify.

A tip earns money only if it leads to an arrest, including one by police outside Japan, or to an international wanted notice, such as an Interpol Red Notice. GMO decides how much each tip helped, and one tipster can receive the full $1 million or the total can be split. Tipsters must prove their identity before payment, and if no tip qualifies, no payment is made.

Some people cannot be paid, including anyone involved in the crime, anyone who got information illegally, such as by buying leaked data, and GMO staff. GMO tells tipsters not to break into systems, negotiate with or pay the attackers, or send leaked data, credentials, or malware.

Tips are shared with police and other authorities in Japan and abroad as needed. GMO has already given police all its evidence on the threats, including communication records.

GMO will never ask tipsters for passwords, authentication codes or fees, and it writes to them only from addresses ending in @cybercrimebounty.gmo.

The Breach and the Trading Accounts

GMO Internet, the subsidiary that runs the service, found on October 20 that a third party had installed malicious programs on some customers' servers. It shut down the servers on every plan from October 21. It counts 26,739 servers as potentially affected, which is not the number of confirmed break-ins or data thefts.

On October 24, GMO said it had confirmed a security problem in the service's systems, unauthorized access to the service, and the exfiltration of customer information from the company.

Anything customers stored on the servers may have been viewed, including login credentials saved in trading software such as MetaTrader 4 and 5 (MT4/MT5). GMO does not keep customers' payment card data on the servers.

Customers began reporting trades they did not recognize on October 21. A broker, OANDA Japan, has confirmed that a third party logged in to and traded on some of its customers' accounts using ID and password pairs it believes were leaked from the GMO servers. It has restricted trading on accounts that may be affected, and as of October 26 it had not found a break-in or leak in its own core systems.

Another broker, FXTF, warned on October 22 that third parties may have stolen the logins of some customers who use VPS servers, in an attack it believes hit another company's VPS servers. They may also have used the logins to log in and trade. It told customers who had connected to Desktop Cloud to change their FXTF passwords from a device that had never connected to it.

GMO Internet Group said in a stock exchange filing on October 28 that it had not yet confirmed how many customers its payments will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify for compensation. It had not confirmed any impact from the breach on its other services.

The Threats and the Leak

GMO says the attackers threatened to keep manipulating customers' accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms, to publish information about the service and about customers' PCs, to hit those PCs with ransomware, and to publish details of GMO's systems.

They set noon on October 27 for publishing customer information and launching the ransomware attack. No ransomware attack had been confirmed as of 1:55 p.m. Japan time that day.

The material posted on October 27 was what the attackers called one customer's personal information, ITmedia NEWS reported that afternoon. GMO was checking it that day.

The attackers collected information about anyone who visited their site, according to GMO, which tells visitors to run a full antivirus scan. It asks people not to visit the site or any new one, and not to repost or link to the material.

How the Attackers Got In

As of October 28, GMO had not said how the attackers got in.

Masatoshi Kumagai, who heads GMO Internet Group, wrote in an October 25 blog post that the group's own white-hat hackers had warned the team running the service about problems in advance.

The response was neither fast nor thorough enough, he wrote, and the attackers took advantage of the gap.

On their website, the attackers claimed that one administrator account was shared across all the servers and that customers' PC drives were visible from the servers by default when they connected, ITmedia NEWS reported.

They also claimed they used a flaw in the service to reach customers' own PCs. GMO had not publicly confirmed these claims either.

By October 26, GMO had collected PCs from customers who offered them for analysis, as of 11:59 a.m. Japan time on October 27, it had found no malware, including ransomware, on the PCs it had finished checking. That does not confirm that every customer's device is safe, and the analysis is still ongoing.

What Customers Should Do

GMO has told Desktop Cloud customers to take these steps:

Change trading-account and trading-software passwords from a device not used for FX trading, such as a phone.

End every logged-in session, through the broker if needed, even after changing the password.

Check trading history and balances, and report unrecognized trades to the broker first.

Turn on two-factor authentication where the broker offers it.

Change passwords reused on other services or saved in the browser.

Run a full antivirus scan on devices used to connect, and back up data.

Do not reply to messages from anyone claiming to be behind the attack, or open their links or files.

Ignore offers to recover lost money for a fee. GMO will never ask for a password or authentication code.

GMO Internet will pay every current user ¥5,000 and cover actual trading losses and fees from trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. Customers whose information it confirms was published will also get ¥10,000 to ¥25,000 for each type of information exposed.

GMO will not restart the service on the breached systems as they are. Customers who want a Windows desktop will be offered a move to a separate service, free for six months and only with their consent, with details due by October 30.

Title: Tailscale Patches SSH Flaws That Could Let Hacked Devices Gain Root Access on Other Servers
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Tailscale has released version 1.104.4 to fix flaws in its built-in SSH server that could let an attacker reach services and files on other servers that only the root user should be able to touch.

The flaws are in how Tailscale SSH forwards network connections, a job the Tailscale background process carries out with root privileges. To use them, an attacker must already control a device that the network's access rules permit to open an SSH session to the target, with forwarding allowed in that rule.

The flaws come from a report called Tailworm, published days before the fix by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs, who tested released versions of the Tailscale client and the self-hosted headscale control server in a lab.

Tailscale SSH decides who can connect using a device's identity and the network's policy file, not a password or key, so an attacker does not need stolen credentials, only a foothold on a device the policy already trusts.

The flaws "don't allow an unauthenticated attacker to connect to arbitrary Tailscale SSH servers," Tailscale said, and an attacker can still reach only the machines the policy file already allows.

Tailscale SSH's server runs only on Linux and the open-source macOS build; the attacker's own device can be any platform.

The problem is in socket forwarding. When a permitted SSH session forwarded a connection to a Unix socket on the server, the Tailscale process checked the path but then operated as root. A timing trick let an attacker swap in a different path after that check, defeating the safeguard meant to limit which sockets forwarding could reach.

In Windisch's own tests, forwarding to the Docker control socket produced a root shell and read the system password file, /etc/shadow, with no administrator rights. Tailscale's bulletin describes the reach more narrowly, saying an attacker could get to root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API.

In 1.104.4, Tailscale changed the server to carry out forwarding as the logged-in user rather than as root, and to rely on the operating system's own file permissions in place of its earlier path check. The release covers 4 security bulletins:

TS-2026-014: the SSH socket-forwarding flaws above, which let a permitted session reach root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API.

TS-2026-015: a way for a permitted SSH session to use up a server's memory and crash the Tailscale process, cutting all Tailscale networking on that node.

TS-2026-016: a flaw in tailscale serve where a forward to a Unix socket could reach the tailscaled local API, giving remote control of the node, plus a related socket-swap issue.

TS-2026-017: a flaw where, with TLS serve and 2 or more mounts, one request could receive another mount's permission headers.

What to Do

Users of Tailscale SSH should update to version 1.104.4 or later. If you cannot update a server yet, you can turn off SSH forwarding on it by setting TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restarting the service, which Tailscale says turns off forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH and blocks several of the more serious findings.

Tailscale also recommends reviewing SSH access rules so that only the users and devices that need access have it.

Tailscale suggests using SSH check mode, which requires a user to sign in again before a session starts, for sensitive systems. Check mode does not stop these forwarding flaws: it guards the start of a session, whereas the forwarding occurs within a session that has already been approved.

If a server may already have been compromised, Windisch's report says the fix alone is not enough. A stolen device key stays valid until the device is deleted at the control plane, because reimaging the machine does not revoke it. Tailscale's notices do not cover this case.

The picture is worse on headscale, the self-hosted control server. On headscale, SSH forwarding is granted on every accepted session and cannot be turned off in the policy, so Windisch's report says every SSH grant there should be treated as giving root. The newest headscale release, version 0.29.5 from October 13, does not fix the reported issues.

Is It a Worm?

Windisch called the chain "wormable." In her tests, one compromised device could spread to every device the policy allowed, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

Two controls stopped the spread in those tests. Writing access rules as single device-to-device pairs held it back, and binding device keys to hardware such as a TPM kept a stolen identity from being reused elsewhere.

Tailscale rejected the worm description. The findings do not describe self-replicating malware that spreads between machines on its own, the company said, but lateral movement limited to the connections a policy file already allows.

It called the privilege-escalation problems "serious security issues," said it had reproduced the main ones, and added that it is still working out which configurations are affected.

Disclosure and Earlier Fixes

As of publication, the 4 bulletins carry no CVE identifiers or severity scores, and none state the oldest affected version. The report also covered Tailscale's app connectors and its serve and funnel features.

Tailscale said the app-connector finding is in conn25, an experimental feature it has not released, and that the connectors customers use today are not affected. Of 5 serve and funnel findings, it fixed 3 and said the other 2 work as designed.

Windisch published the report without coordinating the release with Tailscale first, which she has described as "reported but not coordinated." Tailscale said it received the report on the morning of Saturday, October 24, about 2 hours before Windisch published it, and that its engineers were already looking at the same parts of the code.

Neither Tailscale nor the report says the flaws have been used in real attacks. The proof-of-concept code is not public, and Windisch said she gave it only to Tailscale's security team.

The report is the latest in a run of fixes in the same part of Tailscale this year. In June, Tailscale fixed a separate flaw in Tailscale SSH's Unix-socket forwarding that let an unprivileged user reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

Title: ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained Flaws
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.

Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.

The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.

In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.

CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.

In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.

ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.

The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.

PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.

From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.

The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.

In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.

What to Do

The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response.

Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching.

If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions.

If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion.

One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

Title: Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature
Context: Cybersecurity Operations Cyber Risk Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Threat Intelligence News Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around...
Full Text:
A two-month operation in Africa led to the arrests of nearly 1,500 cybercrime suspects across 20 African countries and the US, the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds, and the shutdown of nearly 11,000 malicious networks.

The third annual roundup of cybercriminals and financial scammers, dubbed Operation Serengeti III, aimed to take down groups responsible for ransomware, phishing, and cyber-enabled fraud, Interpol stated. The operation expanded the impact of cyber-focused investigations from previous law enforcement efforts in 2024 and 2025, which netted 1,006 suspects in the original Operation Serengeti and 1,209 suspects in last year's effort, dubbed Operation Serengeti 2.0.

The increasing arrests show that the national law enforcement partners are becoming more mature in their investigative practices and collaboration across jurisdictions, says Neal Jetton, director for cybercrime at Interpol.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

"Rising arrest figures reflect stronger enforcement activity, not a change in the scale of offending," he says. "The success of law enforcement efforts should be judged by whether fewer people are victimized over time and not by the number of suspects arrested or victims identified during a specific operation."

The crackdown came as cybercriminals in the region continue to develop more sophistication in their operations, with a survey of African members finding that 72% of the 36 African countries have discovered a criminally operated scam center and more than half of cybercrime cases involved the use of AI — 8% frequently and 47% occasionally, according to Interpol's "African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026."

The data highlights the rapid improvements in cybercriminal infrastructure, says Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of global data partnerships at Team Cymru.

"Scams that once looked like individual schemes now run like businesses, with recruitment pipelines, international staff, and, increasingly, trafficked workers," he says.

Busting Transnational Criminal Orgs

In Uganda, for example, two transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) used a rotating call-center model with scripted communications, fraudulent websites, and fake trading platforms to convince elderly victims in Asia to invest in their financial scams, Interpol said in a statement on Operation Serengeti III's impact. Ugandan law enforcement authorities successfully dismantled the fraud rings, arresting 365 foreign nationals, consisting almost entirely of citizens from various Asian nations, Interpol's Jetton says.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

In another arm of the operation, national police arrested nine suspects in Angola, dismantling two illegal cryptocurrency mining sites and seizing more than 2,000 devices used to mine crypto along with six illegal power transformers valued at more than US $1 million. Cybercriminal mining operations are a common way to generate cryptocurrency, the favored method of cashing out on illegal schemes, Jetton says.

"Cryptocurrency played a significant role in moving the proceeds," Jetton says. "It is now the principal rail for this type of fraud."

In Nigeria, police shuttered two fraud operations: One using 2.1 million email addresses to create a large-scale phishing and business email compromise (BEC) operation, while another scheme focused on international investment fraud and garnered at least US $2.4 million in profits, Interpol stated.

The schemes showed off the role that AI is taking in enabling cybercriminal campaigns. The phishing and BEC campaigns used email addresses and AI agents to scrape information from LinkedIn and other social media to identify high-value targets, Jetton says.

"AI enabled the threat actor to create highly personalized phishing emails by mimicking the writing style of executives, colleagues, and suppliers," he says, adding that "AI helped criminals manage and prioritize millions of email addresses for large-scale campaigns and, in some cases, combined with voice cloning, deepfake videos, and AI chatbots to make social engineering attacks even more convincing."

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

Maturing Collaboration Between Law Enforcement

Law enforcement collaboration is making the individual nations more effective in tackling transnational cybercrime. With international partners, the individual countries are able to gain intelligence on signs of cybercriminal activities in their country, says Team Cymru's Piccolini.

"The biggest change is timing. Since Serengeti 2.0, investigators have gone in with intelligence on suspicious IP addresses, domains, and command-and-control servers before the operation begins, along with training in open source, crypto, and ransomware investigation."

Without such collaboration, TCOs could evade repercussions, especially if they limited their activities to impacting only citizens of other nations, as in the case of the Asian investment fraud ring.

"Actors targeting victims in Europe and North America use infrastructure spread across multiple jurisdictions, which makes it harder to pursue through any single country," Piccolini says. "That’s a big part of why international operations like Serengeti, with partners who can see across borders, matter so much."

Both Interpol and Team Cyrmu stressed that several operations are ongoing, with investigators continuing to use seized data and other information to pursue suspected cybercriminals.

Title: Adobe Commerce PolyShell Attacks Breach Hundreds of Stores as Brotli Exploit Traffic Emerges
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.

CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block.

The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025.

As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope.

"An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder."

ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution.

"The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation."

The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw.

This includes PHP, which has shipped versions 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, as well as Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, Python, ClickHouse, the PHP Brotli extension, and the Ruby "brotli" gem. Links to some of the advisories are below -

Google-owned Wiz has warned that "91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances."

"Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli," Sysdig said. "Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability."

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 10, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes against the two flaws.

Title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
Context: A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second
Full Text:
Executive Summary

In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY, a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer.

Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it.

INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean.

The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it.

Key Takeaways

Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected.

The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere.

Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated.

Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console.

The Campaign So Far

INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY.

The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password-gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts.

Figure 1: INJ3CTOR3 attack chain, September generation. (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub)

Unchanged: the decoded webshell panel, the encoding chain (base64 in the shell script, base64 again in PHP, then ROT13), the persistence channels, the backdoor account password hash, and the borrowed timestamp. Behavioral detections built on our May report still apply.

Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product

The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults.

Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads

Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes.

This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second.

Detection

Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel.

Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them.

For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs

By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else.

Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list.

An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both.

In April, all of these pointed to 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. We assess that the operator replaced the address in plain text and never re-encoded the base64 strings; the credential upload, which names both hosts, appears deliberate. This host is distinct from the scanner 160[.]119[.]76[.]250, which is named in our May report.

Defend: block both hosts in both directions, and decode every base64-encoded string in a crontab or shell profile before deciding which hosts a host talks to. A plain-text review would miss every channel that still reaches 45[.]95[.]147[.]178.

The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers

Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for.

Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections.

One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only.

A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below)

Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password

Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains.

The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap

k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it.

Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it.

Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive.

What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You

FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so.

Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console

Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added.

What Keeps It There

Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below)

Figure 5: Persistence channels that rebuild each other, and the backdoors they stay open

Detecting It Without IOCs

The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be.

On the host: triage with beagle.sh

The script separated one infected server from one clean server of the same FreePBX version, a sample of one, so expect some legitimate findings. However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct.

The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected.

Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works

First move

Why it fails on its own

Delete the webshell

Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags.

Patch FreePBX

Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system.

Change the admin password

The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login.

Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it.

Preserve first

The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run:

Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below.

Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times.

Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs.

Then clean, in this order

Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref.

Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local.

Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled.

Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php.

Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host.

Conclusion

The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account.

The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR.

The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure.

Title: ZDI-26-825: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) Alpine iLX-F511 diagapp Command Injection Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Alpine iLX-F511 devices
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows physically present attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Alpine iLX-F511 devices. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the diagapp component. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute a system call. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of root.

Additional Details

Title: Introducing Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall
Context: A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own...
Full Text:
Your workloads reach most destinations by domain name, but a firewall can only act on what it sees in the traffic. For HTTP and HTTPS, AWS Network Firewall domain rules match the name that the client puts in the request, and the client chooses that name. The connections for protocols such as SSH and SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) don’t carry the domain name. The client uses the name only for the DNS lookup and then connects straight to the IP address that DNS returned. As a result, Network Firewall rules for these protocols have used IP addresses, which change over time. For web and non-web traffic alike, Network Firewall had no view of the answers that your DNS resolver returned, because that shared visibility between DNS and the firewall didn’t exist.

On October 21, 2026, we launched Route 53 Resolved IP Validation for AWS Network Firewall, at no additional charge. Amazon Route 53 Resolver now shares the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name with Network Firewall, and Network Firewall checks each new outbound connection against them. With this launch, you can now filter non-web traffic by domain name, and you can prevent Server Name Indication (SNI) manipulation on TLS traffic without needing to enable TLS inspection.

In this post, we explain how the feature works, show how to turn it on in alert mode, and walk through two common use cases. They’re examples; the same check applies to any outbound traffic that you control by domain name.

How it works

Amazon Route 53 Resolver answers DNS queries from resources in your virtual private cloud (VPC) configured to use it, and it’s available by default in every VPC. With this feature, Route 53 Resolver keeps the IP addresses that it returns for each domain name in a resolved IP cache. When a new outbound connection starts, Network Firewall checks the destination address against that cache.

The workload asks Route 53 Resolver at 10.0.0.2 for files.partner.example.com.

DNS Firewall checks the query first. Domain rules can block or alert on it; an empty rule group lets it through.

Route 53 Resolver answers 203.0.113.10 and records the answer in the resolved IP cache.

The SFTP connection to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 reaches the Network Firewall endpoint.

The policy checks the first packet. The address is in the cache, so the connection continues.

The stateful rule passes it, because Route 53 Resolver returned the address for files.partner.example.com.

The connection leaves through the NAT gateway and internet gateway.

The flow log and alert log record the new fields.

The feature has three parts:

An Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group – It defines the scope. The answers that Route 53 Resolver returns in every VPC associated with this rule group go into the resolved IP cache. The rule group can be empty. Add rules to it and the same rule group also filters the DNS queries themselves, for example, by blocking lookups of known threat domains. Together, DNS Firewall checks the lookup and Network Firewall checks the connection that follows.

The Network Firewall policy setting – On the first packet of each new connection, before your stateful rules run, Network Firewall checks whether Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. If it did, the connection continues to your stateful rules. If it didn’t, Network Firewall applies the action you chose: Alert, Drop, or Reject.

Resolved-domain rules – In your stateful rule groups, these rules match a connection by the domain name that its destination address was resolved for, so they work with every protocol. Use the name that your clients look up.

The following diagram shows this architecture.

Figure 1. How Network Firewall checks the SFTP connection from use case 1 against the answers that Route 53 Resolver returned

The policy setting checks every connection, not only web traffic. A connection to an IP address that no client looked up through Route 53 Resolver, such as a hardcoded address, fails the check. If any of your workloads connect straight to IP addresses, add those addresses to Bypass destination validation IP ranges before you enforce. A stateful pass rule doesn’t exempt them because the policy check runs before your rules. The check is per address: when any client in an associated VPC looks up a name, its addresses pass the check for every client in scope in the same Availability Zone. For details, see Resolved IP validation in AWS Network Firewall in the AWS Network Firewall Developer Guide.

Prerequisites

To follow along, you need:

DNS through Amazon Route 53 Resolver – Network Firewall can check only answers that Route 53 Resolver returned. Queries that reach Route 53 Resolver through Resolver endpoints or Resolver forwarding rules count.

A Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group associated with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against.

The policy setting turned on before you add resolved-domain rules – Rules that use domain filtering (the aws_route_53_resolved_domain keyword) need Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in the same firewall policy. Turn the setting on first, in alert mode, then add the rules.

A supported deployment model – The feature works with distributed deployments, including multiple firewall endpoints, where clients reach a firewall endpoint in their own Availability Zone, and with centralized deployments where the firewall is attached natively to AWS Transit Gateway. If routing sends a client to a firewall endpoint in another Availability Zone, its connections fail the check. To move a centralized deployment to a natively attached firewall, see Why and how to migrate to a Transit Gateway attached AWS Network Firewall.

How to turn it on in alert mode

Start in alert mode because clients cache DNS answers. Network Firewall recognizes only the answers that Route 53 Resolver returns after the DNS Firewall rule group is associated with the VPC and selected in the policy. A client that still uses an answer it cached earlier fails the check until it looks up the name again, usually when its cached record expires. Alert mode lets you see this without blocking anything. Allow about 24 hours in alert mode for clients to refresh their caches.

Create a DNS Firewall rule group (it can be empty) and associate it with the VPCs whose DNS answers Network Firewall should check connections against. For the steps, see Creating a rule group and rules.

Or, to use a DNS Firewall rule group that you already have, make sure it’s associated with those VPCs and only those. An answer returned in any associated VPC is valid for every client that the firewall checks. Which clients are checked is set by source IP ranges in step 6.

In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, choose Firewall policies, then choose the policy that your firewall uses. On the Traffic inspection tab, in the Route 53 Resolved IP validation section, choose Edit and select Enable Route 53 Resolved IP validation.

For Action, choose Alert. For DNS Firewall rule group, choose the rule group from step 1 or 2.

For DNS expiry exception policy, choose what happens to a connection that’s already open when its entry expires from the resolved IP cache. Continue keeps it running, Drop stops it silently, and Reject stops it with a TCP reset. We recommend Continue so that long-running sessions, such as file transfers, aren’t cut off midway. However, choose the option that fits your security requirements.

For source IP ranges, list the clients to check. If you don’t set it, Network Firewall checks clients in the firewall’s VPC and in any additional VPCs attached to the firewall. If your clients are in other VPCs, such as spoke VPCs that send traffic to a firewall attached to a transit gateway, enter their CIDR ranges; otherwise, Network Firewall doesn’t check their connections. Add destinations that you allow by IP address to Bypass destination validation IP ranges. Choose Save.

The following screenshot illustrates these steps.

Figure 2. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation turned on in alert mode

In alert mode, Network Firewall doesn’t block a connection that fails the check, and it doesn’t write an alert of its own. It records the result in your flow logs, in the route53_resolved_ip field of each connection. A value of true means Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for a domain name. A value of false means it didn’t, so enforcement would block the connection. The same field also appears in alert log records that a rule or the policy’s default action writes for the connection. Pass rules don’t write one unless they have the alert; keyword. The DnsUnresolvedFlows metric in Amazon CloudWatch counts the connections that fail the check, and DnsAzUnavailableFlows counts connections from an Availability Zone that doesn’t support the feature. The following alert log record (trimmed, with example values) was written by a default action that alerts, for a connection to an address that Route 53 Resolver returned:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 123, "proto": "UDP", "app_proto": "ntp", "route53_resolved_ip": true, "verdict": { "action": "alert" }, "alert": { "action": "allowed", "signature_id": 3, "signature": "aws:alert_established action" } } }

In alert mode, this record is for a TLS connection that presented an allowed domain name but went to an address that Route 53 Resolver didn’t return for it, blocked by the policy’s default action in use case 2:

{ "firewall_name": "egress-firewall", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "src_ip": "10.0.1.10", "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "api.partner.example.com" }, "route53_resolved_ip": false, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature": "aws:alert_established_app_layer_to_server action" } } }

Before you switch Action to Drop or Reject, check that connections that fail the check are ones you expect and that destinations you allow by IP address are in the bypass ranges. Reject sends a TCP reset, so a blocked TCP client fails right away instead of waiting for a timeout. After you enforce, blocked connections appear in your flow logs with route53_resolved_ip as false, not in your alert logs. For the metrics and log fields to watch, see Monitoring and troubleshooting resolved IP validation.

Use case 1: Filter non-web traffic by domain name

Before this launch, Network Firewall rules for protocols that carry no domain name, such as SFTP, used IP addresses. Now, you can allow them by domain name. In this example, a workload sends files over SFTP to a partner at files.partner.example.com on TCP port 22, and the partner can change the addresses behind that name at any time. The same approach works for SSH, MySQL, and other non-web protocols. You create it as a standard stateful rule. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, and choose the rule evaluation order that your policy uses.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TCP. For Destination port, enter 22. Under Domain filtering, enter files.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

Figure 3. A pass rule for SFTP on TCP port 22, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is shown in the following code. It adds the alert; keyword so that the firewall logs allowed connections. The console rule doesn’t add it.

pass tcp any any -> any 22 (alert; msg:"Allow TCP/22 to files.partner.example.com"; aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"files.partner.example.com"; sid:1;)

When the partner moves its server to a new address, the next DNS answer adds it to the resolved IP cache. There’s no IP list to maintain. The cache keeps earlier answers for longer than their DNS time to live (TTL), so the old address can still pass for a while.

Use case 2: Prevent SNI spoofing without TLS inspection

With SNI spoofing, a client presents an allowed domain name in its TLS request while it connects to a different server. Preventing that has required TLS inspection, which decrypts the traffic. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation prevents it without TLS inspection. In this example, a workload calls a partner API at api.partner.example.com over HTTPS. TLS traffic on port 443 must reach only the addresses that Route 53 Resolver returned for that name. You create a pass rule in a standard stateful rule group, as in use case 1, and the firewall policy’s default action drops everything that no rule passes. Follow these steps:

Under Network Firewall, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Stateful rule group and Standard stateful rule, then choose Strict order.

Choose Add rule. For Protocol, choose TLS. For Destination port, enter 443. Under Domain filtering, enter api.partner.example.com. For Action, choose Pass.

Create the rule group, then add it to your firewall policy.

In the firewall policy, use strict rule order. For the stateful default actions, choose Application drop established (server-directed only) and Application alert established (server-directed only). The alert action logs what the drop action blocks. For why we recommend these default actions, see Firewall policy configuration in the AWS Security Services Best Practices guide.

Figure 4. A pass rule for TLS on port 443, scoped to the partner’s domain name

If you manage rules as code, the equivalent Suricata rule is:

pass tls any any -> any 443 (aws_route_53_resolved_domain:"api.partner.example.com"; sid:2;)

The pass rule matches the destination address, not the name in the TLS request. TLS traffic on port 443 passes only when Route 53 Resolver returned the destination address for api.partner.example.com. If the partner’s addresses also serve other domain names, such as behind a content delivery network (CDN), those names pass too. To also require the partner’s name in the TLS request, add an exact SNI match to the same rule: tls.sni; content:"api.partner.example.com"; startswith; endswith; nocase;.

Without startswith and endswith, the content match accepts any SNI that contains the name.

A connection that presents the partner’s name but goes to another address doesn’t match the pass rule. If Route 53 Resolver never returned that address, the policy setting’s enforcement action blocks the connection before your rules run. In alert mode, the policy setting lets the connection through to your rules instead, and the stateful default action drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match. Its alert log record shows route53_resolved_ip as false, as in the second example previously. If Route 53 Resolver returned the address for a different domain name, the connection passes the policy check. The stateful default action then drops it because the pass rule doesn’t match, and that record shows route53_resolved_ip as true.

Best practices

We recommend that you follow these best practices:

Keep DNS on Route 53 Resolver – Block outbound UDP and TCP port 53 DNS to other resolvers, including DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT), on Network Firewall, so that clients don’t bypass the check. Route 53 Resolved IP Validation alone doesn’t do this. If any client looks up a public resolver’s name, such as dns.google, that resolver’s addresses pass the check.

Keep DNS Firewall rules in those VPCs – Route 53 Resolved IP Validation checks the connections that follow a DNS lookup, not the DNS queries themselves. DNS Firewall blocks lookups of known threat domains with AWS managed domain lists, and its advanced rule groups detect data leaving through DNS queries, such as DNS tunneling.

Start small – Add domain filtering to a few rules at a time, then add more when the results look clean. For domain allow list patterns, see Allow rules and domain allowlisting.

Turn on flow and alert logging and detailed monitoring – Connections that fail the resolved IP check show in your flow logs (route53_resolved_ip: false) and in the DnsUnresolvedFlows metric, not in your alert logs. Pass rules without the alert; keyword don’t write an alert log record.

Pricing and availability

Route 53 Resolved IP Validation is available today in all commercial AWS Regions (Regions other than the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions) where AWS Network Firewall and Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For the list of Regions, see AWS Capabilities by Region. A DNS Firewall rule group with no rules doesn’t incur DNS Firewall charges. Standard DNS Firewall pricing applies after you add rules. See AWS Network Firewall pricing and Amazon Route 53 pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how Route 53 Resolved IP Validation works and how to turn it on in alert mode. Network Firewall now checks each connection’s destination against the IP addresses that Amazon Route 53 Resolver returned for the DNS query. Filtering SFTP, SSH, database, and other non-web traffic by domain name and preventing SNI spoofing without TLS inspection are two common examples of what that makes possible. To get started, turn the feature on in alert mode and review the results before you enforce. For the full walkthrough, see Getting started with resolved IP validation.

To learn more, visit the AWS Network Firewall product page and the feature documentation.
