Title: There's a third PHP2Shell bug, but it won't get an emergency fix
Context: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems
Full Text: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems. But this one won’t receive an emergency fix. The PHP Foundation on Friday told The Register that it has reserved a CVE identifier (CVE-2026-115560) for a third RCE flaw to go with the first two that comprise PHP2Shell, and it will release a full advisory and fixed software with the next regular PHP release. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The informational advisory, published on Friday, suggests that users “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled. This setup, according to the PHP Foundation, is unlikely in real-world applications, and as such doesn’t pose the same massive risk as the earlier two CVEs that set the internet on fire earlier this week. Those, of course, are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell. The related vulnerabilities involve memory-safety flaws in PHP, the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites with a known server-side programming language. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and patched both bugs on Wednesday. Despite reports of mass exploitation attempts, and multiple proof-of-concept exploits both before and after the CVE disclosures, as of Friday there have been no publicly confirmed successful compromises attributed to PHP2Shell. “We have no evidence of successful exploitation of the two vulnerabilities from Wednesday prior to disclosure, and we currently have no evidence of any exploitation of these vulnerabilities on patched PHP versions,” Barron said. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems.” The Register reached out to multiple other security researchers, all of whom said they’ve documented exploitation attempts - but no confirmed successful attacks in the wild. “Nonetheless, exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious,” Mandiant Chief Technology Officer Charles Carmakal said in a Friday LinkedIn post. Google Cloud owns Mandiant, along with cloud security biz Wiz, which is one of the organizations credited with finding and reporting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Despite “no evidence of successful wide scale exploitation,” Carmakal noted that there are several exploit PoCs publicly circulating online. Many of these, he said, “appear to be ‘vibe-coded’ and are incapable of remote code execution. We have validated some PoCs, however, that are capable of RCE against default deployments of mod_php but not PHP-FPM.”®

Title: Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice
Context: Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of...
Full Text:
New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

Step 1: Find PHP, Everywhere

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

Not So Simple as Clicking "Update"

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Each PHP2Shell Case Will Be Different

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

Title: Red-team report found OpenAI utterly failed to monitor its agents during Hugging Face attack
Context: "The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st,"...
Full Text: An independent evaluation of OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system revealed that the system was not fit for purpose during a period when the company's bots were breaking into model-hosting platform Hugging Face. The safeguards weren't nearly strong enough. "The METR and Redwood employees discovered a number of novel vulnerabilities in the asynchronous internal misalignment monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21st," said evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research in a report released on Thursday. The system, since improved according to OpenAI, was intended to monitor AI agent behavior. But as described by METR and Redwood Research, its monitoring capability was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor. Bypassing the system wasn't always necessary because it wasn't always operative. Monitoring was suspended, for example, during compaction events. Compaction is a process by which AI models condense the data in their context window to make room for further input. And between May and July 2026, about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report. That gap was theoretically large enough to allow AI agents to postpone monitoring indefinitely: agents could further suppress monitoring by continuing to take actions without returning control to the user. "At the time of the exercise, the monitoring system triggered when agents returned control to the user, so during the time period when compaction events were not being monitored, agents could indefinitely postpone being monitored by simply continuing to take actions," the report explains. This is not to say that OpenAI agents necessarily did so – the actions they did take, against Hugging Face and other organizations, have now been well documented. But OpenAI's internal monitoring system could easily have missed any misbehavior, were the company's AI agents inclined to conceal their activities – by acting during compaction – or simply to operate in system blind spots. The report continues in this vein, citing not only monitoring gaps but poorly constructed software – dare we say vibe-coded? – that gave OpenAI agents the means to evade the shoddy monitoring. "We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take," the report says. "We also discovered an exploit agents could use that would prevent hundreds of recent actions (including the actions involved in the exploit itself) from being monitored." The details of this exploit were redacted by OpenAI, but to summarize: the monitoring system that missed some traffic could be avoided by agents that were constrained by a non-working sandbox and had access to an exploit to evade monitoring. But that's not all. The evaluators found that AI agents could craft inputs that caused monitoring to fail, that there were two client-controllable headers capable of disabling the monitoring of new agents, and that there were two unmonitored agentic tools that were thought to be read-only but could be exploited to take arbitrary action in the sandbox – which as noted above leaked like a sieve. In conclusion, METR and Redwood Research propose that the agent monitoring systems used by AI companies actually work and are robust enough to "withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale." ®

Title: AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost
Context: Cybersecurity Operations Cyber Risk Cybersecurity Analytics Vulnerabilities & Threats News AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost One campaign targets 105 sites...
Full Text:
Over five days in September, a Chinese-speaking attacker used three different AI harnesses and both open-weight and public AI models to target 105 different e-commerce sites.

Usually within a day, and often with hours, the autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 different companies. Malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two, installed credit-card skimmers on the websites of five, and gained some degree of illicit access to the rest, which includes at least one Fortune 500 company, according to Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign.

The total bill for the attackers? An average of $25.46 per completed target.

"The scale and success of this campaign are remarkable for just one week, especially considering the size of some of the victims," says Sa'ar Elias, co-founder and chief research officer for Gambit Security. "Work that would previously have required a coordinated team of skilled attackers can now be carried out by one person without much prior knowledge."

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

The autonomous credit-card and data-stealing campaign is not an outlier. Agentic AI has sped up vulnerability research, leading to a massive surge in CVE assignments. Attackers are increasingly using AI to automate attacks, exploit systems faster, and even act as fully autonomous hackers.

In another instance, researchers with AI cyber-defense firm Silverfort conduct lab tests using an orchestrating agent and publicly available versions of Claude Opus to explore how quickly autonomous AI can turn initial access into a full compromise. The "attacker" gained complete domain control in eight minutes, says Colin Ferris, threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

The total cost: About $12.

"The barrier to entry is falling," Ferris says. "What it takes is a basic foothold, not exotic skill, and that’s why this won't stay confined to sophisticated actors."

Security Teams Looking for Cheap Defenses

Prices in dark markets have reflected the reduction in costs for attackers. Because of increasing supply in the underground markets, the average price of sold initial access declined from just over $1,400 to $429, according to figures from threat intelligence firm Flashpoint. While fewer companies are paying ransoms — 28% in the first half of 2026 — ransomware activity continued to grow by 45%, the company said.

"Initial access is where we've measured the price drop," says Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence for Flashpoint. "Elsewhere in the attack chain, we see AI making operations faster and easier to scale."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In many ways, the situation resembles the one on current battlefields: Cheap autonomous or directed attacks by drones are making expensive defenses uneconomical, which means that defenders have to find cheaper ways to defend and harden systems. In the latest campaign, cyberattackers used the agentic AI system Hermes and two AI penetration-testing frameworks, Strix and Cairn, according to Gambit Security.

"Attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal costs, while defenders must maintain a high level of reliability across complex environments," says Gambit Security's Elias. "Defending against every individual attempt can quickly become an unsustainable economic proposition."

Applying AI to existing security processes will be necessary, but not enough, he says. Instead, companies need to look at their business processes, determine which ones matter most, and find ways to protect them and prevent disruption.

No Place to Hide From AI

For the past two decades, cybersecurity experts have warned that companies can't expect to avoid attacks simply because they are in an obscure business or have a relatively small attack surface. Every part of a company that is attached to the Internet or connected to a partner connected to the Internet will be attacked, says Albert Ziegler, chief information security officer at offensive cybersecurity firm XBOW.

Related:Beware the Slasher: AI Could Kill Off Cybersecurity Pros' Skills

"These are not incredibly expensive attacks, but also these are attacks that work because the sites haven't been hardened enough," he says. "It's that it's not enough to protect a couple of crown jewel sites that you are very concerned about."

One way to bolster defenses is to focus on the basic paths that AI agents tend to exploit — overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts — and automate access decisions, so humans do not slow down responses, Silverfort's Ferris says. When Silverfort researchers improved controls, especially authentication and access, the same agent that took the domain in minutes hit 21 dead ends and gave up, he says.

"AI didn't create these weaknesses; it just finds them faster," Ferris says. "Controls that stop the attack at the point of access are cheaper than cleanup afterwards."

Companies should focus on the economics of recovering from an attack and how to protect their minimum viable business processes, says Gambit Security's Elias. Business leaders should focus on what investments will have the most business impact.

Unfortunately, that may mean budgets need to grow to adapt to the economics of AI, he says. However, "spending should increasingly be measured by how effectively it protects business operations," he notes, "rather than simply how many threats or tools a security program can manage."

Title: Warning: Attackers Are Using Calendar Invite Files to Evade Security Filters
Context: ” Notably, this technique has been incorporated into popular phishing kits, lowering the bar for unskilled threat actors to launch these attacks
Full Text:
Phishing attacks are increasingly using legitimate calendar invites to bypass security filters, according to researchers at Netcraft. Attackers send ICS calendar invite files that plant phishing lures directly on users’ calendars, often under the guise of work-related meetings.

“When an invite is sent to a user, having the item penciled into their calendar helps identify conflicts when scheduling,” the researchers write. “In this case, however, it allows attackers to go from the target’s inbox to their calendar without user interaction. Ultimately, the lure’s injection into the target’s calendar is a normal and intended behavior of their email client. In many email clients, this allows the invite to persist in the target’s calendar even after the original phishing email is deleted.”

Notably, this technique has been incorporated into popular phishing kits, lowering the bar for unskilled threat actors to launch these attacks.

“Calendar invite abuse has been adopted as a delivery mechanism by widespread campaigns such as those using EvilTokens, a token-stealing phishing toolkit targeting Microsoft 365 accounts that was previously reported by Netcraft,” the researchers write. “This campaign often used ICS files as low- friction lures, attempting to bypass scrutiny, appearing directly in a user’s calendar, and remaining even if the original phishing email was deleted. Invites associated with this campaign are often disguised as meetings, alerts, or voicemail notifications. When users follow them, they are taken to an attacker- controlled page that gives them a device code and instructions to enter it into Microsoft’s device authorization page.”

Users need to maintain a healthy sense of suspicion and stay up-to-date on evolving social engineering tactics in order to thwart these attacks.

“Email-attached calendar invites are now so ubiquitous that the average user may barely scrutinize them,” the researchers write. “In fast-paced, tech-reliant workplaces, new events appearing in the calendar without manual entry have become normalized. This combination of automatic behavior by email clients, users’ normalized expectations that events simply appear, and persistence even after the original email is deleted gives threat actors an easy route to the user’s attention.”

Netcraft has the story: https://www.netcraft.com/blog/how-attackers-get-into-your-calendar-the-easy-way

Why Caribbean Threats Cascade Into Global Cyber-Risk

The region is demonstrating what happens when exploits accelerate but assurance does not.

Marlon Cooper,CEO,Symptai Consulting Limited

October 23, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: FrankRamspott via Getty Images

COMMENTARY

On July 24, 2025, Curaçao's Tax and Customs Administration found ransomware on its network. Counter services, the call center, and internal processes went dark for more than a week, and the island's recovery depended on specialists flown in from the Netherlands.

A day earlier, the Joint Court of Justice had gone down as well. Because that court serves Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Bonaire, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, a single intrusion degraded the judicial system of six jurisdictions at once.

One platform, six governments.

That is the Caribbean's defining security characteristic, and it is why the interval between an exposure appearing and an exposure closing matters more here than almost anywhere else.

The Speed Gap

Consider what that interval currently is.

Fortinet's "Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition" recorded roughly 325 million attack attempts across the English-speaking Caribbean in 2025, an extraordinary volume against a small economic base, with critical vulnerabilities now targeted within 24 to 48 hours of disclosure, down from an average of nearly five days.

Related:Nigeria Deepens Cybersecurity Efforts as Cybercriminals See More Profits

IBM's 2026 "Cost of a Data Breach Report" puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, up 2.5% and reversing five consecutive years of improvement.

Both of those numbers moved this year, and they moved in opposite directions. Exploitation got faster. Finding and containing it got slower, for the first time in five years.

When Assurance Falls Behind

Here is the part that the security industry has not absorbed: third-party assurance still runs on an annual cycle. A global insurer assesses its Caribbean claims processor once a year.

A hotel chain reviews its regional franchisee's controls at renewal. A correspondent bank collects an attestation and files it. Every one of those instruments is calibrated to a threat landscape that stopped existing several years ago.

The questionnaire signed in March describes a network that was materially different by April and unrecognizable by October. Twelve months of assurance against 48 hours of exposure, and nobody has repriced the difference.

Global Issue

That mismatch is not a Caribbean failing. It is a global control design failing, and the Caribbean is simply where it shows up first because of what sits inside the interval.

The plumbing is ordinary. A business process outsourcer holds live credentials into a North American insurer's claims platform. A hotel group's property management system federates to a global loyalty program. A regional bank sits inside correspondent rails that clear in New York. An attacker who compromises the small end inherits trust at the large end, and does it inside a window where the large end's assurance process has no way to notice.

Related:Mexico's New Cyber Plan Faces Its First Real Test

The obvious response is that Caribbean organizations should simply patch faster.

Having spent two decades running security operations across these markets, I can tell you why that answer keeps failing. Security teams here are frequently two or three people covering an entire institution.

Critical systems often cannot be taken offline because there is no redundant capacity to fail over to. Vendor support is remote and time-zoned away. And where six jurisdictions share one platform, no single institution can authorize a maintenance window on it.

These are structural constraints, not attitudes, and telling the region to try harder has not moved the number in years.

Measure remediation against exploit velocity, not the audit calendar. Report critical MTTR as a distribution against a 48-hour benchmark. An average conceals the tail, and the tail is where the exposure lives.

Replace annual attestations with continuous evidence. If your assurance over a supplier is a document signed in March, you are not managing that risk; you're recording that you once looked at it.

Related:UK Social Media Ban for Minors Has Privacy Experts Worried

Assume some things can't be patched in time, and design for that. Segmentation, compensating controls, and explicit, owned, time-boxed decisions about what stays exposed. An undocumented exception is the same as no control.

Instrument the federated paths, not just the perimeter. Stolen credentials remain the primary route into cloud environments, and federated access is where a stolen credential stops being your incident and becomes your partner's.

Assess the shared provider, not just the institution. Where multiple entities run on one platform, assessing each separately measures the same risk repeatedly and reduces it once, at best.

The Caribbean isn't asking for allowances. It is showing the rest of the industry, early and in public, what happens when exploitation accelerates and assurance does not.

Anyone whose supply chain touches this region is measuring a snapshot of a system that has already changed.

Title: eMudhra Incident: A Practical Audit to Inspect Tools
Context: Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident
Full Text:
Browser protections were an important first response to the eMudhra certificate authority incident. But they don't answer a harder question for organizations: which other tools and environments still trust the affected certificate chains?

Certificate trust can come from different places. A tool may use the operating system's trust store, a bundled certificate list, or a runtime-specific store such as a Java JDK's cacerts. One machine can therefore have different trust behavior across its browsers, developer tools, and runtimes. Updating one trust store doesn't update them all.

That makes eMudhra remediation a software supply chain problem. Teams need to find where trust is configured, identify which systems need attention, and confirm that updates reach the tools developers and build processes actually use.

Start by Finding What Each Tool Trusts

Paul Horton, Sonatype's Open Source Program Office (OSPO) Global Director, created the open source eMudhra Audit and Fix script to help teams inspect selected developer tools on Unix-like machines.

The script checks tools such as Java, Node.js, Python, Go, and Git, along with system certificate bundles and other components. Where supported, it makes live HTTPS requests to two test hosts whose certificates chain to the affected intermediates, then checks GitHub as a control. The control helps distinguish certificate rejection from other connection problems, such as a lack of network access. The script also compares some tool versions with fixes listed in the incident reference. When a live probe and version check disagree, the live probe takes precedence.

By default, the audit does not install, change, or delete anything on the machine. It creates temporary probe programs and makes ordinary HTTPS requests. Those requests send no file contents. If network probes aren't appropriate for an environment, the --no-network option skips them and runs version checks only.

Teams can use the results to identify tools that need attention and decide what to investigate next. An audit result is a starting point for remediation, not confirmation that every system in the organization is protected.

Use the Results to Guide Remediation

Teams can use the script's output to:

Identify affected or potentially affected tools on a workstation.

Confirm how each tool is installed and which trust store it uses.

Apply the relevant operating system, runtime, or application vendor update.

Re-run the checks and record which systems still need remediation.

The script also has an optional --fix mode that can apply some changes it supports, asking before each change. Those actions can include upgrading a supported tool or changing a system or runtime trust store. Review the README and the proposed action before proceeding; the --dry-run option shows what a fix would do without changing anything. Prefer vendor updates where available, and test any workaround against the systems and services that depend on the trust store.

Know What the Script Can't See

The script audits the machine where it runs. It does not scan remote hosts, containers, or per-project dependencies. Its coverage is limited to specified tools and installation paths. Some tools receive version checks rather than live probes. A result from a developer workstation therefore cannot establish the status of a CI runner, container image, production host, or another employee's machine.

Organizations should treat those environments as separate parts of the investigation. Update and verify container images, build agents, and managed systems through the processes and vendor guidance that apply to them. For Sonatype products, follow the current Help documentation for product-specific updates and instructions.

The eMudhra incident showed why browser status alone can't answer whether an organization is remediated. Trust stores are distributed across tools and environments, and each one needs an owner and a way to verify its status. Paul's script gives teams a practical way to examine part of that landscape. Completing the work still requires a broader inventory, vendor updates, and follow-up checks.

The script is part of the Sonatype Nexus Community. If you have feedback or would like to contribute, engage with the project by following its Contribution Guidelines. As a community project, it is not officially supported by Sonatype.

For background on the eMudhra incident and Sonatype's response, see our published blog post.

Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 23, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: Mohamad Faizal Bin Ramli via Getty Images

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Broader Threat Landscape Means Stricter Underwriting Requirements

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

Cyber Insurers Become Active Players

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

In this article

Capcom’s breach exposed 11.7 million account records.

Leaked details could fuel convincing phishing messages.

Passwords on 196 accounts were changed without permission.

Use CAPCOM ID? Check your account and enable two-factor authentication.

Gamers are being warned to watch their inboxes after someone gained unauthorized access to Capcom’s online membership service.

Capcom, the Japanese video game developer and publisher behind Resident Evil, Monster Hunter, and Street Fighter, disclosed a breach affecting more than 11.7 million CAPCOM ID records worldwide.

The exposed information includes email addresses, account activity details, and IP addresses. A much smaller number of records also contained personal details such as dates of birth.

The company says credit card information was not affected, and it has not confirmed that passwords originally chosen by customers were compromised, but someone changed the passwords on 196 accounts without authorization. Capcom has since reset those passwords.

CAPCOM ID is the company’s unified account system for its websites and services, including online features in certain games. Users can also link it to gaming platform accounts, including PlayStation, Xbox, Steam, Epic Games, and Nintendo accounts.

For players, the exposed information could help scammers make fake Capcom messages more convincing, potentially tricking them into handing over passwords or verification codes.

Capcom discovered the incident on October 19, and says it has addressed the attack method. Games and services remain available, and the company plans to notify affected customers.

The 11.7 million figure refers to affected records, so it may not represent that many individual users. Capcom is still investigating the impact, including how the passwords on 196 accounts were changed without permission and whether any other unauthorized activity occurred on those accounts.

How to stay safe

As with any breach, watch for phishing messages, particularly those using the breach to create urgency. If an email claims your account needs attention, open your browser and go to cid.capcom.com independently to check it. Capcom warns users not to follow URLs or open attachments in suspicious messages.

You can also take these steps:

Enable CAPCOM ID’s two-factor authentication: This adds an authenticator-app code to the sign-in process, helping protect your account if someone obtains your password. Set it up from your Account page using a smartphone or tablet. Capcom recommends Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator.

Check your account, especially if you received an unexpected password-change notice: Review your registered information and linked platform accounts from your Account page. If you cannot sign in, use Forgot your password? on the login page. See Capcom’s support page for instructions.

Use official support channels if you need help: Find the appropriate regional contact in Capcom’s breach notice, rather than trusting contact details in an unexpected message.

Title: FBI Warns of Phishing Attacks Ahead of the US Midterm Elections
Context: Additionally, attackers are launching more targeted social engineering attacks against people involved in politics, using AI tools to craft extremely realistic messages
Full Text:
The U.S. FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) have issued joint advisories warning of election-themed scams targeting voters and spear phishing attacks targeting election officials.

“Scammers use the names, images, logos, and slogans of candidates to fraudulently solicit campaign contributions, sell merchandise that is never delivered, or steal personally identifiable information (PII) that can be used for other fraud,” the FBI says. “Scammers also exploit artificial intelligence (AI) tools to generate highly realistic voices, images, and written messages that impersonate candidates, campaigns, government entities, and trusted contacts. The realism makes these schemes harder for victims to detect and increases the likelihood of financial loss or exposure of PII.”

These scams include soliciting donations for phony Super PACs, campaign investment pool schemes and phishing attacks using voter registration as a lure.

Additionally, attackers are launching more targeted social engineering attacks against people involved in politics, using AI tools to craft extremely realistic messages.

“Election officials, candidates, and their political organizations are attractive targets to malicious cyber criminals due to their access to voter registration data, current government officials, or sensitive campaign information,” “In recent years, these actors have crafted increasingly sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications, making it difficult for targets to distinguish fraudulent messages.”

The FBI and CISA advise organizations and individuals to follow security best practices to thwart social engineering attacks:

“Implement or enhance existing security infrastructure. Ensure your organization has the latest antivirus/anti-malware software installed that detects and defends against inbound malware, spam, and new and sophisticated phishing campaigns. Further, ensure your organization has implemented phishing-resistant MFA. For information on newly exploited vulnerabilities please refer to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Educate employees on how to identify phishing and smishing attempts. Advise employees to be cautious when providing sensitive information — such as login credentials — electronically or over the phone, particularly if unsolicited or anomalous. Employees should confirm, if possible, requests for sensitive information through secondary channels.

Create processes for employees to send suspicious emails to IT departments for confirmation and advise personnel within your organization not to open email attachments from senders they do not recognize.”

The FBI has the story: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA261015-3

Title: Hacker leaks 281 GB of data from Germany’s far-right AfD party
Context: cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local...
Full Text:
Germany's far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) party has confirmed that it has suffered a security breach, after a hacker published what appear to be hundreds of thousands of the controversial political party's internal emails.

Earlier this week, the AfD admitted that its hosting provider had been hacked in September, and that some of its mailboxes had been copied. The party claims that most of the affected mailboxes had not been used for years, but the leaked archive reportedly includes messages dated as recently as 12 September 2026.

The news came as the Hexane.cc leak site published AI-written summaries of hundreds of thousands of the messages into categories such as racism and antisemitism, graded Low to Critical, according to local media reports.

To add to the AfD's discomfort, reports suggest that the hacker's access may have been gained in an embarrassingly simple fashion, via a website that had allegedly been left unpatched. However, this has not been independently verified.

What is unusual is that the leaked emails are not published on the site directly. Instead, AI-generated summaries are shown, categorised and rated from Low to Critical. The site encourages anybody who wants to read a complete original email, including headers, message bodies, attachments, and DKIM signatures, to download it via a torrent.

Of course, everyone should be wary of trusting AI-generated summaries, as artificial intelligence has a history of making sometimes large mistakes with great confidence. Indeed, party sources told the media that although the leaked emails appeared to be authentic, the AI-generated summaries appeared to contain several inaccuracies.

The full corpus of 281 GB of stolen messages and files has been made available for download via the torrent, and claims to contain 421,179 stolen internal party emails as well as more than 100,000 files.

The hacker says the leak is intended to expose the party's "degeneracy and hypocrisy."

They have also claimed that someone with a Proton Mail email address reached out to them offering 100,000 Euros if the leak site was taken down.

Should you be tempted to download the torrent and explore the contents of the messages yourself? I would advise against it. In the past, cybercriminals have used torrents of trending topics in the public eye to distribute malware. That's before you even consider the possible legal questions that can arise from handling stolen personal data, whatever you might think of the individuals exposed.

It's not the first cybersecurity headache that the AfD has suffered recently. On 3 September, a press spokesman for the party's group in the Thuringia state parliament warned that his work email account had been used to send phishing emails, and urged recipients not to open PDF attachments they may have received.

Whatever you may think of the AfD, there appear to have been security failures in this case that are far too common. It's not unusual for websites to be overlooked or half-forgotten, and left unpatched. It's not rare for shared infrastructure to not be segmented properly.

Furthermore, whether you are an individual or an organisation, you should be aware that an email account can be a treasure trove of sensitive information. Even if it has not been used for years, it can hold vast amounts of correspondence that can be exploited by hackers and fraudsters.

Title: Gaming Giant Capcom Confirms Data Breach Exposed Users’ Personal Information
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Capcom, the gaming giant behind Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, has warned that players’ personal information may have been compromised following a data breach.

In a notice published October 22, the Japanese company said customer information associated with CAPCOM ID was subject to unauthorized access by a third party.

CAPCOM ID is a unified account operated by Capcom that players can use to play Capcom-licensed games online as well as to access various web services.

As of October 22, Capcom estimated that the data compromised include:

11,774,247 records of email addresses and system-specific identifier information (e.g. date and time of account creation, date and time of last login, number of logins, client IP address used during last login)

43 records of date of birth, gender, country/region and nickname

Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of CAPCOM ID account login passwords originally set by customers themselves. However, it has observed that passwords were changed without authorization on 196 customer accounts.

“The passwords associated with these accounts have already been reset, and the company continues to investigate the scope of any impact resulting from this incident,” the company said.

It also confirmed that credit card information remains unaffected by the breach.

Capcom has warned that the affected information could potentially be misused in fraudulent emails or other communications impersonating the company or related parties.

It has advised customers to exercise caution when receiving suspicious messages and avoid clicking on links or opening attachments.

The company also confirmed that services using CAPCOM ID, including its games, remain available

Timeline of Capcom Data Breach and Company Response

Capcom detected suspicious activity involving its CAPCOM ID account system on October 19, 2026, indicating potential unauthorised access.

The company said it immediately moved to block the access, investigate the cause and scope of the incident, and implement emergency response measures. Later that day, Capcom confirmed that unauthorised access had occurred and began identifying and addressing the attack method.

On October 20, Capcom established an internal incident response headquarters to coordinate its investigation and prevent further impact.

The investigation confirmed that certain customer information registered with CAPCOM ID had been accessed without authorisation. The company also discovered that passwords associated with a limited number of accounts had been changed without permission.

Capcom subsequently reported the incident to its external Information Technology Security Oversight Committee.

By October 21, Capcom had completed emergency response measures and identified and addressed the attack method and reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.

Title: AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack
Context: Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may...
Full Text:
Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Project Perception's Second Act

The new release turns the system inward.

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Remediating Vulnerabilities With LLMs: Inside Ivanti's Automation Push

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Intelligence vs. Authority

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

One Stack vs. Multivendor Specialists

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

Controls Still Work in Progress

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

Title: Torvalds: AI is fine for competent devs, but spare us the 'drive-by' patches
Context: They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods
Full Text: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I. Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as "Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop." In the podcast Pivot to AI, podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: "This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI." I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous. I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse, which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place. Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them. All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful. Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today. In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception. Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to "deprecate the Assisted-by Tag." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions. That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool." Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so. As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe: "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming. Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real." True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers. Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides "tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it." By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers. In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question." He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself." It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®

Title: Compromised TLS Certificates
Context: One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive...
Full Text:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.
