Title: TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions
Context: Vendor Breach Puts TiDB Customers at Risk In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access...
Full Text:
UPDATE

A breach of an open source database provider may have inadvertently highlighted a serious gap in the way companies think about their cloud security.

On Oct. 19, software maker PingCAP, which sells an SQL database program called TiDB, disclosed that it had been breached. According to PingCAP's website, it serves major American corporations like Atlassian, Square, and Pinterest, as well as major players in China's AI space, including Manus, Kimi, and more.

The perpetrator — the somewhat deceptively named "Fulcrum Security," or FulcrumSec, for short — is a relatively new extortionist group whose leak site already includes major organizations like LexisNexis, Novo Nordisk, and the Manchester Airports Group (MAG). Earlier this fall, FulcrumSec appears to have compromised PingCAP, enjoying something shy of unfettered access to all of its cloud management, financial, analytics, storage, and other systems for a month or more.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

The even bigger issue is whether the breach exposed downstream customers' sensitive data. Investigators are still working out the details, but early evidence suggests that customers may be at some risk. Though their actual databases weren't breached, the information their vendor stored about them may have been enough to cause serious issues.

Vendor Breach Puts TiDB Customers at Risk

In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access to its systems from Sept. 9 to Oct. 7. Using stolen service account credentials, the company wrote, the unauthorized party accessed internal company systems and then copied data and source code.

PingCAP's own third-party-assisted investigation found no evidence that attackers ran malicious commands or maintained persistent access in their systems, nor did they access any customers' databases. Instead, it said, the threat actors accessed customers' billing and other business data, such as contract terms and pricing, as well as various information pertaining to cloud accounts and product usage — email addresses, SQL editor text and errors, etc. They also exported a table with encrypted API keys, though investigators said the encryption protected the keys from actually being used maliciously.

Dark Reading reached out to PingCAP for comment. A company spokesperson provided the following statement:

"Between September 9 and October 7, 2026, an unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code. PingCAP identified the activity on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials that day. As of October 14, all identified compromised credentials have been invalidated, all identified unauthorized access paths have been blocked, and four vulnerabilities reported by our external incident response firm have been fixed and independently verified as remediated.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

"Our investigation, supported by outside counsel and third-party forensic specialists, has found no evidence that data stored by customers in our TiDB cloud production services was impacted, and no evidence that the attacker ran commands or maintained persistent access in the production systems reviewed. Exported records included certain TiDB Cloud account information, business and billing details. API-key values in the exported data were encrypted, and we have found no evidence that any were decrypted or used. As a precaution, we have advised all customers to rotate their TiDB Cloud management API keys and remain alert to targeted phishing attempts. We will notify affected customers directly as customer-specific impact is confirmed, and we will continue to share verified updates on our Trust Hub: pingcap.com/trust-hub."

FulcrumSec, however, painted a bleaker picture.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Attackers Leak TiDB Customer Data

In a name-and-shame post to its leak site, the hackers claimed to be in possession of all of PingCAP's service management records, its financial records, its files stored within Google Cloud, Jira support tickets, customer relationship management (CRM) data, analytics data, source code, plus a four-year-long log of every connection every one of its customers ever made to the TiDB Cloud service.

Crucially, the hackers did not claim to have stolen any TiDB databases straight up. Instead, they indirectly obtained a wealth of potentially exploitable user data like those aforementioned API keys and other secrets, and potentially sensitive internal data exposed by cloud database commands.

The attackers fingered individual enterprises caught in the crossfire: brand-name US companies like Airbnb and Booking.com, Asian corporate giants like Baidu and Fujitsu, and a few of the world's biggest video game companies, including Capcom, Konami, and Square Enix. Asia represented the biggest slice of the pie, with nearly 2,000 affected organizations in Japan, China, and Hong Kong, with another 500 from India.

Additionally, FulcrumSec said its unauthorized access lasted for nearly two months, not just one. It was so comprehensive and unthreatened that, in the meantime, they were able to stand up a mirror of PingCAP's own service management system. Instead of having to manually exfiltrate data, their replication feed automatically pulled fresh copies of the company's internal database every six hours, for 22 days.

Claims made by threat actors must always be met with a degree of skepticism, and Dark Reading did not independently confirm FulcrumSec's. Still, the group does have some record of reliability.

Last summer, for example, the group breached Manchester Airports Group (MAG), claiming to have stolen 86GB of data. That data turned out to contain far more genuine personally identifiable information (PII) than MAG copped to, according to reporting by BleepingComputer. And whereas some hackers exaggerate their winnings, this case was something of the opposite: That initial 86GB claim represented compressed data. The hackers clarified that the actual, uncompressed total stolen was 640GB.

Orgs: Be More Critical of Your Service Providers

Even if one were to completely ignore the hackers' account and take PingCAP's more limited assessment as the truth, it would still represent a potentially serious risk to customers.

Arguably the most acute dangers — more than the broad customer data, or the API keys if they are in fact protected — lie in the less obvious exfiltrated data. This includes Jira tickets, SQL histories, and places where organizations unknowingly leak internal data. For instance, when customers use their cloud-managed database services, they send commands to the vendors' servers. Those interactions can often carry corporate secrets or sensitive data of many other types.

"Vendors don't typically set out to store secrets. However, customers often pass them over to use features built for convenience, and the data can settle in places few people think of as credential stores," explains Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at Sysdig.

Take PingCAP's SQL editor text and errors, for example, she says. "That's query history and error output, which is where secrets can accumulate when someone pastes a connection string to debug something on the fly," Morin adds. In FulcrumSec's name-and-shame post, for example, it highlighted exfiltrated SQL statements that listed in full view one medical clinic's roster of patients, and another's list of medical professionals.

Keeper Security chief information security officer Shane Barney seconds Morin's point. "The PingCAP incident illustrates a daily reality in enterprise security: Attackers do not need to compromise a customer's primary database directly if they can systematically harvest upstream credentials," he says. "In modern software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecosystems, customer metadata, API keys, and diagnostic query logs routinely seep into vendor environments through everyday operational telemetry. When service account credentials or administrative API tokens are stolen from a provider, that aggregated operational data transforms into a road map for exploitation."

Barney emphasizes the importance of cloud security hygiene — such as rotating vendor-facing API keys and eliminating hardcoded and long-lived secrets in developer workflows — and vetting one's managed service providers by demanding continuous third-party risk assessments and independent certifications and attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001.

Morin urges organizations to ask a few specific questions when vetting cloud providers. "Teams should seek to understand what customer-provided data the vendor retains and what its retention policy is. They should also ask whether they scan for secrets at ingest and redact what they find," she says. "Teams may also want to understand how service account credentials are handled, whether they’re short-lived, how they’re scoped, how often they rotate, and what detections fire on anomalous credential or account use."

And, she says, don't forget: "Inquire about breach notification, specifically the timeline and what triggers it."

This story was updated at 9 p.m. ET on Oct. 22 to reflect a statement from PingCAP.

Title: No time to PHP around.
Context: Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.
Full Text:
Critical PHP flaws threaten millions of websites. Weak certificates from an Indian authority spark a global security scramble. Investigators probe a U.S. consulting executive’s alleged ties to ShinyHunters. SafePay ransomware hits at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations. Researchers find troubling security biases in Chinese AI-generated code. A $10 million initiative bolsters cybersecurity for small U.S. utilities. An American pleads guilty to stealing from thousands of servicemembers and veterans. Leo Scott, Managing Director of DataTribe, is talking about their upcoming Cyber Innovation Conference and the 9th annual DataTribe Challenge. Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

Today is Wednesday October 21st 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

PHP vulnerabilities put millions of web sites at risk.

PHP is a widely used, open-source programming language that powers the behind-the-scenes functionality of websites. It runs on web servers, handling tasks like processing forms, managing user accounts, interacting with databases, and generating web pages. Popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla rely on PHP. Because it’s so widely used, a serious PHP vulnerability can potentially affect millions of websites.

Now, PHP administrators are bracing for two potentially critical vulnerabilities that could put millions of websites at risk. PHP maintainers have announced plans to release patches for two flaws, each carrying a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.

The warning follows leaked, but unverified, details of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell, reportedly capable of executing code on servers running popular platforms including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento.

Security firm watchTowr says it has confirmed the vulnerabilities are real, while researchers at Sansec warn that widespread attacks could begin within minutes of the patches becoming available.

One researcher estimates that 1.3 million internet-connected hosts may be affected.

Administrators are being urged to inventory their PHP applications, prepare backups, and arrange emergency maintenance windows. Patches are scheduled for release at 14:00 UTC, though maintainers warn they could arrive earlier if exploitation is detected.

Given PHP’s enormous footprint, the potential consequences extend across much of the web.

An Indian cert authority unlocks a global security headache.

Security teams worldwide are scrambling to contain a potentially massive Internet security problem after researchers discovered eight digital certificates with private keys so weak that attackers could use them to impersonate virtually any website.

The certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra. They’re intermediate certificates, meaning they can be used to issue other certificates that browsers and applications automatically trust.

Normally, cracking their encryption would be practically impossible. But these keys were astonishingly weak, containing as little as three to eight bits of entropy. One researcher described the situation as “bonkers.”

Major browsers and several applications have already blocked the certificates, and there’s currently no evidence they’ve been maliciously exploited. But cleaning up the broader Internet could take years.

Cryptography expert Filippo Valsorda compares the challenge to the 2014 Heartbleed vulnerability, warning that this recovery could be even more complicated. Linux systems, embedded devices, forgotten servers, and Internet of Things equipment may require individual updates.

The immediate concern involves attackers intercepting encrypted communications, particularly VPN connections. Exploitation requires positioning oneself between communicating parties, something that’s easier for attackers controlling local networks or possessing sophisticated surveillance capabilities.

Most modern browsers have implemented protections, although Microsoft’s Edge on Windows 10 reportedly remained vulnerable in some circumstances.

The incident exposes a fundamental weakness in Internet trust: even the strongest encryption depends on the security of the organizations issuing certificates.

And when one of those organizations gets the fundamentals spectacularly wrong, the cleanup becomes everybody’s problem.

Investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters.

Federal investigators examining the ShinyHunters hacking group are scrutinizing executives at two ransomware negotiation firms over their alleged relationships with the cybercriminals.

According to KrebsOnSecurity, investigators believe an executive at a major U.S. consulting firm helped operate ShinyHunters’ extortion website, which pressured nearly 100 victims to pay ransoms.

Authorities have also arrested Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky on extortion-related charges. Investigators reportedly uncovered communications linking him and other negotiators to ShinyHunters after Dutch police arrested a suspected group member and accessed his Signal messages.

The investigation raises troubling questions about conflicts of interest in the ransomware negotiation business. Some firms reportedly collect fees based on the size of ransom payments, creating financial incentives that may favor the criminals over their victims.

The allegations remain under investigation.

SafePay ransomware has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide.

The SafePay ransomware group has compromised at least 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since emerging in August 2024, according to a joint advisory from U.S., German, and British authorities.

SafePay has become one of 2026’s most active ransomware operations, targeting organizations across four continents.

The group gains access through stolen credentials, brute-force attacks, vulnerable VPNs, and exposed network devices. Once inside, attackers escalate privileges, move laterally using legitimate administrative tools, disable security software, and steal sensitive data before encrypting systems.

SafePay employs double extortion, demanding cryptocurrency payments in exchange for decryption tools and promises not to publish stolen information.

The group also reportedly calls victims directly to pressure them into paying.

Authorities are urging organizations to strengthen defenses against SafePay’s increasingly widespread operations.

New research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

The United States has banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, citing national security concerns. The Department of Homeland Security says DeepSeek’s China-based infrastructure could expose sensitive American data to Chinese authorities.

Beijing condemned the restrictions and warned of possible retaliation, adding another complication to already strained U.S.-China technology relations.

Meanwhile, new research raises questions about the security of code generated by Chinese AI models.

Cybersecurity startup Hirundo tested Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder and found it produced significantly more vulnerable applications for American defense contractors than Chinese ones. Seventy percent of applications generated for U.S. contractors were exploitable, compared with 59 percent for Chinese contractors.

Applications built for a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group were also more likely to leak secrets.

Hirundo says the discrepancies disappeared after researchers modified the model to remove what they characterize as Chinese Communist Party political alignment.

The findings suggest that AI coding assistants may introduce security risks influenced by their training and underlying model behavior.

A $10 million initiative looks to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

Accenture, Dragos, and the SANS Institute are launching a $10 million initiative to help smaller U.S. utilities defend against cyberattacks.

The new nonprofit Community Cyber Resilience Foundation will initially provide free cybersecurity technology, hardware, deployment assistance, and training to as many as 500 water, wastewater, electric, and natural gas utilities.

The announcement follows a surge in cyberattacks affecting more than 100 American water systems across over a dozen states.

Eligible utilities must have annual revenues below $100 million, a threshold covering more than 50,000 organizations nationwide.

Participants will receive access to Dragos security technology, Accenture implementation support, and SANS operational technology training.

The initiative aims to address a growing cybersecurity divide between large infrastructure operators and smaller utilities struggling with limited budgets, aging equipment, and staffing shortages.

An American pleads guilty to an identity theft scheme targeting U.S. service members.

A 45-year-old American has pleaded guilty to orchestrating an identity theft scheme that targeted thousands of U.S. servicemembers and veterans.

Robert Wayne Boling Jr. operated from the Philippines, using stolen personal information to access victims’ bank accounts and steal money and veterans’ benefits between 2014 and 2019.

Prosecutors say Boling obtained sensitive records from a former U.S. Army medical records contractor stationed in South Korea.

The operation relied on dozens of money mules in the United States who received stolen funds and transferred portions of the proceeds to the Philippines.

Boling was deported to the United States and arrested in May. Two accomplices have already been sentenced, while two others remain fugitives.

Boling faces up to 40 years in prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering.

Two pallets of GPUs never make it to baggage claim.

A Brazilian electronics distributor is looking for nearly half a million dollars’ worth of missing graphics cards, and it’s taking its search to Instagram.

Oderço says two pallets of high-end Nvidia RTX 5090 GPUs arrived at São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, then apparently vanished.

After getting nowhere with official inquiries, the company turned to social media, saying nothing like this has happened in its 38-year history.

The missing shipment is valued at roughly $470,000, although the company hasn’t disclosed exactly how many cards disappeared, or when.

The timing is particularly unfortunate. RTX 5090s are already in short supply, with retail prices reaching thousands of dollars per card.

Whether the shipment was stolen, misplaced, or swallowed by some bureaucratic black hole remains unclear.

For now, Oderço is hoping the internet can help locate its missing hardware.

Which is perhaps fitting, considering how many people have already been searching the internet for an RTX 5090.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security
Context: “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry
Full Text:
PRESS RELEASE

SANTA CLARA, Calif. — October 13, 2026 — Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads.

Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

“An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.”

“As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.”

“An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.”

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

About OCP and the New Security Working Group

The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure.

As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California.

Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project.

About Marvell

To deliver the data infrastructure technology that connects the world, we’re building solutions on the most powerful foundation: our partnerships with our customers. Trusted by the world’s leading technology companies for over 30 years, we move, store, process and secure the world’s data with semiconductor solutions designed for our customers’ current needs and future ambitions. Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.

Oracle offers integrated suites of applications plus secure, autonomous infrastructure in the Oracle Cloud. For more information about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), please visit us at www.oracle.com.

Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Research finds that, among respondents experiencing data loss, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incidents before data left the organization.

October 21, 2026

4 Min Read

PRESS RELEASE

SEATTLE — (BUSINESS WIRE) — Data loss prevention (DLP) tools are often functioning as after-the-fact forensic systems rather than prevention controls, according to DLP in the AI Era, a new survey from the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), the world's leading not-for-profit organization committed to AI, cloud, and Zero Trust cybersecurity education. The study, conducted in collaboration with Jazz, found that 73% of organizations said they experienced at least one confirmed data loss incident in the past 24 months. Among the respondents, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incident before data left the organization.

“Enterprise DLP has moved beyond the question of whether it should be deployed to whether it’s doing what it is intended to do. Enforcement is being softened, analyst capacity is consumed by noise, and new data-exit channels created through GenAI are exposing gaps legacy DLP was never meant to handle,” said Hillary Baron, AVP/Research, Cloud Security Alliance. “In the AI era, where employees and applications can move sensitive data through more channels than ever, organizations can’t afford to discover gaps after the fact.”

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Among the report’s findings:

Perceived visibility exceeds demonstrated capability. While close to half (48%) of security teams ranked GenAI as their top exfiltration risk, less than a third (29%) are able to produce a routine 30-day report showing sensitive data sent to GenAI tools.

Modern risks lack modern enforcement. Paradoxically, the highest-ranked risks are among the least strictly enforced, and the lowest-ranked are among the most strictly enforced. Both GenAI (48%) and cloud storage uploads (41%) were cited as top exfiltration risks, but only 22% of organizations strictly block on GenAI and 19% on cloud storage uploads. Conversely, removable media, which ranked last (10%) as an exfiltration risk, is strictly blocked by 31% of respondents, the highest strict-block of any channel measured.

DLP alert overload fuels fatigue. Fifty-four percent of teams are triaging DLP alerts where the majority turn out to be false positives, and 90% report at least one measurable impact from alert fatigue in the past year, including 21% who report voluntary staff departures directly attributable to DLP alert burden.

Business friction determines enforcement posture. Seventy-one percent of respondents reported that their security teams received pushback on DLP enforcement during the past two years. Among those teams, 66% reduced enforcement for specific teams/use cases; 8% reduced enforcement broadly across the organization; and 3% reduced or paused the program entirely. Across the full respondent base, 54% softened enforcement in some form.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

“Security teams know GenAI is creating new ways for sensitive data to leave the business, but many still cannot see the full impact,” said Ido Livneh, Co-Founder & CEO, Jazz. “Across the customer environments we observe, the average organization uses nearly 170 AI tools and fewer than 10 are sanctioned. Teams need to understand how data is actually moving so they can focus on real risk without blocking legitimate work.”

The survey was conducted online by CSA in June and July 2026 and received 433 responses from IT and security professionals. Respondents represented organizations ranging from fewer than 1,000 to more than 50,000 employees and were primarily located in the United States and Canada. Jazz funded the research and co-developed the questionnaire with CSA research analysts, while CSA independently performed the data analysis and interpretation.

Jazz is the DLP platform built to understand your business. Its agentic investigator, Melody, delivers pre-investigated findings with the business context already attached with no rules, no regex, and no browser extension required. A single lightweight agent runs at under 1% CPU and covers GenAI use, shadow IT, desktop applications, and personal cloud accounts. Jazz is a Gartner Cool Vendor and the winner of the 2026 CrowdStrike, AWS and NVIDIA Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator, selected out of nearly 1,000 startups. Learn more at jazz.security.

The Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) is the world’s leading not-for-profit organization committed to awareness, practical implementation, and credentialing of forward-looking cybersecurity topics, including AI, cloud, and Zero Trust. In an era where digital transformation drives business success, CSA stands as the global authority ensuring organizations can operate securely while harnessing cutting-edge technology. Through the 501(c)3 CSAI Foundation, volunteer-driven research, globally-accepted standards, and award-winning vendor-neutral education programs that unite varied associations, governments, chapters, and corporate members, CSA bridges the gap between innovation and pragmatic security execution. Title: 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security Industry
Context: " On the other hand, "that same early warning was available to attackers, who were undoubtedly spinning up AI and LLMs to find the vulnerabilities, identify targets, and start...
Full Text:
A pair of critical vulnerabilities tied to open source scripting language PHP appear to have significant consequences for much of the server infrastructure holding the Internet afloat.

These vulnerabilities, dubbed "php2shell" by some researchers, include CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. CVE-2026-109618 enables remote code execution (RCE) via out-of-memory corruption, and CVE-2026-109619 enables RCE via a stale global state. The vulnerabilities, discovered by infosec consulting firm Calif, were designated with a critical CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

According to a WatchTowr blog post, both PHP vulnerabilities let an attacker run their own code on a Web server without logging in. "It stems from stale internal data that survives after its memory is freed; a later request handled by the same worker can use that leftover data, and PHP confirms this can let an attacker run their own code on the server without logging in. Reaching the server over the network is enough; no account or prior access is needed," researchers said in the blog post.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Patch Your Web-Facing PHP Servers Now

Organizations should update affected servers to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to protect against the flaws. As 8.2 through 8.5 are the supported versions of PHP, lower-numbered versions do not have a patch available, meaning organizations must either upgrade their PHP versions to a supported branch or use a backported fix. PHP's security advisory urges that while only an update is a complete solution, organizations can take certain actions to reduce exposure until that time.

PHP's maintainers initially said yesterday that an emergency security release was scheduled for Oct. 22 at 14:00 UTC alongside coordinated disclosure, but as WatchTowr's blog post explained, the embargo broke. A proof-of-concept tool called "PHP2Shell" came to light, and WatchTowr claimed to be able to recreate both vulnerabilities.

John Hammond, senior principal security researcher for Huntress, tells Dark Reading that there was a silver lining in the leak in that it "pushed defenders to inventory systems, prepare mitigations, and get ready to patch sooner."

On the other hand, "that same early warning was available to attackers, who were undoubtedly spinning up AI and LLMs to find the vulnerabilities, identify targets, and start developing or adapting exploits," Hammond adds.

This may not be theoretical risk, either; WatchTowr reported it has observed exploitation attempts of both flaws in the wild. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for WatchTowr, tells Dark Reading that while no one has been successful yet, the company does not expect this to be the case for very long.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The vendor said the potential for exploitation is broad across vulnerable PHP installations, and security teams should prioritize "internet-facing servers running PHP as an Apache module," as the PHP Foundation highlighted that configuration as having the highest risk.

"Every PHP installation that serves web requests is in scope, including PHP-FPM, Apache’s mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, and PHP says the risk is highest on mod_php, where an attack can succeed before any application code runs," WatchTowr's blog post read. "Session Upload Progress, a feature turned on by default, offers one confirmed path to the problem, so most default deployments meet that precondition."

More Critical Bugs Involving Open Source Projects

PHP is a common, highly supported programming language run on servers across the globe and used for Web development. The scope of organizations using PHP spans the Internet, from enterprises to small businesses, critical infrastructure, and municipalities. Many organizations, like the Netherlands' National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), took websites and services down to limit exposure and/or facilitate emergency patching.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

As the Independent Federated Intelligence Network, a not-for-profit cyber intelligence group, warned in a Mastodon post, "If you are able to contact folks at local schools, governments, nonprofits, and other services to warn them about the PHP vulnerabilities, please consider doing so. These locations often do not have dedicated security staff and almost certainly have PHP assets exposed."

In a blog post, Huntress' Hammond recommended inventorying every PHP install, identifying end-of-life PHP installs, and alerting on "PHP worker processes launching shells, interpreters, or download tools."

Despite the leak and the resulting chaos, PHP maintainers acted quickly to give organizations lead time for two challenging vulnerabilities. Patrick Münch, chief security officer at Mondoo, praised the PHP Foundation's response. He worries, however, about the resources of open source organizations, which have to support this kind of work, often on a volunteer basis.

"I think the PHP team handled this well. They warned people a day ahead, Linux distributions got the patches early, and they even wrote fixes for old versions they don't support anymore. A lot of commercial vendors wouldn't do that," he says. "Where it gets harder is everything after php.net. PHP gets packaged and shipped by distributions, hosting companies, and software vendors, and a lot of those are volunteers or very small teams."

Indeed, the PHP2Shell flaws echo the Log4Shell vulnerability in Log4j 2 nearly five years ago, which similarly required the security industry to come together to collectively patch a major flaw in a popular open source project.

Title: PHP Foundation Says Chainguard Broke Security Embargo Ahead of Emergency Patches
Context: The PHP Foundation says Chainguard broke a coordinated security embargo by releasing patched PHP container images hours ahead of schedule, making the fix available for attackers...
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation says Chainguard broke a coordinated security embargo by releasing patched PHP container images hours ahead of schedule, making the fix available for attackers to study while other distributors were still preparing updates.

In a postmortem published October 21, the Foundation described a disclosure process disrupted by leaked CVE identifiers, an accidentally published exploit demonstration, and Chainguard’s decision to release early. It also acknowledged that work on the underlying memory management problem had stalled repeatedly after developers first noticed signs of it in 2024.

The account follows PHP’s emergency patches for two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Researchers demonstrated attacks that could execute code on web servers without logging in.

Chainguard released early citing exploits in the wild #

The PHP Foundation wrote:

On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.

Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc described the decision in a Hacker News comment posted earlier that day.

“I made the call to get these out early when exploits hit in the wild,” Lorenc wrote. He praised the maintainers’ work, said Chainguard had extensively tested the patch, and said the images were free and would remain so.

In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Lorenc defended his decision and apologized for the additional stress on PHP’s maintainers.

Lorenc said Chainguard independently discovered the vulnerability after receiving an initial warning on Friday, using its testing harness and a frontier AI model, and later helped test the fixes. By Tuesday night, he said, several other security vendors involved in the disclosure had reported exploits in the wild.

“After talking to several of the other researchers on a video call, I made the call to ship the fixes and immediately notified the group,” Lorenc wrote.

He cited those exploitation reports, the ease of independently discovering and exploiting the vulnerability, and information already circulating publicly as reasons for releasing early. He said the patched artifacts were publicly accessible to everyone, including organizations that were not Chainguard customers.

The Foundation offered a narrower assessment of the exploit code circulating before disclosure. Its security team inspected public proof-of-concept exploits after the leak but had not identified any functional ones by release time.

Lorenc did not name the vendors or publish supporting evidence of exploitation in his post. The Foundation’s assessment of the public PoCs it examined does not rule out exploitation elsewhere.

Cloudflare’s Dane Knecht had also reported early attacks before the patches arrived and said the company had deployed temporary WAF protections. His warning did not establish that those attacks had successfully compromised servers.

Chainguard allows early disclosure but commits to continued coordination #

Lorenc has previously argued that embargoes are essential to protecting users before vulnerability details become public. In his July 5 post, Summer of Clearinghouses, he explained how a published fix can help attackers locate the underlying vulnerability.

“Pre-disclosure protection extends exactly as far as the people you can vet and hold to an embargo,” he wrote.

Chainguard’s vulnerability disclosure policy, last updated September 22, says the company may shorten disclosure timelines in response to active exploitation, publicly available details, or other exceptional circumstances. Those are the company’s own criteria for releasing early. They do not establish that PHP’s maintainers authorized publication of the patches shared under embargo.

The policy also promises to “notify the reporter of any changes to the disclosure timeline” and continue coordinating to reduce harm. Lorenc said he immediately notified the coordination group after deciding to release early. The Foundation characterized the release as unilateral.

The Foundation’s account drew criticism of Chainguard in Reddit’s r/PHP and r/cybersecurity communities, where commenters questioned whether other projects would trust the company with embargoed patches again. Others urged businesses that depend on PHP to fund its maintainers, while pushing back on suggestions that the team had knowingly left a demonstrated RCE unfixed since 2024.

The release had already been moved forward a day #

The disclosure schedule began breaking down on October 20. At around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE identifiers appeared on forums and social media alongside an incorrect release time and an incorrect CVSS score of 10.0. The Foundation says that initial leak contained no technical details.

PHP brought its public warning forward to 19:30 UTC and moved the scheduled patch release from October 22 to October 21, keeping the planned 14:00 UTC release time.

Distributors were still packaging the fixes. According to the Foundation, an immediate release would have left many users without a straightforward way to update.

Around 20:00 UTC on October 20, Calif accidentally published a video showing its exploits working against several targets, the Foundation said. Although the video was deleted, copies spread on social media. The Foundation said the demonstration exposed limited additional details and accelerated development of public PoCs.

The Foundation also said mitigation guidance shared with some critical infrastructure providers around 23:00 UTC may have leaked. It did not identify who leaked the initial CVE information.

The underlying problem surfaced in 2024 #

The Foundation’s account also explains why the out-of-memory problem behind CVE-2026-109618 took so long to resolve.

A PHP core developer found the first signs while addressing an issue from a 2024 Quarkslab audit organized through OSTIF and funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency. At that point, exploitation was theoretical. Developers had not identified concrete attack vectors, and other vulnerabilities with clearer impact took priority.

Several proposed fixes came with serious costs: breaking compatibility, creating new denial-of-service risks, or requiring changes across third-party extensions. The security team’s consensus process struggled to settle on an approach, and the small number of developers with deep engine expertise had other responsibilities. Work stalled and restarted over months.

“We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources,” the Foundation wrote.

The situation changed in August. The Foundation says Calif reported an unconditional RCE with the same root cause on August 11, and OpenAI independently reported that root cause the same day. Wiz and OpenAI subsequently supplied additional attack vectors.

Calif’s own timeline adds that it shared an RCE proof of concept with PHP on August 14 and received confirmation that it worked on August 15. The Foundation says fixing the issue became its security team’s top priority from August 11.

PHP is changing how security decisions get made #

The security team has begun moving toward majority decisions so difficult fixes do not remain stuck waiting for consensus. The Foundation also says serious vulnerabilities involving hard trade-offs should reach its leadership sooner.

The pressure on that team is growing. According to the Foundation, PHP has published 15 CVEs since July 1 while also working through more than 100 reports that were invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible. AI tools help validate findings, but engineers still have to choose, implement, and review the fixes.

The Foundation is asking companies, hosting providers, cloud platforms, and governments that depend on PHP to fund more engineers with deep knowledge of the engine. AI tools can help validate findings, but engineers still have to choose, implement, and review the fixes.

Title: Limits of Java Certificate Bypass: Fingerprint Blocklist Insights
Context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

Title: eMudhra CA Incident: Sonatype's Assessment and Guidance
Context: For self-managed deployments, install the applicable updated Docker image or patch release when available
Full Text:
Sonatype is responding to the industry-wide eMudhra certificate authority incident, which affects certificate trust stores used by certain Sonatype products and distributions. We are updating affected components. In the meantime, apply certificate trust-store updates provided by your operating-system, runtime, and application vendors.

What Happened

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) could be recovered because they were generated with insufficient randomness. Six affected intermediates were for TLS certificates and two were for code signing. Someone with an affected TLS key could create a certificate for a website or service, which could be accepted by clients that still trust the affected chain.

Browser and operating system vendors have taken steps to block the affected certificates. Other software may rely on separate or bundled certificate trust stores that need updates, so organizations should also check systems beyond browsers and operating systems.

Sonatype Impact

We are preparing updated Docker images and patch releases with current certificate trust data. The tables below list the impacted Sonatype products and their remediation status. Existing Docker images and bundled JVMs do not update automatically.

For self-managed deployments, install the applicable updated Docker image or patch release when available.

What Customers Must Do

Update certificate trust stores and any software that bundles a trust store, including containers and applications.

Organizations may also see related advisories, including CVE-2026-113470 for Amazon Linux packages and RHSB-2026-012 from Red Hat. These identifiers support tracking across affected software and trust stores; remediation may differ by product and environment.

Title: Best practices for integrating IAM Roles Anywhere with your PKI
Context: This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs
Full Text:
Using temporary credentials is a security best practice to reduce the risk from credentials getting compromised. With AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, now your workloads outside of Amazon Web Services (AWS) will be able to access AWS resources by obtaining temporary security credentials in AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). IAM Roles Anywhere relies on public key infrastructure (PKI) to establish trust between your AWS account and certificate authorities that issues certificates to your workloads that run outside AWS. PKI involves the generation, distribution, and verification of digital certificates through public key encryption.

In this post, we show you some best practices, considerations, and solutions for integrating your PKI with IAM Roles Anywhere. In this post, we assume that you have a foundational knowledge of IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere. For more information, see the IAM and IAM Roles Anywhere documentation.

Note: As of July 2026, AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) supports exportable public certificates that can be used on workloads outside AWS (containers or on-premises). Additionally, ACM supports the ACME protocol for automated certificate issuance and renewal on external workloads. These capabilities complement IAM Roles Anywhere by providing both identity (using X.509 certificates for IAM Roles Anywhere) and encryption (using ACM public/private certificates) for hybrid environments.

X.509 certificates for workload identity

If you’re running multiple workloads in your infrastructure, you’re probably assigning unique workload identities and specific user permissions. In this environment, your workloads can use PKI tools like Active Directory Certificate Services to centrally manage and monitor the identities and permissions at scale. The same principles of segregating unrelated workloads apply to PKI and IAM Roles Anywhere. If you’re issuing certificates to your workloads today, they can probably be used with IAM Roles Anywhere without any changes.

As shown in Figure 1, the access boundary and permissions of Workload A can be very different from that of Workload B when accessing AWS resources, depending on the organization’s needs. In such scenarios, it’s recommended to establish a unique machine identity for each workload. This can be achieved by issuing a separate X.509 certificate with distinct identity attributes signed by your certificate authority (CA). To set up an effective PKI solution for machine identities, you must configure the appropriate certificate attributes and anchor the trust model around those attributes.

Figure 1: Workloads outside of AWS accessing AWS services

Temporary access credentials

Workloads with distinct CA signed X.509 certificates exchange certificates with IAM, as shown in Figure 2, to get temporary security credentials for the session. The signature validation process used by IAM Roles Anywhere verifies the certificate issuer and the subject before providing the temporary credentials. To enable this verification process, an IAM Roles Anywhere trust model should be set up by either uploading your CA’s digital certificate as a trust anchor or by referencing an existing AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) certificate. In this post, we focus on using a trust anchor.

To help define the appropriate scope for the temporary credentials, it’s recommended to configure distinct IAM roles for each workload to assume. Workloads must use X.509 certificates issued by your CA. These certificates are exchanged with IAM to get temporary security credentials for the session.

Figure 2: Getting temporary credentials from IAM using CA issued X.509 certificate

Setting up a trust model for IAM Roles Anywhere is a three-step process, see Extend AWS IAM Roles Anywhere to workloads outside of AWS for more information.

Create a trust anchor.

Set up IAM roles with the IAM Roles Anywhere trust policy that will be assumed by your non-AWS workload.

Configure profiles with IAM roles and attach relevant session policies. This instructs IAM Roles Anywhere to use your selected session policies whenever you request credentials for any of the attached roles.

Trust model

The trust model is centered around setting up the right trust relationship between IAM Roles Anywhere and your CA by configuring a trust anchor. The model connects the role, the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal, and identities encoded in X509 certificates that are issued by a CA.

Certificate attributes

Certificates are a binary record with encoded key/value pairs as certificate attributes. Let’s look at one of the X.509 certificates to understand different attributes of certificate that are important for IAM Roles Anywhere PKI validation.

The following is an example PEM encoded certificate file that can be decoded with tools like openssl.

-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIKOzCCCSOgAwIBAgIQDlnyZvBeKjgHm1jJ++CbgDANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQsFADBE MQswC ........... -----END CERTIFICATE---- Certificate: Data: Version: 3 (0x2) Serial Number: e0:5d:b7:72:56:fa:75:e3 Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 Issuer: C=US, ST=CA, L=San Francisco, O=MyCompany Inc., OU=AC, CN=MyCompany CA Validity Not Before: Sep 15 00:09:17 2023 GMT Not After : Sep 18 00:09:17 2023 GMT Subject: C=US, O=MyCompany, OU=eCommerce, CN=WorkloadA Subject Public Key Info: Public Key Algorithm: id-ecPublicKey Public-Key: (384 bit) pub: 04:3b:74:e1:68:06:fa:b0:3d:fe:f7:5f:74:80:05: X509v3 extensions: X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:ecommerce.mycompany.com, DNS:*ecommerce.mycompany.com, URI:spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical CA:FALSE X509v3 Key Usage: critical Digital Signature Signature Algorithm: ecdsa-with-SHA512 30:64:02:30:19:a7:a0:33:49:ce:e1:cb:76:6e:c0:f3:c5:66:

IAM Roles Anywhere extracts values from the subject Common Name (CN), issuer, and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) fields of the authenticating certificate and makes them available for policy evaluation through the sts:sourceIdentity and principal tags. When configuring your PKI, set short validity periods on the certificates issued to workloads. Short-lived certificates limit the window of exposure if a certificate is compromised and reduce the need for active revocation.

"aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/DNS": "ecommerce.mycompany.com" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/URI": "spiffe://mycompany.com/workload/ecommerce" "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA"

Note: An empty Subject CN in a certificate isn’t supported by IAM Roles Anywhere.

Trust policy and effective permissions of credentials

IAM Roles Anywhere clients fetch temporary credentials for IAM Roles using the API method CreateSession. To successfully authorize this API call, the IAM role trust policy should trust the IAM Roles Anywhere service principal as shown in the following example.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession", "sts:SetSourceIdentity" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN": "MyCompany CA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/CN": "WorkloadA", "aws:PrincipalTag/x509SAN/Name/CN": "WorkloadA" }, "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": [ "arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID" ] } } } ] }

As a security best practice, consider using additional condition statements to evaluate the session PrincipalTag attributes extracted from the certificate to further restrict authorization of temporary credentials. If the workloads have ephemeral certificates with a dynamic subject CN, then the issuer or SAN principal tags can be used to define condition statements in the trust policy. The trust anchor shown in the preceding trust policy helps establish the trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and the CA in your PKI.

Plan for trust anchor placement

Depending on the CA platform, you can configure one or more intermediate certificates in your PKI certificate hierarchy, as shown in Figure 3. The certificate level the trust anchor is placed at affects which end-entity certificates IAM Roles Anywhere accepts, and therefore which workloads are authorized to assume a role. To create a trust anchor, export the certificate bundle for the issuing CA certificate from your external CA platform in PEM-encoded format and upload it to the trust anchor console.

Figure 3: Certificate hierarchy in an external PKI

See the Solution deployment section to onboard a sample solution and verify your certificate bundle.

Fine-grained access control is vital for security because it allows organizations to precisely define and restrict permissions, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. The effective permissions of the temporary security credentials are an intersection of resource-based, identity-based, and session policies as shown in Figure 4. By setting up the trust anchor and profile configuration in IAM Roles Anywhere with session policies, you can limit the permissions for each session.

Figure 4: Effective permissions of session credentials

Credential helper

To obtain temporary security credentials from IAM Roles Anywhere, use the credential helper tool. This tool is compatible with the credential_process feature available across the AWS SDKs. The credential helper manages the process of obtaining temporary security credentials using IAM Roles Anywhere and returns them in JSON format. The private key of the workload and its CA signed certificate are the two critical parameters provided to the credential helper tool. To use this tool, you need both an end-entity certificate and a trust anchor created in IAM Roles Anywhere. As of December 2024, the credential helper (version 1.4.0 and later) supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0.

The following is an example of how to obtain temporary security credentials:

$ ./aws_signing_helper credential-process \ --certificate /path/to/certificate \ --private-key /path/to/private-key \ --trust-anchor-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:trust-anchor/TA_ID \ --profile-arn arn:aws:rolesanywhere:region:account:profile/PROFILE_ID \ --role-arn arn:aws:iam::account:role/role-name-with-path

When credential-process is used with AWS SDKs, the temporary credentials are stored in memory and refreshed automatically. However, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) invokes credential-process on every command. Each invocation creates a new IAM Roles Anywhere session, which adds latency to every CLI call. To avoid this delay when using the AWS CLI, we recommend using the update command, which writes refreshed credentials to a file that the CLI reads on each invocation without calling credential-process again.

When you use update, credentials are written to a credential file on disk and any user or process who can read the credential file might be able to read and use those AWS credentials, so it’s recommended to use serve unless your business has a specific use case that needs to read AWS credentials from a file. The serve command can be used to vend temporary credentials through an endpoint running on the local host using the same URIs and request headers as Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (IMDSv2). When using serve, no AWS configuration files are needed because the AWS SDKs can discover the server endpoint.

Just-in-time compared to short-lived certificates as workload identities

To help mitigate the risk around the exposure of your business-critical resources to compromised certificate user sessions, it’s recommended to use certificates with just-in-time credentials or short-lived access credentials. Just-in-time certificates are issued by a CA for immediate use for authentication on a system or application. The CA uses the roles and policies defined in IAM to determine when, and under what conditions, a workload can establish a session. With just-in-time access, admins don’t have to worry about revoking access if the users’ access roles change. Because the access credentials are recreated for each access request, any role changes can be applied in real time. Just-in-time access requires support from your CA, so verify compatibility with your CA before implementing it.

It’s recommended to tailor the validity periods for short-lived certificates to align with business requirements, workload lifecycle, and your organization’s risk tolerance. AWS Private CA offers a short-lived CA mode specifically designed for certificates with validity periods under 7 days. This mode is priced at $50 per month (compared to $400 per month for general-purpose CA mode), making it cost-effective for high-volume, ephemeral workload identities such as containers and serverless functions. For more information, see AWS Private Certificate Authority and How to use AWS Private CA short-lived certificate mode. See Zero trust on AWS for information about how short-lived credentials support a zero trust architecture.

Best practices for private key storage

Safeguarding private keys is of paramount importance in any environment. A private key is created by the certificate owner when requesting certificates with a Certificate Signing Request (CSR). The CA providing your certificate doesn’t create or have your private key. In fact, it’s recommended that no one outside your administrators should ever be given access to this material. Guardrails should be implemented to make sure the keys aren’t stored in an online repository.

Using the credential helper with IAM Roles Anywhere, you can integrate with PKCS #11-compatible modules. For implementation details, see How to implement cryptographic modules to secure private keys used with IAM Roles Anywhere. With the credential helper (version 1.1.0 and later), IAM Roles Anywhere supports PKCS #11 integration, so you can use private keys stored in hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-based secure stores and avoid storing them to disk. Additionally, as of December 2024, the credential helper supports Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0, enabling private keys to be generated inside the TPM and marked as non-exportable. With TPM-backed keys, the private keys can’t be extracted even if the workload host is compromised. This is the strongest private key protection available for on-premises and hybrid workloads using IAM Roles Anywhere.

If your organization doesn’t implement PKCS #11–compatible modules, IAM Roles Anywhere supports credential helper version 1.0.5 for X.509 certificates and private keys stored in macOS and Windows certificate stores. This delegates the signing operations to keys stored within those OS-specific certificate stores. In Windows, both CryptoAPI and Cryptography API: Next Generation (CNG) are supported; in macOS, Keychain is supported. In these environments, the private key will never be directly readable, and the signing operation would be delegated to the secure store instead, which will improve security posture of your environment. If you have multiple certificates, then use the --cert-selector flag of the credential helper tool to search for a specific certificate (and associated private key) through the certificate subject, issuer, and serial number. The corresponding keys are x509Subject, x509Issuer, and x509Serial, respectively. These keys can be specified either through a JSON file format or through the command line. The following is an example of both approaches:

If you want to use a JSON file, it should be similar to this:

[ { "Key": "x509Subject", "Value": "CN=Subject" }, { "Key": "x509Issuer", "Value": "CN=Issuer" }, { "Key": "x509Serial", "Value": "15D19632234BF759A32802C0DA88F9E8AFC8702D" } ]

If the preceding example is placed in a file called selector.json, it can be specified with the --cert-selector flag through file://path/to/selector.json.

The same certificate selector argument can be specified through the command line as shown in the following:

--cert-selector Key=x509Subject, Value=CN=Subject Key=x509Issuer, Value=CN=Issuer Key=x509Serial, Value=15D19632

Monitoring trust anchor certificates

Monitoring certificate expiry in PKI is crucial for maintaining secure communication, because expired certificates can lead to authentication failures, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized access. Compliance and regulatory requirements often mandate timely renewal of certificates, making monitoring certificate expiry essential to avoid legal penalties and maintain organizational integrity.

Using IAM Roles Anywhere, you can receive notifications for CA certificate expiry and end-entity certificate expiry. IAM Roles Anywhere can send metrics, events, and notifications through multiple notification channels as shown in the following table:

The preceding notifications thresholds are default settings, which you can customize using the steps in Customize notification settings in IAM Roles Anywhere.

Best practices for trust anchor certificate rotation

Consider rotating your certificates using blue/green deployments to seamlessly roll out new certificates without affecting service availability. Use automation to integrate certificate rotation testing in your blue/green deployment pipeline. See the sample AWS CloudFormation template in the Solution deployment section to build your automation pipeline.

As shown in Figure 5, two trust anchors have been created; one for each environment. Using this approach, you can test the certificate rotation process in a controlled staging environment before applying it to the production environment, thus reducing the risk of certificate-related outages.

Figure 5: Trust anchor certificate rotation in blue/green deployment

The sample solution template is available in the IAM Roles Anywhere — External PKI Integration repository on GitHub. It contains the following main steps:

Creates a distinct IAM role with policies scoped to the resources that workload requires.

Assigns a trust relationship to a IAM Roles Anywhere principal.

Creates a trust anchor using a certificate bundle from an external CA.

Creates a profile with the required IAM Roles.

If you request a longer session than the role allows, the CreateSession API returns an error. The companion template keeps both values in sync by setting the role’s MaxSessionDuration to the same parameter value. If you configure the role separately, update its MaxSessionDuration to match your desired session length. For more information, see IAM Roles Anywhere CreateSession API.

If the workload’s subject CN (WorkloadSubjectCN) doesn’t match the x509Subject CN of the authenticating certificate, the CreateSession call is denied. The same conditional verification applies to WorkloadIssuerCN and WorkloadSANCN.

Additionally, the trust policy scopes role assumption to the specific trust anchor Amazon Resource Name (ARN), preventing other trust anchors in the same account from assuming that role.

Conclusion

In this post, we discussed how AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, empowered by X.509 certificates, introduces a dynamic and secure way to manage workload identities and issue temporary access credentials. By understanding the trust model, using certificate attributes, and implementing fine-grained authorization, organizations can gain granular control over the effective permissions of these credentials.

The choice between just-in-time and short-lived certificates as workload identities depends on your specific requirements.

Adhering to best practices for private key storage is essential to maintain the integrity of your security infrastructure. Regularly rotating trust anchor certificates helps ensure the long-term trustworthiness of your system.

As you embark on your journey to implement IAM Roles Anywhere and integrate it with your PKI, remember that a well-architected approach to certificate management is a cornerstone of robust and resilient cloud security.

Title: Signal bug could keep your mic - and camera - on after hangup
Context: The vulnerability, CVE-2026-113380, was published by MITRE on Tuesday and given a CVSS score of 9
Full Text: Make sure you don’t say anything mean or secret after hanging up a call on Signal, as a bug in the encrypted messaging app’s calling library could prevent a call from ending properly, potentially leaving audio and possibly video active. The vulnerability, CVE-2026-113380, was published by MITRE on Tuesday and given a CVSS score of 9.3, marking it as a critical issue in Signal’s open-source RingRTC library in every single version before 2.72.0. That update was pushed out last month, but the vulnerability wasn’t made public until now. RingRTC is Signal’s own calling library built on top of WebRTC, a technology introduced in 2011 that has since become widely used for voice and video communication over the internet. RingRTC provides Signal-specific calling functionality using WebRTC, which already encrypts media traffic, but that isn't stopping RingRTC from failing to hang up calls in certain conditions, according to the CVE report. What’s happening is, in essence, a denial-of-service attack on RingRTC’s finite state machine (FSM) event queue, which handles events involved in managing calls. If one of the people on the call saturates the FSM queue with requests, it can become overwhelmed and fail to process a hangup request, preventing the call from terminating properly. The vulnerability is classified as CWE-754, or improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions, according to a report posted to GitHub. A conceptual proof of concept is available in the GitHub report linked above, using a Python script to simulate how flooding an event queue can prevent a hangup request from being processed. Were a malicious actor to exploit this, the person on the other end may think the call has been terminated, but either or both of their video and audio channels could still be open. The attack complexity is considered low according to the CVE, and while CISA’s known exploited vulnerabilities catalog doesn’t indicate this has been spotted in the wild, Signal users ought to ensure they’ve updated their apps - mobile and desktop - to the latest versions to ensure they don’t end up being caught on a hot mic without any notice. Comparing RingRTC 2.72.0 to the previous version indicates that Signal's fix allows the call's finite state machine (FSM) to detect termination requests independently of the event queue, while adding a timeout to prevent stalled processing from indefinitely blocking a hangup. It's not entirely clear from Signal's release notes when the fixed version of RingRTC reached the Android, iOS, and desktop versions of its apps. Signal Desktop's release history indicates that RingRTC 2.72.0 was incorporated in September, but the precise rollout dates across all platforms remain unclear. We’ve reached out to Signal to learn more, but haven’t heard back. In the meantime, best to update your installation to be sure you’re not still vulnerable. That, and watch what you say after hanging up a call. ®
