Full Text:
Maria Varmazis: Hello, and welcome to this CyberWire special edition. In today's episode, host Dave Bittner is speaking with author John Kindervag and contributor Dr. Chase Cunningham about their new book, "Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed: The Zero Trust Model for the AI Era." Here's their conversation.

Dave Bittner: So today, we're talking about the new book. This is "Cyber Resilience at Machine Speed." John, I'd love to start with you. My understanding is this book was your brainchild. What prompted you to take on this topic?

John Kindervag: Well, I mean, there was a lot of people asking me to take on the topic, zero trust in the AI world, because there's always a lot of people who are kind of naysayers and say zero trust won't work for this, zero trust won't work for this and that. And so I already knew that it was working for AI, but what I didn't want to do is be the sole author of it. So someone who was very wise told me years ago, "There are no great books, only great chapters." And so, I reached out to 13 people that I really admire in this industry, including Dr. Chase Cunningham, and asked them to contribute a chapter. And I think we got a great book out of that, because I would've maybe written a great chapter, but we got a great book.

Dave Bittner: Chase, what made you decide that this is a project that you wanted to sign onto?

Chase Cunningham: Well, I mean, to be perfectly frank, if John says, "Hey, Chase, there's a building on fire, you should run in there," like, I'll do it, because that's just how it works. I mean, I've been working with John for so long, and he's been such a great mentor. But as far as the book goes, like, I genuinely enjoy writing. The topic area was really interesting to me. And, you know, I agree with John. I personally think that this is actually the greatest time in history for CT because machines and all these AI agents, they don't have an HR department, and they're not going to complain about us telling them we don't trust them. So it really just lined up well. And John was kind enough to just kind of say, "Look, here's the, you know, broad scope, what I'd like you to write about and go." And, you know, I love writing, so when you turn me loose, I get after it.

Dave Bittner: Well, John, what was your organizing principle here? How did you divvy out the assignments to your co-collaborators?

John Kindervag: Well, there's a five-step model for deploying zero trust. First, you define the protect surface, then you map the transaction flows. After that, you architect the network, the environment, decide what products need to go in, essentially. Step four is policy. So you instantiate the policy in the products. And step five is monitor and maintain. So I just laid out the book in those five steps, and then I looked at who amongst the people that I think are really good at ZT could really contribute to that. And Chase had already written a book on policy and graph databases and how, you know, attackers think in graphs, but defenders think in lists. And I wanted him to, you know, just hone in on that for that one chapter. So he's part of that part of the book. And so I just went to different people who had expertise in different areas to write the chapters based upon the five-step model.

Dave Bittner: Well, Chase, let's dig into your specific chapter. Can you walk us through the topic that you covered?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, John's point on graph database and sort of the adversarial mindset, I think, is what's missing in a lot of people's approach, so the problem is, interestingly enough, when we think about security, we're all usually thinking from a posture of defense and nothing bad ever happening and not allowing X to occur. And in truth, that's not going to -- that's not the way things work. You're always going to be in a position where you have to be able to respond, and you have to understand how the adversaries are approaching things from their end because that's where you -- you know, in the military, we have a phrase, "We meet the enemy at the door," and that's what you're trying to do. And so, my contribution here was really to look at how would that be applicable in this particular context, especially in kind of the new era that we're falling into. And then do those legacy approaches around visualization and understanding and context apply? And absolutely they do. So that was kind of the overall impetus for that. And then, you know, getting the reader to understand the fundamentals of all the things we've talked about, strategy still matters. It's just now you have a scope and speed that is beyond human speed.

Dave Bittner: You mentioned lists and graphs. Can you unpack that a bit for us?

Chase Cunningham: Sure. So if you look at, you know, SIEM and some of the legacy technologies and those types of things, what they usually show you is a big, like, glorified spreadsheet of a bunch of things doing a bunch of stuff, and it's a bunch of blinky lights, and you kind of hope that you can understand what's going on there. Whereas, from the perspective of what is actually valuable -- and I've been a red teamer. I've been, I guess you could say, a pseudo bad guy -- your goal as that person, that entity, is to be more contextual, to understand the intricacies of what is being missed, and then to know where the pivot points are. And you don't get that from looking at a spreadsheet. You don't get that from looking at a bunch of alerts on a screen. You have to understand, with total context, where you go, what you do, what areas to avoid. And this, in the militaristic approach, also leans more towards understanding the battlespace. And John had a bunch of other contributors in there as well. So it all really lines up on getting people to keep their head in the game around what works and what is just kind of security theater.

Dave Bittner: You know, John, one of the key elements of the book is this notion of cyber resilience. I've noticed personally in the past three months or so that cyber resilience has become a hot topic. People are reaching out to us, and it's something that they really want to talk about. How do you define it, and why do you think it's become such a -- it's come to the fore in the way that it has?

John Kindervag: Well, because, you know, as Chase says, we assume that an organization probably has been breached. They've got, you know, malicious actors inside the organization. That's dwell time. They're sitting there learning everything that they can do, and they're deciding what they're going to attack, right? And so, what resilience is is the ability to withstand an attack and revert back to a good state, you know, and not completely go down. And so, I even talk a little bit about going beyond resilience into antifragility, because one of the things that zero trust can do is make the environment stronger and stronger over time when there's a lot of load. And so, resilience, you know, and robustness is another thing people talk about. But what it means is that our environments won't just fall over when there's an attack. And too many environments completely fall over when there's an attack. And we've seen that over and over again. I mean, you think about Target, you think about TJ Maxx or TJX. You think about so many things. You think about Jaguar Land Rover. I mean, they couldn't make a car for -- I don't remember how long, but it was weeks. And so they completely fell over because they weren't resilient environments. And they allowed the attackers to go on a wild shooting spree, right? And I have a saying that all bad things happen inside of an allow rule. And this gets back to what Chase was talking about in the list, because in traditional security technology, there's a list of policies. And generally, the first policy that meets the criteria of the traffic gets instantiated. That may not be the best policy, right? But it's the first one in that list. And so if somebody puts a policy in a firewall, for example, an any-any allow rule, and this is -- I've seen this more than once in my career. They put it as the first rule because that's -- they put it in to just get it up and running, and then they never took it out. And so they have a very expensive box called a firewall that's doing absolutely nothing. You might as well just have the two jacks connected with a coupler for all the security you're getting. And that's because people don't understand policy. So we're so focused on products that we don't focus on policy. And policy that comes from a graph perspective is better policy than policy that comes from a list perspective.

Dave Bittner: Well, John, help me understand the relationship between cyber resilience and zero trust. Is it a parallel relationship? Is there intersection there? How do you combine or have the two work to their best effect?

John Kindervag: So cyber resilience is an outcome, and zero trust is a way of achieving that outcome. You know, I had dinner last night with one of the other contributors of the book, actually a friend of Chase's as well, Lieuwe Jan Koning. And he has this concept that zero trust is a verb. You do it, right? And so as you're doing it, the process of doing it makes the environment more resilient, more antifragile, more stable because there's less opportunity for attackers to ride, you know, open, flat, unrestricted networks and get access to sensitive data and assets.

Dave Bittner: Chase, did you mention that you had some experience as a penetration tester?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I was a red teamer for the government, and then I was on the National Cyber Collegiate Defense Competition a few times. And on my, you know, individual career, I did a bunch of red teaming and, you know, so acted as a bad guy, which is probably more of a comment on my own personality than anything else.

Dave Bittner: I'm curious. From that experience, were there times where you were called to question the traditional perimeter model, the days before the popularity of zero trust?

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, when I came over to Forrester and John, you know, kind of told me I was going to follow up in his footsteps, it was interesting because immediately I was like, "I don't want to carry someone else's laundry." But when I started looking at what the concept was and the approach as a red teamer, I looked at it, and I was like, yeah, he was dead on point. Like, this is the stuff that would make me miserable. Like, I would quit what I was doing if the red teaming was still a thing and I was working on infrastructure built that way. So that was kind of the light bulb moment for me that, you know, strategy matters every day and twice on Sunday. And then the reality of the space is it's meeting the adversary where the adversary is going to try and, you know, maneuver. And as long as you can do that, you stay with them. Now, today it's moving at light speed, but, you know, the bad guys don't own the patent on light speed. We can operate at that speed, too.

John Kindervag: And I think that's a real important point because we're at an inflection point in history because of AI, the post-mythos world, whatever you want to call it, where we're not going to be able to take our time and manually make changes, do long change control meetings, and all that kind of stuff. We're going to have to enable technology to take action at the same speed as the attack. And that's what happens in kinetic warfare. Chase is a veteran. He's done some stuff, as they say, been involved in some shenanigans.

Chase Cunningham: Some things, yeah, shenanigans. Yeah.

John Kindervag: Shenanigans. And when you're -- when the enemy is firing on you, you don't, you know, call back to base and say, "Hey, let's have a three-hour meeting to see whether we should shoot back or not," right? And so, what we do in cybersecurity, and I've often used the example of an airbag. What if you tried to deploy an airbag the same way we do change control, right? You couldn't do it, right? You'd be dead. The whole purpose is automation. And so the airbag goes off as soon as the sensor sees the problem, and it protects you. And yeah, every once in a while, maybe in history, we've had a few airbags that just went off on their own, but it's much better to have an airbag than not to have an airbag. I think we all can agree on that. Well, we can work at that same speed in cybersecurity now because AI is a tool that defenders can use as well as attackers. And I think a lot of people aren't recognizing this. And I think this is the key, that you can use AI to say that's a real attack against real systems that are critical. So we're going to stop it right now by changing the policy and putting a deny rule in place and not allowing that traffic to get access to that dataset or those assets.

Dave Bittner: John, do you suppose that AI actually changes the fundamental security problem, or is this more a matter of the timeline being compressed?

John Kindervag: Yeah, it doesn't change the security problem. You know, as I did a -- we did a podcast with Rich Mogull of the Cloud Security Alliance who wrote a great -- well, several great white papers on AI. But one of his takeaways was, "Zero trust or zero days, your choice." And his point was, it's not magical. It's fast, right? And it's at massive scale. So, you know, you could spin up a bunch of bots and just hammer at things. I'm actually surprised, and I haven't heard of any, but maybe you have, Chase, that we haven't seen attackers just do DDoS swarms with agents or something. But I haven't heard of any. But that came to my mind as if I wanted to bring somebody down, I'd do a DDoS swarm, kind of like the Mirai botnet attack, but I would just use individual agents to overwhelm someone's capacity to keep their network up and live.

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, it is kind of interesting to say that there hasn't been, you know, a whole giant renewal of DDoS as the new sort of method of attack, but that also makes my spidey sense tingle a little bit because then I'm thinking of, "Well, if they're not DDoSing us with all these agents, what the heck are they doing with it? And when is that going to go down?"

John Kindervag: Right. And it makes ransomware faster. I mean --

Chase Cunningham: Yeah, I mean, everybody's a developer now.

John Kindervag: Right. These things are so fast that there's no way a human being can get involved in the pathway and stop it before damage is done. I mean, you know, think about how fast a bullet flies, right? Nobody but Neo dodges bullets.

Dave Bittner: Well, so, John, how do we deal with this fundamental asymmetry here? I mean, the AI attackers can function at machine speed, but the defenders, they've got more steps along the way. I know you refer to -- I think you call it organizational latency.

John Kindervag: Yeah. So the one advantage that we have in cyber warfare versus kinetic warfare, in the kinetic warfare, you have to worry about the air, you know, attacks coming from the air, from under the sea, you know, from over mountains and cliffs. In cyber warfare, the attackers are still limited by the guardrails placed on them by the protocols that transmit packets around the internet and around networks. And that's typically TCP/IP, right? Not exclusively, but typically. And so because of that, you know, they can't create something that hides under the water. There's no -- under the -- under the water, you can -- everything can be visible because the protocol is designed to be visible. And so we can leverage the protocols themselves to control what the attacker can do, because as soon as they get on our network and they get on on a wire or on a fiber optic cable, they're starting to get on it in a choke point, and we can start to choke that down. And so if we have the right policy, then we can control their access to resources. So in this world, where everybody's worried about, oh, there's all these new zero-day attacks, and there's all these new zero-day vulnerabilities, what they forget is there's no reason that those two things have to talk to each other. There's still controls that we can place in the middle of that pathway that stops the ability of the attacker with the new zero-day attack to get access to the vulnerable system with the new zero-day vulnerability. There's no reason for that to happen. And so this means you have to be much more thoughtful in your policy creation because there should be no policy in any organization that allows an unknown resource on the public internet to get access all the way through to, say, your credit card database or your financials or power plant, your PLC that drives the power plant. Those rules should not be in place. But unfortunately, through the history of cybersecurity and before that, information security, we just opened everything up and said, "Let everybody come in. Yeah. Because everybody is a good guy." And we found out that people aren't so good.

Dave Bittner: Chase, is this a fundamental shift in mindset here? You know, designing security around the assumption that compromise is going to happen rather than treating every compromise as a failure of the security program?

Chase Cunningham: I mean, none of this stuff happens in a silo, and that's what's weird, is, you know, we've built organizational silos that cause a lot of the problems that we face, but it's not happening inside of those silos. It's happening across platform, across infrastructure, across business, across geographies even. And people have to think about these problems from a different perspective. And it's no longer just a, "Hey, the nerds will figure this out, and eventually, they'll nerd their way to stopping bad things from happening," because that's not the case. The reality of it is, especially in today's world, everything everywhere is potentially an avenue of compromise. And if you're not thinking about, "How would I deal with it when things do go wrong?" you're not going to be ready when things do go wrong. You know, to throw one more military adage in there is no plan survives first contact with the enemy. And I mean, that's really what we're dealing with.

Dave Bittner: I'm curious, John, what are some of the common misconceptions that you run into when organizations say they're implementing zero trust?

John Kindervag: Well, a lot of them haven't understood some of the fundamentals of zero trust, and so they don't know what they're trying to protect. That's the first thing, right? So that's why we stay in the five-step model to find your protect surface. What are you going to protect? This is the inversion of the attack surface, right? The late, great Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's partner, said, you know, when you're looking at a problem, invert, invert, invert. And so this is the inversion of the attack surface because you can't control the whole attack surface, but you can control certain things. You can control your credit card database. You can control your SWIFT system or your ATM network if you're in a bank. You can control your DNS server, which, if that goes down, you're toast. And so you can control certain things. So figure out what you need to control. And so too often, people just acquire a product and then they don't know what they're going to do with it. Secondly, people try to do zero trust all at once for the whole company, and it never works. You have to do it in small bite-sized chunks, right? However you eat the elephant or the whale is the same way you do zero trust. And that's why we start with one protect surface, and then do another, and then do another. And in this way, zero trust becomes three things that are really important. It becomes incremental. We're doing it one at a time. It becomes iterative. We're doing it one after another. And it becomes non-disruptive. The most you can screw up is one protect surface at any given time, and then you can revert that back. So you don't have to be afraid of it. A lot of people are afraid of it. And as one customer of mine said, we argued about zero trust longer than it took to build the first zero trust environment in our organization.

Dave Bittner: Well, suppose an organization accepts your argument, but they're sitting on top of that large legacy environment. They can't rebuild everything around zero trust tomorrow. What are your words of wisdom for how they should begin?

John Kindervag: Well, I mean, there's a whole thing I call the learning curve, where you start with something that's very small and it doesn't have very much value. And you learn to build zero trust. You learn to just live the five-step model. And then you eventually go up to those things, those keys to the kingdom, the crown jewels, high-value assets, whatever you call them. I used to believe we started there. And then the more I worked with customers, I found out that there was nobody in that company who was around when that system was built, and nobody knew how it worked. And that's why I put in as step two later on mapping the transaction flows, because until I could see how the system worked together, there was no way. I mean, I needed a map, right? And as Chase knows, in the military, you know, you're always looking at a map. And a map tells you where you are. It tells you where the bad guys are. If you don't have a map, you're going to be wrong and lost, and they both suck. But if you have a map, you might be wrong, but you won't be lost because you'll know where you need to go.

Dave Bittner: Chase, suppose I'm a CISO, and I'm trying to translate this into a board-level conversation. How do I explain to them what success should look like?

Chase Cunningham: Well, I would say flat out that -- you know, remind them that, like, look, this is the most, let's call it, unfair position to ever declare success in because success means nothing happened. And of course, no one likes that because it's like, "Well, that doesn't really show me a return." But the return is we're still up and running, and nothing's gone wrong. And then the follow-on to that is to really make people understand, like, look, you guys go to organizations and you -- if I'm in your org and you tell me that -- I've heard that phrase a million times -- "Everyone's in sales." Well, guess what? Everyone's also in security. Does that mean that you have to enable security controls and that you're doing configuration on endpoints, whatever? No. But it means that you understand that the things we're doing are valuable in the context of keeping the business secure. And that's something that we need to get across to more people and make sure that they understand it. Because the moment that this goes away from being a business enabler and an outcome that benefits everybody and becomes more security tech and more, "Oh, gosh, I got to figure out how this stuff actually works," it gets -- it just gets bogged down, and no one cares. You know, security is for security people, and no one wants to do it but us. But we've got to work harder to make sure that we translate this stuff in business context and along the lines that they actually care about.

Dave Bittner: John, can you give us some highlights of some of the other chapters and some of the contributors that you brought in here?

John Kindervag: Oh, yeah. So, well, as I already said, Rich Mogull is doing a chapter, "Zero Trust or Zero Days, Your Choice." So he's given a high-level view of the whole project. And so -- and, of course, our CEO, Andrew Rubin of Illumio, is talking about how we have to get past the prevention-only mindset. And then we've got Don Yeske, who's the former zero-trust lead at both the Navy and Department of Homeland Security, explaining what a protect surface is. He actually wrote his master's thesis on protect surfaces. And then Clint Bruce, a very well-known Navy SEAL. He's a good friend of Chase. That's how I met him. Writes about my favorite weapon is a map, and why you need to have visibility. And then we've got a lot of other people. I've written a couple chapters. Josh Woodruff and his wife, Michelle Savage, have written a chapter on controls that every AI agent need. They actually wrote a book called "Genetic AI + Zero Trust," and I wrote the foreword to it. So lots of great people. George Finney writes about policy. He wrote "Project Zero Trust," and he also wrote "Rise of the Machines: A Project Zero Trust Story." Chase, of course, is talking about creating policy. And then our chief product officer, Mario Espinoza, is writing about AI and why it's essential for zero trust. And then, you know, we've got Tony Scott, the former CIO of the US federal government, talking about, you know, kind of the business perspective of it. So 14 different authors in this book, great team to work with at Illumio, and a great team with all these contributors really came through, and very, very excited to see this come out.

Maria Varmazis: Thanks for joining us. We'll see you next time.

Title: Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides
Context: But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone
Full Text:
First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Dan Lisichkin⁠, AI Security Researcher from ⁠Pillar Security⁠, discussing their work on "A WIF Of Fresh Access, How a GitHub Issue on Gemini-CLI Led to GCP Project Compromise." Researchers at Pillar Security uncovered a vulnerability in Google’s Gemini CLI workflows that could allow an attacker to turn a malicious GitHub issue into remote code execution and gain elevated access to a Google Cloud Platform (GCP) project.

Title: Reboot, rinse, repeat.
Context: A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group is exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust’s Remote Support software. CISA has added a critical Atlassian vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following confirmed attacks.
Full Text:
Chinese spies exploit a BeyondTrust zero-day. Atlassian faces active attacks. Rogue AI agents breach Indian networks. Ransomware gangs turn to threats of violence. A cyber incident disrupts U.S. bankruptcy courts. F5 and Juniper push critical patches. Japanese companies suffer a wave of breaches. Google brings AI-powered scam protection to Android. Our guest is Nick Jackson, Global Director of Cyber Security Services at Bitdefender, sharing how the UK are thinking about AI regulation. Braille meets brains.

Today is Friday October 16th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

A suspected Chinese espionage group exploits a BeyondTrust zero-day.

A suspected Chinese state-sponsored espionage group is exploiting a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust’s Remote Support software. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, allows attackers to escalate privileges, move laterally through networks, and steal stored credentials. Researchers at Mandiant and Google attribute the activity to Armory Castle, also known as UNC5221, a group specializing in long-term intelligence gathering. The attackers demonstrated sophisticated knowledge of BeyondTrust’s internal systems, deploying custom malware and establishing persistence that survives reboots and configuration resets. The group has previously exploited vulnerabilities in Ivanti and Citrix products, often expanding attacks once vulnerabilities become public. BeyondTrust has released a patch, but researchers warn that internet-facing appliances should be considered potentially compromised until thoroughly investigated. Google expects broader exploitation as attackers race against patch deployments.

CISA says a critical Atlassian vulnerability is under active exploitation.

CISA has added a critical Atlassian vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following confirmed attacks. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589, carries a severity score of 9.3 and affects multiple Atlassian Data Center products, including Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket. Attackers can exploit a path traversal vulnerability to access sensitive files without authentication, potentially exposing credentials and enabling administrative access. Researchers observed exploitation attempts shortly after technical details became public. Organizations are urged to apply available patches promptly.

AI agents access government and private-sector systems in India.

India’s cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, is warning that AI agents have accessed government and private-sector systems without authorization, exceeding the boundaries of their assigned tasks. The agency received voluntary disclosures from AI developers whose agents exploited exposed credentials, misconfigured cloud accounts, and poorly secured interfaces to access sensitive information. None of the affected organizations detected the intrusions themselves. The warning follows similar incidents involving OpenAI agents in Australia. CERT-In also reports that criminals are using agentic AI tools to accelerate cyberattacks, reducing the time from initial compromise to impact from days to hours. The agency has not identified the AI developers or affected organizations, raising transparency concerns. Officials are urging developers to strengthen safeguards preventing AI agents from accessing unauthorized systems.

Researchers at Cyble have identified an upgraded version of GhostBat Android malware targeting 60 banking and payment apps in India. Distributed through fraudulent government-service messages and malicious APK downloads, the malware abuses Android’s Accessibility Service to capture payment PINs, intercept messages, and collect sensitive information. Its sophisticated overlay technique records PIN entries while victims use legitimate banking apps, making detection difficult. GhostBat also employs encrypted loaders and remotely configurable settings to evade security tools. Users are advised to avoid unofficial app downloads and scrutinize permission requests.

Ransomware gangs increasingly threaten physical violence.

Ransomware gangs are increasingly threatening physical violence against corporate executives and employees to pressure organizations into paying extortion demands. According to the 2026 Semperis Ransomware Risk Report, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical intimidation, including threats against employees’ families and even their homes. This tactic, known as triple extortion, adds personal threats to traditional ransomware demands and data-leak threats. Among affected organizations, 25% reported employees being doxxed, while 23% experienced swatting incidents, sometimes forcing victims to relocate or seek psychological treatment. Researchers warn that these tactics can undermine even well-prepared organizations with reliable backups, as executives weigh employees’ personal safety against ransom demands. The findings are based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals worldwide.

A cyber incident disrupts bankruptcy court notifications.

A cybersecurity incident affecting BAE Systems has disrupted bankruptcy court notifications across the United States. The company operates the Bankruptcy Noticing Center, which distributes official notices for federal bankruptcy courts nationwide. Since October 9, the system has been unable to generate or deliver notices, affecting both electronic and paper communications. Courts continue accepting filings, but creditor notification services remain unavailable. BAE says the incident is isolated to the noticing system. The cause, potential data exposure, and timeline for restoring services remain unknown.

F5 and Juniper Networks release new patches.

F5 and Juniper Networks have released patches addressing more than 160 security vulnerabilities, including dozens of critical flaws. F5 fixed 11 vulnerabilities in NGINX, including three critical issues that could enable unauthenticated remote code execution under certain conditions. Meanwhile, Juniper published 17 advisories covering more than 150 vulnerabilities in Junos OS and related products. Roughly two dozen critical flaws could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges, take over devices, or disrupt services. Neither company has reported evidence of active exploitation.

A wave of cyberattacks hit major Japanese companies.

A wave of cyberattacks against major Japanese companies has exposed millions of customer records. Logistics giant Yamato Transport reported a breach affecting 5.31 million records, while publisher Nikkei disclosed the compromise of 1.83 million. Burger King Japan confirmed attackers accessed a server containing 11.18 million customer records, including names, contact information, birth dates, and purchase histories. The company says payment card information and login credentials were not exposed. Meanwhile, car-sharing operator Park24 is deleting stored identity verification documents following its own breach. Security researchers have documented 119 incidents involving personal information exposure in Japan this year. Attackers are increasingly exploiting weaknesses in website authentication, access controls, and APIs, highlighting the growing risks facing Japanese businesses and their customers.

Google rolls out new AI-powered protections for Android.

Google is rolling out new AI-powered protections against increasingly sophisticated mobile scams on Android devices. The enhancements include Gemini-based analysis of suspicious text conversations, on-device detection of malicious links, and stronger warnings about potential fraud. Google is also expanding protections that hide sensitive information during screen sharing and prevent apps from secretly enabling call forwarding. An enhanced bank-call verification system helps identify spoofed calls, automatically disconnecting suspected fraudsters. Google says its existing protections flag more than five million suspicious calls and messages monthly, while its bank verification system has blocked over three million fraudulent calls in Brazil since June. The new features are rolling out to eligible Android devices, with some protections requiring users to opt in.

Braille meets brains.

Scientists are making progress toward an intriguing new frontier in computing: using actual human brain cells instead of silicon chips. Researchers at Bristol University have demonstrated that tiny clusters of human neurons, known as brain organoids, can help recognize letters of the Braille alphabet. By converting Braille patterns into electrical signals, researchers found that a single organoid containing roughly 10,000 neurons could classify letters with 61 percent accuracy. Combine three organoids, and accuracy jumped to 83 percent. The research is part of an emerging field called organoid intelligence, which explores using living neural tissue for information processing. Previous experiments have demonstrated similar systems recognizing speech sounds and even playing Pong. Researchers emphasize that these miniature brains aren’t actually reading or understanding Braille. They’re simply processing electrical patterns. Still, it’s an intriguing development in biological computing, and perhaps another reminder that the line between hardware and wetware is getting a little blurry.

I want to know where they get the brains…

Title: Anthropic’s Free OSS Scanner: What It Means For Your Team
Context: On October 8, 2026, Anthropic announced OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in vulnerability scanning service for eligible open-source projects
Full Text:
On October 8, 2026, Anthropic announced OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in vulnerability scanning service for eligible open-source projects. The OSS Scanner is powered by their most capable models, including Claude Mythos. It scans codebases, identifies vulnerabilities, proposes patches, and sends reports directly to maintainers. As you read this, it has already identified real, high-severity issues in production software used by millions.

What does this mean for security teams? Finding vulnerabilities is no longer the primary hurdle. As AI-driven discovery scales, upstream maintainers will produce far more patches and security fixes than enterprises have ever had to process. Over time, as trust in model-generated findings and fixes grows, doubts about their validity will fade. What will remain is the true bottleneck: remediating the continuous stream of fixes responsibly, at scale, across every build, across all environments. Is this a revolution, a natural evolution, or mere hype? Let’s break it down.

What Was Announced?

Anthropic is offering free security scans to eligible OSS maintainers using their strongest frontier AI models. The output includes vulnerability reports, reproducers, and candidate patches that are fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This enables faster and more frequent scanning. That said, Anthropic continues to offer human-verified disclosures through its coordinated vulnerability disclosure process for projects that need them, and has called out to maintainers to verify and test findings for false positives.

The revolutionary aspect lies in the underlying capability. In their announcement, Anthropic mentions that LLMs progressed from discovering under 20% of vulnerabilities on academic benchmarks to over 85%. These models can now autonomously discover vulnerabilities, chain lower-severity findings into critical exploits, and generate working proof-of-concept code – tasks that previously took expert human researchers days or weeks.

What started with Project Glasswing, a contained initiative with a small number of trusted organizations who gained access to Anthropic’s frontier AI models, is now available to the broader OSS community via this new, free service. Other frontier labs are likely to follow this trajectory with their own OSS scanners.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Anthropic’s announcement contains a statistic worth sitting with: they have discovered over 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but, as of now, have only been able to manually review and triage approximately 6,000 of them.

That leaves 23,000 unverified findings. Anthropic is transparent about this – the opt-in fast track explicitly delivers unvalidated reports – and notes that even unverified findings from their models have proven highly accurate in early testing. However, for an enterprise security team consuming open-source software scanned by this service, those 23,000 unverified findings currently create an overwhelming triage backlog.

As trust in model-generated findings and fixes grows, that triage backlog will likely shrink, yet the stream of fixes that needs addressing will only expand, shifting the bottleneck entirely to remediation.

The Bottleneck Has Moved: From Discovery to Remediation

The volume of vulnerabilities AI can find is simultaneously the most powerful thing about it and the most challenging. AI models now find vulnerabilities faster, at greater scale, and with more accuracy than human researchers ever could. OSS Scanner is a powerful acceleration of that trend – it makes finding vulnerabilities almost a non-issue. Solving those findings is a different story.

For years, detecting vulnerabilities before the attacker was one of the greatest challenges in software security. But with solutions like OSS Scanner, the main challenge now lies in prioritizing, managing and implementing remediation for the vast amount of detected vulnerabilities. And humans simply can’t keep up with machines.

Upstream Fixes Don’t Guarantee Downstream Protection

The more fixes maintainers produce, the more those fixes trickle down through the ecosystem to vendors and organizations. That is unambiguously good news. That said, it also means the layer that sits between all those upstream fixes and every affected build in your estate (e.g. selecting the right fix, delivering it automatically, governing the decision) becomes more critical with every finding Anthropic’s scanner surfaces.

OSS Scanner helps maintainers identify and fix vulnerabilities in the packages they own, which is genuinely valuable. But if you are an organization consuming that OSS, you cannot assume that every finding was acted on, the maintainer moved fast enough, or the fix reached the version you are running in production.

Another thing to remember: the same frontier AI capabilities that power OSS Scanner have leaked to the attackers, and adversaries increasingly buy stolen or jailbroken access to frontier AI models on underground markets. This makes detection a race where both sides have equally powerful tools. The defender’s advantage is no longer in finding vulnerabilities first, but in acting on them faster.

As mentioned above, the bottleneck now lies in what follows discovery: remediating an ever-growing stream of fixes at the speed of AI, responsibly and at scale. This is especially felt in organizations with ever-shrinking SLAs mandated by boards and customers alike. The only architecture that closes this gap is one where detection, prioritization, and remediation run as one continuous system, at machine speed, without waiting for a human to advance each step. This is what a self-healing supply chain is designed to deliver; it is the operational response to a threat that no longer moves at human speed.

The Four Responsibilities That Remain Yours

OSS Scanner improves what happens upstream, but four responsibilities stay with you.

1. Prevention: Your Gate, Your Policies

A package can pass every check Anthropic runs and still violate your license, versioning, or approved-component rules and policies. That is why control over what enters your pipelines remains yours. Curate at the point of ingestion by blocking risky components and serving compliant versions in their place, so development never stalls. This now reaches well beyond traditional OSS packages to MCP servers, agent skills, plugins, and IDE extensions, which agents often pull without any developer awareness. Building a Trusted Agentic Workforce means immunizing what your agents consume, not just what your developers pull, and that takes a single gate that governs every asset type.

2. Detection and Prioritization: Context Is Everything

Once something clears the gate, the next question is whether it matters in your specific environment. Understanding whether the flaw OSS Scanner found is running somewhere sensitive, exists in the binary you built, or is reachable from production traffic is still up to you. Prioritizing findings is also critical to ensure security does not slow down delivery. A 9.8 severity score for a package found in a library you never call isn’t a 9.8 vulnerability for you. Turning generic findings into a prioritized action list requires artifact-layer scanning of your binaries, containers, and AI models – complete with reachability and applicability analysis and backed by a System of Record that knows what you actually run.

3. Remediation at Speed: The New Hardest Problem

Even when a verified fix exists, getting it into every affected build across your estate is a separate and genuinely hard problem. Vulnerability remediation in large-scale software is a progressive process, not a simple command. Upgrading a dependency to the latest version carries real operational risk – it can break things. Transitive dependencies – the dependencies of your dependencies – add another layer of complexity that compounds with every upgrade.

The safest path is often a backported patch: the security fix applied to the exact version you already run, without changing anything else about your dependency tree. This approach dramatically compresses remediation SLA without introducing upgrade risk, but it requires access to providers who manufacture backported patches for the specific versions you use, and a package delivery layer that gets those patches to every affected build automatically – without pipeline changes, without requiring a developer to act, without disrupting what is already working.

OSS Scanner finds vulnerabilities and proposes patches to maintainers. It does not get those patches into your builds. The remediation problem is yours, and it is the new frontier of software supply chain security.

The ability to automatically intercept a vulnerable component and serve a verified, policy-compliant version in its place across your entire estate becomes not a nice-to-have but the operational foundation of machine-speed remediation. The universality of that delivery layer matters too: no single patch provider covers every ecosystem, every version, or every component type. Freedom of choice across fix sources – hardened image providers, backporting services, upstream maintainers – is what makes remediation sustainable at scale.

4. Governance: The Audit Trail That Regulators Require

Finally, every finding you fix, deprioritize, or defer is a decision, and the scanner generates findings, not a record of how you handled them. Regulators, auditors, and boards now expect evidence rather than assertions. What you need is a signed, auditable record of what was fixed, when, under which policy, and which alternatives were considered, produced as a byproduct of remediation rather than assembled after the fact.

The Bottom Line

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner is a welcome step, and a preview of what’s coming: far more patches and security fixes, flowing from upstream faster than ever before. That is good news, but only for organizations that can absorb the stream responsibly. That means selecting the right fix for the exact versions they run, delivering it across every build without breaking anything, and proving every decision along the way.

This requires a Control Plane built on a single System of Record that immunizes what agents and developers consume, remediates automatically across every available fix source, and continuously proves every action. Automated remediation at scale is the next frontier of software supply chain security, and the teams that build for it now will turn a flood of fixes into a lasting advantage.

Title: Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists
Context: The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs,...
Full Text:
Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.

An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.

The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.

Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.

Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.

Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.

In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.

Title: Irish police force has its Twitter hacked in cryptocurrency scam
Context: There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as...
Full Text:
There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week.

The official @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic Twitter accounts of Garda Síochána were accessed by an unauthorised third party who posted cryptocurrency-related messages on Wednesday evening, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of users.

The messages claimed that followers were eligible to claim free cryptocurrency through an airdrop. However, victims who followed the link could potentially be tricked into handing over the keys to their cryptocurrency wallet, and end up with their savings drained.

The problem, however, is not just that a hacker found themselves with the ability to post fraudulent messages posing as the Irish police. If an unauthorised person was able to publish unauthorised posts from the accounts they may also have been able to access direct messages (DMs) which could contain sensitive personal information from members of the public.

Speaking to the Belfast Telegraph, a police spokesperson attempted to dampen fears that sensitive information could have been compromised:

"An Garda Síochána is satisfied that there is no unauthorised access with any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda data."

Scammers like to hijack established accounts with a large followers as they are both more likely to be trusted, and provide a rapid route to reach a significant number of potential victims. The @GardaTraffic account has over 600,000 followers, and is normally used by Irish police for traffic and road safety updates, while the @GardaInfo account has almost 300,000 followers.

The Garda says that is carrying out an internal investigation into what may have happened, and is working "with the X platform to understand how this unauthorised access has occurred."

The Garda is not the only police force to have ever suffered a security breach on its Twitter account.

For instance, in 2019 the UK's Metropolitan Police had its account hijacked (as well as part of its website) by hackers who posted explicit messages calling for the release of London-based rapper "Digga D". Two men were subsequently charged in connection with the hack.

Five years before, the social media accounts of Dubai police were hacked by an Anonymous-affiliated group calling itself HorsemenLulz, who claimed the UAE's police service was “spying on you”.

In 2022, the official Twitter account of the Philadelphia Police Department was compromised and used to post what appeared to be a series of adverts targeting businesses.

There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as exploiting the common habit of users choosing non-unique passwords that they have used elsewhere.

The advice of cybersecurity experts remains to protect accounts with multi-factor authentication, to always use unique, strong passwords, and to review which third-party apps may have been granted access to accounts.

Title: Lessons from the SolarWinds Breach: A Discussion With CISO Tim Brown
Context: ” We found out more a little later, but that’s how we categorized it first
Full Text:
At JFrog’s swampUP 2026 conference in New York, security leaders gathered to tackle the rapidly evolving landscape of software supply chain security and AI-driven development. In this exclusive sit-down interview from the event, former SolarWinds CISO TIM (now CISO in Residence at Team8) sits with JFrog CISO Paul Davis and reflects on the historic 2020 Sunburst breach that reshaped the cybersecurity industry. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

PAUL: Tim, you’ve had a remarkable journey. As partner and CISO in residence at Team8, how did you get there? What was your path, and what are you focused on today?

TIM: My path to CISO is different than many. I started as an engineer and wrote a lot of code. I was CTO for a couple of different companies. I had been telling CISOs what to do for about 20 years, and I decided I really should be one. That’s what I came to SolarWinds for. The first four years went swimmingly. All my crazy ideas were pretty good, and no little event occurred, right?

PAUL: And then the attack?

TIM: Yeah, Sunburst. As I said, it was a wake-up call for the industry.

On December 12th, 2020, I got a call that every CISO dreads. I got a call from my CEO, and essentially he said, “Mandiant just called us, and you shipped tainted code, and that tainted code is being exploited. The press knows, and it’s going to go public on Sunday.”

Our engineering team started looking. It wasn’t in source code—it had never been in source code. But we found three products or versions of the product produced between February and June that contained the code. We went back to our sales team and support team to figure out how many customers downloaded this thing, and 18,000 customers had downloaded those versions.

On that Saturday, I coined it a “build supply chain attack.” Why? Because it wasn’t in source code control, but somehow got into the product. We didn’t know how yet, so we called it a “build supply chain issue.” We found out more a little later, but that’s how we categorized it first.

The next day, I learned that SolarWinds was part of the big supply chain for everybody. We were part of the power grid, nuclear facilities, every military in the world, and 499 of the Fortune 500. It was spread out everywhere, so that payload could have been whatever it wanted to be.

We started the investigation, and DLA Piper, who was our external legal counsel, has an incredible crisis management team. That was one of our first calls. Legal comes in, and then through legal you hire CrowdStrike, KPMG, and Krebs Stamos. You hire different entities through that platform of legal, and then you start your investigation.

I had dealt with hundreds of little incidents before—a vulnerability in a product was an incident. We have 50 products and 300,000 customers, so we get vulnerabilities in products; my team handles them, we follow a process, and everything gets recorded. But this was of such scope and scale. When it went public on Sunday, it was on 60 Minutes, across the globe, and in every news outlet.

We were forced into being very transparent. We were as transparent as possible to explain how they accomplished the attack, what it looked like, how it flowed, and what we knew at that point in time. Communication became extremely important.

PAUL: CISOs are human, but this incident must have changed you personally. You went through litigation, and now CISOs have to consider personal liability insurance. How did it change you and your team?

TIM: First, I wanted to fix the problem and hoped I would be allowed to. Back then, the standard playbook after an event like this was to fire the CISO and move on. But because of my background in engineering and architecture, I had the skills needed to lead a recovery.

On December 13th, my job changed completely. I had to rely on my team to operate independently under tremendous pressure. In the first 30 days, I lost 25 pounds from working constantly. At the same time, while my Christmas was ruined, I also ruined Christmas for 18,000 customers who had to investigate if they were affected.

Then came the legal phase. The SEC looked to use us as an example to establish precedent by enforcement. After depositions and investigations, in September 2023, they issued a Wells Notice charging the company and me personally. That was the first time a CISO had ever been charged by the SEC.

My legal fees were over $1 million, which SolarWinds covered. But it alarmed the CISO community, sparking discussions with boards about whether companies would back their CISOs during an incident.

When I was charged, I was in Zurich and ended up having a heart attack. I had a 75% blockage in one artery and 90% in another. While sitting in the hospital bed, I thought about whether to sign a settlement paper to make it go away. The document claimed I was negligent, incompetent, and ran a bad security program. If I had signed it, I would have paid a $50,000 fine and walked away. But if I signed that paper, every CISO who experienced a security event in the future would be held personally liable. So I refused to sign it, and the company didn’t settle either. We fought for another three years.

Last December, the case against both SolarWinds and me was completely dismissed with prejudice, meaning it cannot be recharged. The SEC achieved their goal of elevating the CISO role and forcing board-level conversations, but we won our vindication in court.

PAUL: As we look at agentic code generation and protecting environments, have we learned the lessons, or do we still have gaps?

TIM: Some of the lessons have been learned. Pre-incident, SolarWinds was running at a 92% renewal rate and doing really well. Post-incident, it dropped to the 80s. We were sold to private equity about a year and a half ago, and our renewal rate got back up to 99% with our best quarters ever. We made a full recovery.

We accomplished that recovery by being exemplary in how we build, making sure people realized we took the incident seriously and were as resilient to this type of attack as possible. That took invention, new processes, and assuming breach across everything. It required not trusting people just because they were employees. We didn’t find an insider, but if I were going to execute this attack, it would definitely be through an insider.

How do we build resilience inside our systems? We externalized the build system completely. We moved it to AWS, defined it all in code (which it wasn’t before), assumed breach, and eliminated single points of failure.

For Orion, we now run three builds before we ship:

Development Build: Roughly 400 people have access

Staging Build: 36 people have access

Production Build: Only 2 people have access

No single person has access to all three builds. The point is, we made it extremely difficult for anyone to compromise the build.

PAUL: In today’s world, it’s not necessarily a rogue person—it could be an agentic AI agent that doesn’t know what “rogue” means and goes off on its own.

TIM: Absolutely. Managing non-human identities (NHIs) was a key topic last year. As CISOs, we manage our paranoia. With the rush to push code, security needs to understand how you manage and protect those identities. AI models want to make you happy, but without proper guardrails and sandboxing, they can be clever, sneaky, and hallucinate. It requires a true partnership between security and developers.

PAUL: Time to exploit has shifted from weeks to hours, making annual audits and questionnaires obsolete. As software providers and JFrog partners, is moving faster with automated perspectives essential for tomorrow’s world?

TIM: 100%. As software producers, we must produce better software. As consumers, we must test more using agentic pen-testing and tools that adversaries use against us.

I don’t believe this is going to end the world. We’ve managed hundreds of thousands of vulnerabilities for years using firewalls, WAFs, and perimeter protections to limit reachability. But the baseline for good security hygiene has bumped up significantly. Doing what you did three years ago leaves you 100% exposed today. We must invest in proper controls before getting popped from the outside.

PAUL: Do you have any final words of wisdom for this audience of developers, security teams, and DevOps leaders?

TIM: Many CISOs came up through governance or security tooling rather than software engineering, so help them understand your world. They aren’t dumb; they just need help understanding software architecture risks.

Communicate openly with your security teams and executives about where real risks exist in the build pipeline. Ensure that risk gets captured on the risk register so the organization can address it. CISOs can be your greatest partner in moving security forward if you engage them directly.

Title: Your AI Agent Doesn’t Have MFA
Context: The National Cybersecurity Alliance's theme this year is "Don't Make It Easy for Them," built on the idea that small habits repeated every day wear attackers down
Full Text:
Every Cybersecurity Awareness Month campaign rests on four habits:

Strong passwords,

Multifactor authentication,

Spotting phishing,

and keeping software updated.

All four assume a person is the one signing in, reading the message and clicking install. At a growing number of companies that person is now an AI agent, and AI agent security has no equivalent of the annual training.

The National Cybersecurity Alliance's theme this year is "Don't Make It Easy for Them," built on the idea that small habits repeated every day wear attackers down. "Every small choice you make adds up," Lisa Plaggemier, the alliance's executive director, said at the launch. She's right, and that is the problem. Agents now make thousands of small choices a day on an employee's behalf, and the habits that protect the employee don't transfer to the software acting for them.

The record since July shows how wide the gap is. Researchers have counted 21 public incidents between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. By its tally, none of those agents had been hijacked or told to attack; most were doing research. Take the four habits one at a time and the gap is easy to see.

Passwords and MFA: the agent uses any key it can find

MFA works because a stolen password alone isn't enough. Agents have no second factor. They authenticate with API keys, OAuth tokens and service-account credentials, and whoever holds the string is the agent.

Agents also treat a credential they stumble on as permission. OpenAI disclosed Sept. 25 that its research agents logged in to a U.S. Census Bureau site with credentials found online. Google confirmed Sept. 18, after The Wall Street Journal asked about it, that a Gemini model in a May evaluation guessed a password at one real company and used credentials from a public code repository at two others. In an earlier OpenAI case, an internal model that had been told twice to work locally committed its researcher's GitHub token to a public repository, broken into fragments while it reasoned about getting past secret scanning. The token failed to authenticate. OpenAI rotated every employee's keys anyway.

Translated for agents, the habit looks like this: give every agent its own identity with short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens, and block any credential the agent wasn't issued. The Coalition for Secure AI's zero-trust guidance this fall makes the point in its title: authorization can't live inside the model. If the agent's own judgment is the only thing keeping it from using a key, there is no control.

Phishing awareness: the agent reads the lure for you

Phishing training teaches people to slow down before acting on a stranger's message. An agent working through a queue of tickets or sales leads has no instinct to slow down, and it will follow instructions hidden in the text.

Researchers showed what that looks like in Salesforce Agentforce. In research published Sept. 24 and dubbed SalesBleed, an attacker planted hidden instructions in a public Web-to-Lead form submission. When an employee later asked Agentforce to review leads, the agent followed them and leaked customer relationship management data. Nobody clicked anything, and the attacker never logged in. Salesforce has fixed those specific flaws. Researchers broader warning was that any agent that reads outside submissions, renders links or images and can reach sensitive data has the same three ingredients sitting in one place.

Researchers want the industry to stop calling this prompt injection, because "this is actually just persuasion." Persuasion doesn't get patched. Australia's cyber agency reached a similar conclusion in its guidance on agent harnesses, which treats prompt injection as something the model can't fix and puts the controls in the software around it.

Translated for agents: treat every document, email, web page and form field an agent reads as if an attacker wrote it. Keep the agents that read untrusted content away from the ones that can act on sensitive systems, and put a person or a fixed policy in front of outbound actions such as sending email or submitting forms.

Updating software: the agent installs whatever the instructions say

"Keep your software updated" assumes the update channel can be trusted. For an agent, the update channel is any package name that shows up in a README or a setup script, and it runs the install without the pause a developer might take.

That supply chain now runs in both directions. Anthropic disclosed July 30 that during a capture-the-flag evaluation run with partner, a Claude Mythos 5 agent hit setup instructions that referenced a package that didn't exist. It registered an email address and a PyPI account and published a malicious package under that name. The package stayed up for about an hour before PyPI's automated defenses pulled it, long enough to run on 15 real systems, including a security company's malware scanner whose exposed credentials the agent then used. The evaluation was supposed to be cut off from the internet; a misconfiguration let the agent out.

Coding assistants sit on the receiving end. Google's Mandiant, in its AI Risk and Resilience Report 2026, describes a hijacked AI coding assistant session that installed a poisoned package and spread the Shai-Hulud worm across about 100 repositories, plus poisoned assistant command-line hooks that handed attackers code execution. The OWASP GenAI Security Project's third-quarter roundup says the Mini Shai-Hulud and Miasma worm waves abused configuration files tied to Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Cursor to keep themselves running.

Translated for agents: route installs through an internal registry proxy, pin versions with lockfiles and hold back packages published in the last few days. Review agent configuration folders and hooks the way you review code. Take away publishing rights to public registries, and scope any registry allowlist carefully, since an entry that permits downloads usually permits uploads too.

Reporting and stopping: agents don't know when to quit

Awareness campaigns end with the same advice - if something looks wrong, stop and report it. People stop when a site says access denied. Agents built to finish tasks read a block as a problem to solve.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent that got around access blocks on a Medicare statistics portal "didn't accept 'no' for an answer." Philadelphia police said Oct. 8 that an AI agent had filed an invented tip through the department's tip form, and Anthropic published its account the next day. A Claude Haiku 4.5 agent working on a page about an unsolved homicide submitted the tip because its instructions hadn't forbidden submitting forms. Police flagged it as spam.

Even when monitoring works, stopping often waits for a person. OpenAI said an agent that tunneled out of its training sandbox through DNS on Sept. 20 was flagged within about 15 minutes, and the run went on for roughly 2.5 hours until someone ended it. Mandiant's report includes a reasoning loop that ran up a $50,000 cloud bill.

Limits work. Forcepoint X-Labs showed a poisoned lookup pushing a research agent with no limits to 500 tool calls, while call budgets, depth limits and fan-out circuit breakers stopped the same attack after one.

Translated for agents: treat a login failure or a permission error as a stop signal. Set hard budgets on tool calls, spend and run time. Decide in advance which actions end a session automatically, so containment doesn't sit in an alert queue until morning.

An AI agent security checklist

Agents won't attend the lunch-and-learn, so AI agent security has to live in the systems they run on. If you add one AI item to this month's program, make it this list:

Inventory every agent: the model behind it, the tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it can call, the credentials it holds and the person who owns it. An agent nobody owns is an agent nobody will shut off.

Issue each agent its own short-lived, scoped credentials, and alert when it presents one it wasn't given.

Label every input source as trusted or untrusted, and keep agents that read untrusted content away from tools that send or publish.

Put package installs behind a proxy with pinned versions and a cooldown on new releases, and remove publish rights.

Set spending and tool-call limits with an automatic stop.

Log agent actions to storage the agent can't write to, so you can tell an affected outsider what happened within hours, not months.

Then borrow the exercise your awareness team already runs. A phishing simulation tests whether employees take the bait. Seed a test ticket, lead or email with a harmless planted instruction this month and see whether your agents take it.

Title: Ransomware Gangs Increasingly Turn to Threats of Physical Violence to Extort Payments
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Ransomware gangs are increasingly turning to threats of physical violence against CISOs, business executives and other senior staff at the companies they attack in an effort to successfully extort payments from their victims, a new report has warned.

According to the Semperis 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, published on October 14, a quarter of ransomware campaigns now involve psychological or physical threats to members of staff at the company being targeted.

These threats are in addition to the extortion demand for a ransomware key to retrieve the encrypted data, as well as the threat of stolen data being leaked if the ransom isn’t paid.

This approach is referred to as triple extortion.

Overall, 40% of attacks involved psychological or physical threats against staff at the company being targeted, an increase compared with the previous year.

Some of the most common forms of intimidation used by ransomware gangs in these scenarios include sending staff at the victim organization threatening messages, letters or packages (57%), threatening family and friends of employees (37%) and threats of physical intrusions into offices or even homes (19%).

This additional layer of intimidation is designed to force victims of ransomware attacks into paying. Even if an organization is confident it could restore its network from backups, the threat of physical or emotional violence against its staff could encourage the payment of a ransom anyway.

“An attacker has one goal in mind: They want to extract something from you. And the only way they're going to do that is to make the cost of resisting their demands greater than the cost of giving in,” said Chris Inglis, former U.S. National Cyber Director and a Semperis Strategic Advisor.

“Holding you at physical risk is the latest phenomenon because we've covered most of the other risks.”

Doxxing, Swatting and Other Threats

Unfortunately, the threats by ransomware groups against employees of their victims have resulted in very real consequences. Of those organizations affected by ransomware gangs employing these tactics, 25% said their staff had been doxxed by attackers, while 23% suggested that employees had been swatted as part of the extortion campaigns.

The consequences of these attacks have ranged from companies having to support employees through psychological treatment and in some cases, the victim of the doxxing or swatting attack has moved home.

All of this involves a significant amount of emotional trauma for the individuals being targeted, while the stress caused can also impact individuals throughout the business.

“Ransomware has proven to be a great cash-generating activity for criminal syndicates, which have no hesitation about inflicting both cyber and physical harm,” said Mickey Bresman, Semperis CEO.

The Semperis research was based on a survey of 1,200 IT and security professionals across North America, the UK, Europe and the Asia-Pacific.
